text: O Phoebus, lend thy golden lyre; Give me the beams of thy coelestial fire; Avaunt, ye vulgar! poets listen round, And all Parnassus thunder with the sound, While the muse hails that great dramatic name, And down time's rapid tide bears Shakespear's endless fame.
author: Hawkins, W. (William), 18th cent.
title: Poems on various subjects: By William Hawkins, ...

text: Hence then we guess, nor vain is our surmise, Why some are fools, and none are always wise; Why Genius differs in life's every stage, Runs wild with youth, and creeps with hobbling age, The soul uncumber'd with the mortal clay Knows no increase of strength, nor fears decay.
author: Hawkins, W. (William), 18th cent.
title: Poems on various subjects: By William Hawkins, ...

text: I speak with rev'rence for the gown — He preaches of his kind the best in town; And boasts a Sunday's congregation, The quietest in all the nation: For then with hum-drum sounds in drawling tone express'd, He lulls his calm parishioners to rest.
author: Hawkins, W. (William), 18th cent.
title: Poems on various subjects: By William Hawkins, ...

text: I knew a wretch (record him, O my rhymes) That strove to ape the manners of the times.
author: Hawkins, W. (William), 18th cent.
title: Poems on various subjects: By William Hawkins, ...

text: O then you'll exactly recite The raptures fond Gratitude shews, When, blest in his mistress's sight, The heart of a swain overflows.
author: Hawkins, W. (William), 18th cent.
title: Poems on various subjects: By William Hawkins, ...

text: 'Tis lofty precedent that makes us fools, And thro' the world fantastic fashion rules: We set no limits to our vain desires; 'Squires rival lords, and yeomen rival 'squires.
author: Hawkins, W. (William), 18th cent.
title: Poems on various subjects: By William Hawkins, ...

text: No useful talent then should dormant lie; — 'Tis service to the common enemy; — And these no-scholars may or swell the sail Of commerce, and attend the shifting gale; Or deck with great exploits a Georgia's reign, And humble Gallic crests, and crush the pride of Spain.
author: Hawkins, W. (William), 18th cent.
title: Poems on various subjects: By William Hawkins, ...

text: Look down the margent of each month; — Observe the weather's train; — Now calm, and clear, attract your eye, Now cloud, and wind, and rain.
author: Hawkins, W. (William), 18th cent.
title: Poems on various subjects: By William Hawkins, ...

text: Ah! how bright wit, possest of ev'ry gift, Dwindled to folly, and went mad in Swift.
author: Hawkins, W. (William), 18th cent.

text: A pleasant orchard too there was, Before his cottage door; Of cider and of corn likewise, He had a little store.
author: More, Hannah, 1745-1833.
title: The carpenter: or, the danger of evil company.

text: A little cottage too he had, For ease and comfort plann'd, And that he might not lack for ought, An acre of good land.
author: More, Hannah, 1745-1833.
title: The carpenter: or, the danger of evil company.

text: With grief the cause I must relate, The dismal cause reveal, 'Twas EVIL COMPANY and DRINK, The source of every ill.
author: More, Hannah, 1745-1833.
title: The carpenter: or, the danger of evil company.

text: The Drunkard Murders Child and Wife, Nor matters it a pin, Whether he stabs them with his knife, Or starves them by his gin.
author: More, Hannah, 1745-1833.
title: The carpenter: or, the danger of evil company.

text: From that same hour the Cooper more, He never wou'd behold; Nor wou'd he to the Ale-house go, Had it been pav'd with gold.
author: More, Hannah, 1745-1833.
title: The carpenter: or, the danger of evil company.

text: One blooming babe was all he had, His only darling dear, The object of their equal love, The solace of their care.
author: More, Hannah, 1745-1833.
title: The carpenter: or, the danger of evil company.

text: No more his Church he did frequent, A symptom ever sad; Where once the Sunday is mispent, The week days must be bad.
author: More, Hannah, 1745-1833.
title: The carpenter: or, the danger of evil company.

text: By lab'ring hard, and working late, By industry and pains, His Cottage was at length redeem'd, And sav'd were all his gains.
author: More, Hannah, 1745-1833.
title: The carpenter: or, the danger of evil company.

text: Each night when he return'd from work, His wife so meek and mild, His little supper gladly dress'd, While he caress'd his child.
author: More, Hannah, 1745-1833.
title: The carpenter: or, the danger of evil company.

text: The pewter dishes one by one, Were pawn'd, till none was left; And wife and babe at home remain'd Of every help bereft.
author: More, Hannah, 1745-1833.
title: The carpenter: or, the danger of evil company.

text: His father left him what he had, In sooth it was enough; His shining pewter, pots of brass, And all his household stuff.
author: More, Hannah, 1745-1833.
title: The carpenter: or, the danger of evil company.

text: No handsome Sunday suit was left, Nor decent holland shirt; No nosegay mark'd the Sabbath day, But all was rags and dirt.
author: More, Hannah, 1745-1833.
title: The carpenter: or, the danger of evil company.

text: He said the Cooper's company, Was all for which he car'd; But soon he drank as much as he, To swear like him soon dar'd.
author: More, Hannah, 1745-1833.
title: The carpenter: or, the danger of evil company.

text: Could'st thou with elegiac GRAY, In slowly, sad funereal lay, Such passion-quelling truths impart, As charm at once, and mend the heart.
author: Gentleman, Francis, 1728-1784.
title: Royal fables. By Francis Gentleman:

text: The ENVIOUS man affects surprize, To hear of grudging hearts, or eyes; Tho' all he sees another gain, Infects his worthless mind with pain.
author: Gentleman, Francis, 1728-1784.
title: Royal fables. By Francis Gentleman:

text: Ungrateful MOUSE!—nay foolish too, Extend thy dim, contracted view; Plac'd in thy native cupboard see, That night GRIMALKIN watch for thee; And had not fortune led from home, An hungry CAT had been thy doom; Then yield to patience fretful strife, Thy FREEDOM lost prolongs thy LIFE.
author: Gentleman, Francis, 1728-1784.
title: Royal fables. By Francis Gentleman:

text: Oh noble youth, return'd the fire, May heav'n thy virtuous mind inspire; Each worthy deed of thine will be A year of added life to me— Thus I may ask, without a crime, To lengthen out with joy my time.
author: Gentleman, Francis, 1728-1784.
title: Royal fables. By Francis Gentleman:

text: Perfect in ev'ry scene of life, Review'd as mother, friend, or wife; The truly ROYAL DOVE was seen, To act, to coo, to look the QUEEN; With charming form, and gentle mind, Almost the CHARLOTTE of her kind.
author: Gentleman, Francis, 1728-1784.
title: Royal fables. By Francis Gentleman:

text: LIFE a dependant chain appears, With links to join its sev'ral spheres; Shew judging reason when you will, One plac'd on high, there's higher still; 'Till strain'd progression mounts the sky, And melts in vast infinity.
author: Gentleman, Francis, 1728-1784.
title: Royal fables. By Francis Gentleman:

text: An emblem of the boist'rous North, When with its most tempestuous gales It desolates hills, woods and dales.
author: Gentleman, Francis, 1728-1784.
title: Royal fables. By Francis Gentleman:

text: A common Proverb has decreed, The more we haste the worse we speed; Yet some with prudence still at strife Post, neck or nothing, on thro' life.
author: Gentleman, Francis, 1728-1784.
title: Royal fables. By Francis Gentleman:

text: Lip-love could now deceive no more; His monarch with tremendous roar, Full in the BEAR'S delighted view, The sycophantic coward slew; Then cried, Henceforth no fawning slave, No fair-fac'd, flatt'ring, heartless knave, Shall ever royal favour share— Henceforth 'tis thine,—my trusty BEAR.
author: Gentleman, Francis, 1728-1784.
title: Royal fables. By Francis Gentleman:

text: And boasts of something, Reason nam'd, Which all his actions have disclaim'd: A monster, shameful to his kind, To ev'ry honest feeling blind; With tongue of guile, with heart of flint, And soul of villainy the mint.
author: Gentleman, Francis, 1728-1784.
title: Royal fables. By Francis Gentleman:

text: Mean while the BEES a message sent, To know their waspish foes intent; Whether submission should release, From threaten'd war, and give them peace, Or resolute in bold defiance, On Fortune they would fix reliance?
author: Gentleman, Francis, 1728-1784.
title: Royal fables. By Francis Gentleman:

text: The songster heard with patient ears, A multitude of daily sneers; And bore them all, howe'er absurd, Nor answer'd once the coxcomb bird; But like a wise domestic did Whate'er his tender master bid; No business minded, but his own, And studied grateful songs alone.
author: Gentleman, Francis, 1728-1784.
title: Royal fables. By Francis Gentleman:

text: It rush'd into the baited trap; The dainty seiz'd, and bless'd that star, Which led to such delicious fare; Admir'd the thought which taught to roam, From tasteless, mouldy scraps at home, Then prais'd, with joy, the happier lot Of this unknown, luxurious spot.
author: Gentleman, Francis, 1728-1784.
title: Royal fables. By Francis Gentleman:

text: The Delicacy of my Love is shocked, by supposing we shall ever repent our mutual Affection, or Engagements; yet, under the Circumstances I have mentioned, it is not impossible that it should happen.
author: Griffith, Richard, d. 1788.
title: A series of genuine letters between Henry and Frances: ... [pt.2]

text: But I should be glad to see one of our modern Philosophers endure the Loss of Health with that Indifference, they recommend to others.
author: Griffith, Richard, d. 1788.
title: A series of genuine letters between Henry and Frances: ... [pt.2]

text: I have had two whole Days sacred to Peace and Contemplation — But they are over, and Noise and Folly re-assume their Throne.
author: Griffith, Richard, d. 1788.
title: A series of genuine letters between Henry and Frances: ... [pt.2]

text: What I meant was sitting up, and lying in Bed, late; both of which are very bad, in a double Sense, at present.
author: Griffith, Richard, d. 1788.
title: A series of genuine letters between Henry and Frances: ... [pt.2]

text: I DO not, indeed, think it would be possible for me to support myself, under the very disagreeable Situation I am in, both of Body and Mind, were it not for the Pleasure I receive from my dear, dear Life's kind Letters.
author: Griffith, Richard, d. 1788.
title: A series of genuine letters between Henry and Frances: ... [pt.2]

text: IN the disagreeable and embarrassed Situation I am at present, I know nothing could tempt me to write, but the Fear of your thinking I poorly declined the Task you have assigned me, without being ingenuous enough to confess myself unequal to it.
author: Griffith, Richard, d. 1788.
title: A series of genuine letters between Henry and Frances: ... [pt.2]

text: I refer my dearest Life to a former Letter, wrote upon this Occasion: The Particulars of it I do not, at present, recollect; but am certain of this, that my Sentiments are still the same, as both my Love and Friendship for you are so.
author: Griffith, Richard, d. 1788.
title: A series of genuine letters between Henry and Frances: ... [pt.2]

text: I thank you for your kind Sentiments with Regard to passing your Time with me; and it is certain that those Portions of Life, which we spend agreeably to ourselves, are all that can be computed in a Philosopher's Kalendar.
author: Griffith, Richard, d. 1788.
title: A series of genuine letters between Henry and Frances: ... [pt.2]

text: Though your dear Letter has made me vastly easier, than I was, I am not yet calm enough to write about my Affairs to Lady —; besides, I am unwilling to determine on any thing, 'till I see, and consult you.
author: Griffith, Richard, d. 1788.
title: A series of genuine letters between Henry and Frances: ... [pt.2]

text: It is in this Manner we speak to our Kings; and the French, who are Patterns of all Politeness and Decorum, salute their Grand Monarque by the Stile of Sire.
author: Griffith, Richard, d. 1788.
title: A series of genuine letters between Henry and Frances: ... [pt.2]

text: Thus Man has a rational Prae-sentiment of future Bliss, and a rational Deduction of it's Eternity; but he has neither one or the other with regard to future Misery, or it's Eternity.
author: Griffith, Richard, d. 1788.
title: A series of genuine letters between Henry and Frances: ... [pt.2]

text: I have not any Thing new to acquaint you with: Every Thing and Person are just in the same Situation, you left them.
author: Griffith, Richard, d. 1788.
title: A series of genuine letters between Henry and Frances: ... [pt.2]

text: Forgive me, Harry, for making so free; but I think it is better to laugh than cry, at Things which we cannot remedy; for I do not believe, what poor Lear makes a Question of, that there is any Cause, or Cure, in Nature, for hard Hearts.
author: Griffith, Richard, d. 1788.
title: A series of genuine letters between Henry and Frances: ... [pt.2]

text: Miss Woodley thought it her duty to be mute, and now the gentle gingle of a tea-spoon, was like a deep-toned bell, all was so quiet.

title: A simple story: In four volumes. By Mrs. Inchbald. [pt.1]

text: He was going to reply, when Mr. Sandford sullenly interrupted him, and making towards the door, cried, "When you come to the point for which you brought me here, send for me again."

title: A simple story: In four volumes. By Mrs. Inchbald. [pt.1]

text: Miss Woodley obediently sat down— and though her thoughts and heart were in the chamber with her friend, she never shewed by one impertinent word, or by one line of her face, the restraint she suffered.

title: A simple story: In four volumes. By Mrs. Inchbald. [pt.1]

text: "Let this be a warning to you, how you deal in future with the friends who wish you well—you have hurried me into a mistake that might have cost me my life, or the life of the man you love; and thus exposed you to misery, more bitter than death."

title: A simple story: In four volumes. By Mrs. Inchbald. [pt.1]

text: "And yet, I believe," replied she with a smile, "I believe, theory, must only be the judge even there."

title: A simple story: In four volumes. By Mrs. Inchbald. [pt.1]

text: It was agreed the attempt should be made — and instead of receiving the proposal with uneasiness, Miss Milner, to the surprise of every one present, immediately consented; and gave her guardian an opportunity of saying several of the kindest and politest things upon her ready compliance.
author: Inchbald, Mrs., 1753-1821.
title: A simple story: In four volumes. By Mrs. Inchbald. [pt.1]

text: He visited Dorriforth on the evening after his engagement with lord Frederick, and again the next morning breakfasted with him in his own chamber; nor did Miss Milner see her guardian since his first return from that engagement till the following noon.
author: Inchbald, Mrs., 1753-1821.
title: A simple story: In four volumes. By Mrs. Inchbald. [pt.1]

text: Unused to resist temptations, whether to reprehensible, or to laudable actions, she yielded to his supplications, and having overcome a few scruples of Miss Woodley's, determined to take young Rusbrook to town and present him to his uncle.
author: Inchbald, Mrs., 1753-1821.
title: A simple story: In four volumes. By Mrs. Inchbald. [pt.1]

text: Miss Milner could scarcely restrain the joy this gave her; but unluckily, Dorriforth said soon after to the child, "and now tell me your name."
author: Inchbald, Mrs., 1753-1821.
title: A simple story: In four volumes. By Mrs. Inchbald. [pt.1]

text: But Mrs. Horton felt for none but the right reverend priest; and often did she feel so violently interested in his cause, she could not refrain giving an answer herself in his behalf—thus, doing the duty of an adversary.
author: Inchbald, Mrs., 1753-1821.
title: A simple story: In four volumes. By Mrs. Inchbald. [pt.1]

text: Conscious of her inferiority in these subjects of her guardian's praise, Miss Milner, instead of being inspired to emulation, was provoked to envy.
author: Inchbald, Mrs., 1753-1821.
title: A simple story: In four volumes. By Mrs. Inchbald. [pt.1]

text: "What do you mean?" repeated Miss Woodley; "I protest you frighten me:"—and this inconsistency in the behaviour of Miss Milner, really appeared as if her senses had been deranged.
author: Inchbald, Mrs., 1753-1821.
title: A simple story: In four volumes. By Mrs. Inchbald. [pt.1]

text: "And now, madam, the reason of my desire to speak with you—is to know from yourself, the means you think most proper to pursue, in order to acquaint his lordship, that notwithstanding this late repulse, there are hopes of your partiality in his favour."

text: The only good quality he has, is that of sometimes keeping secret his own mischief—How does Mrs. Boothby to day?

text: And are not you, madam, equally jealous of my honour, that out of such mistaken tenderness for my personal safety, you would betray the most invaluable treasure of my soul?

text: Why there, Sir! —it is just as I said—You look upon me as your property, your purchased slave; and would doubtless treat me as such, were we married.
author: Kenrick, W. (William), 1725?-1779.
title: The duellist, a comedy: As it is acted at the Theatre Royal in Covent Garden. Written by W. Kenrick, LL.D.

text: This being in your favour, on settling a handsome separate maintenance on your wife you turn her off a mensa et thoro.
author: Kenrick, W. (William), 1725?-1779.
title: The duellist, a comedy: As it is acted at the Theatre Royal in Covent Garden. Written by W. Kenrick, LL.D.

text: Why to come to the point, then, it was on that subject I sent to talk with you.
author: Kenrick, W. (William), 1725?-1779.
title: The duellist, a comedy: As it is acted at the Theatre Royal in Covent Garden. Written by W. Kenrick, LL.D.

text: And yet, for all that, had it not stopped when it did, I should have never have come up with it.
author: Kenrick, W. (William), 1725?-1779.
title: The duellist, a comedy: As it is acted at the Theatre Royal in Covent Garden. Written by W. Kenrick, LL.D.

text: Oh, Mr. Boothby! where—where is my poor Lord? barbarous man! have you indeed then left him dead, or shall I see him again alive?
author: Kenrick, W. (William), 1725?-1779.
title: The duellist, a comedy: As it is acted at the Theatre Royal in Covent Garden. Written by W. Kenrick, LL.D.

text: Ay, ay—and, as you have got so good an Uncle and a wife into the bargain, Barrister, you ought to be satisfied.
author: Kenrick, W. (William), 1725?-1779.
title: The duellist, a comedy: As it is acted at the Theatre Royal in Covent Garden. Written by W. Kenrick, LL.D.

text: If you love me as you have pretended, therefore, you will devise some method of delivering me from the bondage, to which the will of arbitrary and mercenary parents (for so I must call them) have destined me.
author: Kenrick, W. (William), 1725?-1779.
title: The duellist, a comedy: As it is acted at the Theatre Royal in Covent Garden. Written by W. Kenrick, LL.D.

text: I then shall leave my concerns entirely with him, Sir; but must beg he will take sufficient time, to make every thing secure; and proceed in nothing with precipitation.
author: Kenrick, W. (William), 1725?-1779.

text: Nay, General, don't be angry. —But if you stay, and matters stand as I hear them related, you will run the utmost danger.
author: Kenrick, W. (William), 1725?-1779.
title: The duellist, a comedy: As it is acted at the Theatre Royal in Covent Garden. Written by W. Kenrick, LL.D.

text: But sword and pistol were not then in vogue, and the fighting one's friends was not come in fashion.
author: Kenrick, W. (William), 1725?-1779.

text: But the court of love, my dear Emmeline, is a court of common law, and is governed by ancient customs and usages time immemorial; of which none is of longer standing than that of a woman's changing her mind.
author: Kenrick, W. (William), 1725?-1779.

text: Upon my honour, Dublin, after seeing London, looks like Irish-Town or Ring's-End: Oh, every thing I set my eyes on here gives me the ennui, and the countre cure.
author: Macklin, Charles, 1697?-1797.

text: My compliments, Mrs. Katty, to your lady, I will be with her in the twinkling of a star, or in less time than a single glance of her own immortal beauty can pass to the centre of an amorous heart.

text: Nay, Count, voice or no voice I will make an effort—Sol-la-mi-fa-sol, &c.—Upon my honour I have no more voice than a killing.

text: As the old saying is, Lady Bab—you can never do it younger—Live while we live, that's the rule of happiness, you have good spirits, a good jointure, and nobody to controul you—you amiable creature.
author: Macklin, Charles, 1697?-1797.
title: The true-born Irishman: or, Irish fine lady. A comedy of two acts. By Charles Macklin.

text: Indeed and that they have, my dear, and the cows too, and the sheep, and the bullocks, and that as strong as ever your own mother had it, who was an O'Gallagher.
author: Macklin, Charles, 1697?-1797.

text: Au revoir—well, he is a most humourous creature, and mighty witty: don't you think so, brother?
author: Macklin, Charles, 1697?-1797.

text: Never—till Vengeance has been paid its Full, Never will I grow tame, and hear thee more.

text: When I confess, abhorrent of Deceit, That Love, which seem'd to root my Soul in thee, Has new transplanted it, to Elfrid's Bosom?
author: Hill, Aaron, 1685-1750.

text: My Sovereign shall not need Revenge his Wrongs, on Athelwold.—One Pray'r Has Boldness, yet, to urge your royal Ear; Then, I have done with Wishes, and the World.— Prince Leolyn, whom I have made unhappy, Now suffers, for my Guilt.
author: Hill, Aaron, 1685-1750.
title: Athelwold: a tragedy. As it is acted at the Theatre-Royal in Drury-Lane, by His Majesty's servants.

text: What shall I do, to save insulted Majesty From the Contempt of Weakness?—Yet convince thee, That I can bid my Pity be thy Punishment.
author: Hill, Aaron, 1685-1750.
title: Athelwold: a tragedy. As it is acted at the Theatre-Royal in Drury-Lane, by His Majesty's servants.

text: A new-born Love Is full of soft Impatience!—Soon as arriv'd, I was commanded to return, and press you To shorten your meant Absence.
author: Hill, Aaron, 1685-1750.
title: Athelwold: a tragedy. As it is acted at the Theatre-Royal in Drury-Lane, by His Majesty's servants.

text: And can he live to pardon?—Shame to thy Heart, Or give my Glory the Revenge it claims, Or I will brand thee with a Coward's Marks, And teach light Boys to scorn thee.
author: Hill, Aaron, 1685-1750.
title: Athelwold: a tragedy. As it is acted at the Theatre-Royal in Drury-Lane, by His Majesty's servants.

text: I therefore consider'd myself as not deserving Pardon, from the Publick, till I had purchas'd it, with something, Better, on the same Subject.—This was the Original of Athelwold.

text: Hid from thy Sight, by the dark Grot between us, Thy Voice took Pity on my Heart's Impatience, And taught me how to trace thee.

text: Sorrow, like mine, Sinks the sad Heart too low, for Artifice, And my proud Soul out-swells, and floats above it.

text: But, in these times when so little credit is given to principle in political matters, you may perhaps be told, that I have been following the dictates of party, and deluded by vain expectations of popularity to sacrifice myself to their pursuits.

text: I have now recourse only, as far as the mind is concerned, to a clear conscience, perhaps a more tardy, but, I trust, as efficacious an assistance.

text: The testimony of my conduct during that time, of which I was most proud, was the approbation of Lord Strange, under whose auspicies I first offered myself to your favour.

text: Either way I was not to have the benefit of an Enquiry; but he was to have the advantage of the pretence of one, in order to shut the door of St. James's against me.
author: Burgoyne, John, 1722-1792.
title: A letter from Lieut. Gen. Burgoyne to his constituents: upon his late resignation; with the correspondences between the Secretaries of War and him, relative to his return to America.

text: Having pitched upon this expedient for no other end than to exclude me from the presence of my Sovereign, he could hardly be in pain about the event.

title: A letter from Lieut. Gen. Burgoyne to his constituents: upon his late resignation; with the correspondences between the Secretaries of War and him, relative to his return to America.

text: The men with whom I have the honour to act have no objects, but to save their country; if they had, they might long ago have obtained them; and they would scorn to accept, as I should to offer, an union upon any other terms than a participation of that cause.
author: Burgoyne, John, 1722-1792.
title: A letter from Lieut. Gen. Burgoyne to his constituents: upon his late resignation; with the correspondences between the Secretaries of War and him, relative to his return to America.

text: I have slightly touched this progress of my late service, to shew that the situation in which I was placed in the year 1777, was not one of private favour, court intrigue, or personal ambition, but naturally devolving to me from occurrences and from general opinion.
author: Burgoyne, John, 1722-1792.
title: A letter from Lieut. Gen. Burgoyne to his constituents: upon his late resignation; with the correspondences between the Secretaries of War and him, relative to his return to America.

text: What are the military orders I am to give to men who have no arms to fight, and no liberty to march?

text: The first and ſecond Covenant he ſpeaks of there, are nothing but the two Adminiſtrations of the Covenant of Grace (the ſame in Subſtance, ſay our Divines) in regard to the Jews, which preceded, and then to us Chriſtians.

author: Humfrey, John, 1621-1719.

title: A letter to George Keith concerning the salvability of the heathen together with a testimony to the same doctrine, as long held and not newly taken up, out of several former books of him that writ it

author: Humfrey, John, 1621-1719.
title: A letter to George Keith concerning the salvability of the heathen together with a testimony to the same doctrine, as long held and not newly taken up, out of several former books of him that writ it

author: Humfrey, John, 1621-1719.
title: A letter to George Keith concerning the salvability of the heathen together with a testimony to the same doctrine, as long held and not newly taken up, out of several former books of him that writ it

text: I muſt yet ſay further (if it be farther) That there is no Man on the Earth that is ſaved, but it muſt be by the Covenant, the Covenant of Grace, and the Promiſe of it.
author: Humfrey, John, 1621-1719.
title: A letter to George Keith concerning the salvability of the heathen together with a testimony to the same doctrine, as long held and not newly taken up, out of several former books of him that writ it

text: As he was to the Jews a Peculiar Governour; but not without God as Univerſal Soveraign of Heaven and Earth.
author: Humfrey, John, 1621-1719.
title: A letter to George Keith concerning the salvability of the heathen together with a testimony to the same doctrine, as long held and not newly taken up, out of several former books of him that writ it

author: Humfrey, John, 1621-1719.
title: A letter to George Keith concerning the salvability of the heathen together with a testimony to the same doctrine, as long held and not newly taken up, out of several former books of him that writ it

text: They that are Jews inwardly, and in the Spirit then, (I follow my Argument) though not outwardly ſo, and in the Fleſh, do fulfil the Law, in the ſenſe of this place, and are juſtified.
author: Humfrey, John, 1621-1719.
title: A letter to George Keith concerning the salvability of the heathen together with a testimony to the same doctrine, as long held and not newly taken up, out of several former books of him that writ it

author: Humfrey, John, 1621-1719.
title: A letter to George Keith concerning the salvability of the heathen together with a testimony to the same doctrine, as long held and not newly taken up, out of several former books of him that writ it

text: No, no, my Soul, you muſt without delay Your Faculties imploy In ſomething worthy of your thoughts, which may Hereafter yield you Joy.
author: Warren, Robert, 1680-1740.
title: Miscellany poems Written by R. W. C.C. Cambr.

text: Come now my friends, 'tis thus I Treat We'll Eat to live, whilſt others live to Eat.
author: Warren, Robert, 1680-1740.
title: Miscellany poems Written by R. W. C.C. Cambr.

text: And now aroſe His Genial Star, A Bright Directing Pharus ſtood, To light the Nations from afar Thrô Error's Night, and Vice dire-Flood, Where Truth marks out the Radiant way To Bliſs, and the Bright Realms of Day.
author: Warren, Robert, 1680-1740.
title: Miscellany poems Written by R. W. C.C. Cambr.

text: My Eager Soul the Cherub check'd, She told me that no greater Bliſs below A Mortal here could know: She told me, here 'twas all in vain t'expect A View of that Bright Fountain whence it came, I might but taſte the Flowing ſtream.
author: Warren, Robert, 1680-1740.
title: Miscellany poems Written by R. W. C.C. Cambr.

text: His Actions by kind Fate be crown'd, And Plenty flowing ſtill appear, Nor Envy carp, that thus He 'has found Succeſs through each revolving Year.
author: Warren, Robert, 1680-1740.
title: Miscellany poems Written by R. W. C.C. Cambr.

text: For ſure Thou'rt doom'd by an unalterable fate To ſome Immortal State Of Woe or Bliſs; As thou haſt been employ'd in this.
author: Warren, Robert, 1680-1740.
title: Miscellany poems Written by R. W. C.C. Cambr.

text: (And the Ungrate's an Odious Name We all are wont to blame) For ſure 'tis better far to be, Than loſt, for ever loſt in Nature's dread Abyſs, Nonentity.
author: Warren, Robert, 1680-1740.
title: Miscellany poems Written by R. W. C.C. Cambr.

text: The Crazy World's vaſt Hight I fly, And in an Humble corner Lye, There, There enjoy a bleſt Obſcurity.
author: Warren, Robert, 1680-1740.
title: Miscellany poems Written by R. W. C.C. Cambr.

text: But moſt of all Great Nature's work ſurprize, Hence we behold vaſt mountains to ariſe And with their Aiery Tops to pierce the Skies.

title: Merit. A poem : inscribed to the Right Honourable Philip Earl of Chesterfield. By Mr. Henry Jones,:

text: Behold Othello rage, by Frenzy fir'd, When jealous Love, when Fiends, when Fate, conspir'd To rack his tortur'd Thoughts, ten thousand Ways— What dread Variety each Stroke displays!
author: Jones, Henry, 1721-1770.
title: Merit. A poem : inscribed to the Right Honourable Philip Earl of Chesterfield. By Mr. Henry Jones,:

text: When Hope, when Fear, when Love, when Anguish stand, And Terror takes her Tremor from thy Hand, When Pity melts us at thy potent Call, And, at thy Nod, the Passions rise and fall.
author: Jones, Henry, 1721-1770.
title: Merit. A poem : inscribed to the Right Honourable Philip Earl of Chesterfield. By Mr. Henry Jones,:

text: Great Queen of Harmony, who guides the Spheres, Who weds the circling Orbs, who rules the Years; Thy Magic sways the Mind, and charms the Thought, And all the Soul's by thy Enchantment caught.
author: Jones, Henry, 1721-1770.
title: Merit. A poem : inscribed to the Right Honourable Philip Earl of Chesterfield. By Mr. Henry Jones,:

text: "All Cares, but Love, with Pleasure I forego, "And all my Wishes centre in a Beau."
author: Hawkins, William, 1722-1801.
title: Female empire: or, winter celebrated at London:

text: The youthful Hero views th' inspiring Scenes, And martial Ardour kindles in his Veins; While the fond Virgin, on the Brink of Fate, Warn'd by Calista, shuns the dang'rous Bait.
author: Hawkins, William, 1722-1801.
title: Female empire: or, winter celebrated at London:

text: On his deep-furrow'd Brow the Broker wears Schemes yet in Embryo, and unwieldy Cares; While the grave Doctor, from the Tumult free, Lolls in his Chariot, and expects the Fee.
author: Hawkins, William, 1722-1801.
title: Female empire: or, winter celebrated at London:

text: "And when I wed (if such the Will of Fate) "May no learn'd Pedant be my future Mate; "No Wretch, who Gold prefers to Joys like thine, "Nor Sot, enamour'd with the Fumes of Wine.
author: Hawkins, William, 1722-1801.
title: Female empire: or, winter celebrated at London:

text: Subjects so copious ask a longer Day, And Themes so fruitful wear the Hours away: But Pleasure calls, and Scenes instructive glow, With all the mournful Eloquence of Woe; Monimia, fainting, on Castalio cries, And sad Arpasia with Moneses dies.
author: Hawkins, William, 1722-1801.
title: Female empire: or, winter celebrated at London:

text: The witless Fop, unheedful of the Storm, Stands fixt, and wonders at th' angelic Form; Ling'ring, looks back, in Admiration lost, Nor gains his Senses, till he meets a Post.
author: Hawkins, William, 1722-1801.
title: Female empire: or, winter celebrated at London:

text: And now with warmer Pow'r the Sun-Beams glow, And Kennels widen with dissolving Snow, In ev'ry Street officious Shoe-Boys ply, And meagre Poverty prefers its Cry.
author: Hawkins, William, 1722-1801.
title: Female empire: or, winter celebrated at London:

text: So, on the faithless Waves, the Syren-Train, With melting Airs the Mariner detain; Heedless, he sails along the dang'rous Seas, Enchanted with the Music of their Lays, Till, bulg'd upon some Rock, he mourns too late His Stay, and yields unwillingly to Fate.
author: Hawkins, William, 1722-1801.
title: Female empire: or, winter celebrated at London:

text: But Time rolls on, impatient of Delay, And Hunger sends the Citizen away: To Halls well-furnish'd Liv'rymen repair, And feast, in Fancy, on the Bill of Fare: Calmly they drown th' eternal Feuds of State, And bid e'en Business till To-morrow wait.
author: Hawkins, William, 1722-1801.
title: Female empire: or, winter celebrated at London:

text: Theirs is the Task o'er Fashions to preside, And fix the changing Ornaments of Pride; Recount the Arts that captivate the Mind, Subdue th' Inconstant, and attract the Blind; Safe in their Charms, admire the well-form'd Plan, And join their Sex's Pow'r, to conquer Man.
author: Hawkins, William, 1722-1801.
title: Female empire: or, winter celebrated at London:

text: "But Oh! with full Success my Wishes crown, "Long may I reign the Fav'rite of the Town; "Long may I boast th' unrivall'd Pow'r to kill; "Joy more than Life, belov'd beyond Quadrille!
author: Hawkins, William, 1722-1801.
title: Female empire: or, winter celebrated at London:

text: Where-e'er he dwells, ye Muses, round him shine; A Task so arduous calls for all the Nine.
author: Hawkins, William, 1722-1801.
title: Female empire: or, winter celebrated at London:

text: But softer Things the Female Band amuse, Than Wars, Ambition, Politics, and News; To hardier Breasts they trust the Martial Toil; Kill with a Frown, and conquer with a Smile.
author: Hawkins, William, 1722-1801.
title: Female empire: or, winter celebrated at London:

text: Faith, I don't know—they are of all sorts, like the county militia—however, you'll have enough of 'em—our great parlour will be so cramm'd that we sha'nt have room to stir.
author: Cobb, James, 1756-1818.
title: English readings; a comic piece, in one act. Inscribed to George Colman, Esq:

text: A dev'lish good thought, i'faith—I'll meet the lady, Captain—let her chuse her subject, from Johnny Gilpin up to Milton—prose, rhyme, or blank verse, all the same to me—I read 'em all alike.—Pray now, my dear uncle, consent.
author: Cobb, James, 1756-1818.
title: English readings; a comic piece, in one act. Inscribed to George Colman, Esq:

text: "What signifies the year?—I'll not stay an hour in the room if you don't quit it immediately."
author: Cobb, James, 1756-1818.
title: English readings; a comic piece, in one act. Inscribed to George Colman, Esq:

text: The sarvice its own reward—Faith, and so it seems, by our being bother'd so with the wooden-legged gentry—plaguing one at every corner for a tirteener.—What the divil are you so busy about there, Mr. Spatula?
author: Cobb, James, 1756-1818.
title: English readings; a comic piece, in one act. Inscribed to George Colman, Esq:

text: Take it ill!—Oh no—'Tis ten to one if I take it at all—You must know I like to chuse for myself, Mr. Stately.—The pathetic is my forte—A sentimental story makes one so charmingly miserable.—Oh, I love to touch the feelings—and my voice has power, Mr. Stately.
author: Cobb, James, 1756-1818.
title: English readings; a comic piece, in one act. Inscribed to George Colman, Esq:

text: Your servant, Madam—Here we are come to hear you and my nephew Bob knock the hard words about.—Bob, this is Mrs. Poplin.
author: Cobb, James, 1756-1818.
title: English readings; a comic piece, in one act. Inscribed to George Colman, Esq:

text: I'll go to church on Sunday-morning and afternoon, besides pray'r-days, I'll be damn'd if I dont."
author: Cobb, James, 1756-1818.
title: English readings; a comic piece, in one act. Inscribed to George Colman, Esq:

text: AMONG the Performers to whom the Author of the following Dramatic Sketch esteems himself obliged for their endeavours to promote its success, MR. BANNISTER, Junior, MR. WEWITZER, MR. MOSS, and MRS. WEBB, are entitled to his particular thanks.
author: Cobb, James, 1756-1818.
title: English readings; a comic piece, in one act. Inscribed to George Colman, Esq:

text: "Why faith, Kitty, your beauty is so much a type of my dear Charlotte's, that, like a Roman Catholic, I almost adore the image for its likeness to the saint."
author: Cobb, James, 1756-1818.
title: English readings; a comic piece, in one act. Inscribed to George Colman, Esq:

text: 'Tis perfectly the same to me, Ma'am—all subjects, and all styles, are alike to us public speakers.
author: Cobb, James, 1756-1818.
title: English readings; a comic piece, in one act. Inscribed to George Colman, Esq:

text: "Oh! my unlucky fortune—at these years to be taken up before the justices!—I, who was in hopes to have made one of the quorum!"
author: Cobb, James, 1756-1818.
title: English readings; a comic piece, in one act. Inscribed to George Colman, Esq:

text: No doubt, and with equal ability— but, pray Sir, don't you find it necessary, sometimes, to understand your subject.
author: Cobb, James, 1756-1818.
title: English readings; a comic piece, in one act. Inscribed to George Colman, Esq:

text: But what signifies your saying no more—your cursed inflexible countenance has contradiction in every feature.—When I liv'd in London, I dreaded your appearance in the shop—the very sight of you put my customers in ill humour—and they then were sure to swear their shoes did not fit 'em.
author: Cobb, James, 1756-1818.
title: English readings; a comic piece, in one act. Inscribed to George Colman, Esq:

text: To stand too nicely upon small matters, may give others such a mean opinion of our Understanding, that our Admonitions on greater occasions will make no impression, because they have been often applied to such inconsiderable things.
author: Burnet, Gilbert, 1643-1715.
title: Charitable reproof a sermon preached at the Church of St. Mary-le-Bow to the Societies for Reformation of Manners, the 25th of March, 1700 / by the Right Reverend Father in God, Gilbert Lord Bishop of

text: Storms may shatter our Fleets, and if God should for our Sins deliver us so far to an Enemy that they should but once Land upon us, How naked and defenceless are we?
author: Burnet, Gilbert, 1643-1715.
title: Charitable reproof a sermon preached at the Church of St. Mary-le-Bow to the Societies for Reformation of Manners, the 25th of March, 1700 / by the Right Reverend Father in God, Gilbert Lord Bishop of

text: We ought not to lay too much weight on small or disputable things, but should proportion our Zeal to the importance of the Matters we are concerned for.
author: Burnet, Gilbert, 1643-1715.
title: Charitable reproof a sermon preached at the Church of St. Mary-le-Bow to the Societies for Reformation of Manners, the 25th of March, 1700 / by the Right Reverend Father in God, Gilbert Lord Bishop of

text: The Words thus opened, do lead us to examine our Obligations to this Duty of Reproving others: That will be soon setled, if we do consider the Zeal that we owe to God and to his Honour.
author: Burnet, Gilbert, 1643-1715.
title: Charitable reproof a sermon preached at the Church of St. Mary-le-Bow to the Societies for Reformation of Manners, the 25th of March, 1700 / by the Right Reverend Father in God, Gilbert Lord Bishop of

text: This is such a plain Revolt from God, and a rising, as it were, up against him, that we have no reason to think that he will not at last arise and visit for all these things.
author: Burnet, Gilbert, 1643-1715.
title: Charitable reproof a sermon preached at the Church of St. Mary-le-Bow to the Societies for Reformation of Manners, the 25th of March, 1700 / by the Right Reverend Father in God, Gilbert Lord Bishop of

text: Your Enemies wait for your halting, that by your Errors they may bring up a scandal upon Religion and Godliness.
author: Burnet, Gilbert, 1643-1715.
title: Charitable reproof a sermon preached at the Church of St. Mary-le-Bow to the Societies for Reformation of Manners, the 25th of March, 1700 / by the Right Reverend Father in God, Gilbert Lord Bishop of

text: We will feel a lively concern in us for the Honour of Religion; and when we see it dishonoured, we will interpose, if it were but to express a just Indignation at Impiety and Vice.
author: Burnet, Gilbert, 1643-1715.
title: Charitable reproof a sermon preached at the Church of St. Mary-le-Bow to the Societies for Reformation of Manners, the 25th of March, 1700 / by the Right Reverend Father in God, Gilbert Lord Bishop of

text: The sense will then be, the Kisses or Caresses of an Enemy will be redoubled; they will be officious in them both in season and out of season.
author: Burnet, Gilbert, 1643-1715.
title: Charitable reproof a sermon preached at the Church of St. Mary-le-Bow to the Societies for Reformation of Manners, the 25th of March, 1700 / by the Right Reverend Father in God, Gilbert Lord Bishop of

text: Nor is it enough to authorize a man to be a Monitor, that he does not offend just in that sort and manner for which he blames others.
author: Burnet, Gilbert, 1643-1715.
title: Charitable reproof a sermon preached at the Church of St. Mary-le-Bow to the Societies for Reformation of Manners, the 25th of March, 1700 / by the Right Reverend Father in God, Gilbert Lord Bishop of

text: When it appears that our Admonitions are like either to have no effect at all, or to have bad ones, we may reckon that we are not under the common Obligations of Reproving, if there are no probabilities of our succeeding in them.
author: Burnet, Gilbert, 1643-1715.
title: Charitable reproof a sermon preached at the Church of St. Mary-le-Bow to the Societies for Reformation of Manners, the 25th of March, 1700 / by the Right Reverend Father in God, Gilbert Lord Bishop of

text: Flatterers, when they perceive that their base Obsequiousness is acceptable, they follow close upon that Scent; they are Assiduous and Abject in it.
author: Burnet, Gilbert, 1643-1715.
title: Charitable reproof a sermon preached at the Church of St. Mary-le-Bow to the Societies for Reformation of Manners, the 25th of March, 1700 / by the Right Reverend Father in God, Gilbert Lord Bishop of

text: His Candor and Integrity, his Humility and Meekness, his Modesty and Charity, must be so conspicuous, that his light may thereby shine before others; and then he may more reasonably hope, that others may be wrought on both by his Example and Influence to glorify his Father which is in Heaven.
author: Burnet, Gilbert, 1643-1715.
title: Charitable reproof a sermon preached at the Church of St. Mary-le-Bow to the Societies for Reformation of Manners, the 25th of March, 1700 / by the Right Reverend Father in God, Gilbert Lord Bishop of

text: Another Rule to be observed in Reproving is, to do it in such a manner, that it may appear we are their Friends whom we reprove, and that we Correct them for their own Good.
author: Burnet, Gilbert, 1643-1715.
title: Charitable reproof a sermon preached at the Church of St. Mary-le-Bow to the Societies for Reformation of Manners, the 25th of March, 1700 / by the Right Reverend Father in God, Gilbert Lord Bishop of

text: Mistaken zeal, with folly at her side, Oft has the Drama and its sons decri'd; Gave the profession faults which nature knew, And judg'd the many from an erring few.
author: Downman, Hugh, 1740-1809.
title: The drama, a poem:

text: As folly's offspring sport in fashion's glare, Flutt'ring in silks, with well-bred shrug and stare, The insect tribe DODD paints with nicest art, And gives a double edge to satire's dart.
author: Downman, Hugh, 1740-1809.
title: The drama, a poem:

text: His acting's vappid, it wants feeling's soul, To warm and quicken, into life the whole.
author: Downman, Hugh, 1740-1809.
title: The drama, a poem:

text: Cold, and unmeaning, AICKIN fills a part, And never gains the head, or moves the heart.
author: Downman, Hugh, 1740-1809.
title: The drama, a poem:

text: HULL's always perfect, and displays an aim, To catch the poet's spirit, and his flame; At times, he soars beyond chill medium's line, And shews some sparks of excellence that shine.
author: Downman, Hugh, 1740-1809.
title: The drama, a poem:

text: That part, an actor in the bloom of life Plays with success, he takes to him for wife, Simpers and ogles with a wither'd face, And trips the beau with antiquated grace.
author: Downman, Hugh, 1740-1809.
title: The drama, a poem:

text: How few can ever reach that happy line, Where sense, and spirit, by their union shine; And softned into ease, with nicest art, Assail at once, the judgment and the heart.
author: Downman, Hugh, 1740-1809.
title: The drama, a poem:

text: Tho' WOODWARD once might boast of sprightly ease, And ev'ry frolic wantonness to please, Why must he gambol after youth is fled, And winter scatters hoar upon his head?
author: Downman, Hugh, 1740-1809.
title: The drama, a poem:

text: When partial nature gifts a fav'rite son, With more than toiling art had ever won, Should not the muse, if sloth the bounty mar, Censure the culprit who neglects her care?
author: Downman, Hugh, 1740-1809.
title: The drama, a poem:

text: REDDISH wants pow'r, th'emotion strong to raise, But his attention gains, and merits praise; Tho' voice and feeling small assistance lend, He oft has pleas'd, and seldom does offend; Unless, when folly fain would have him great, And rant and stare usurp expression's seat.
author: Downman, Hugh, 1740-1809.
title: The drama, a poem:

text: Apollo pleads his cause; and dare the muse, To hear her prince, and patron's voice refuse?
author: Downman, Hugh, 1740-1809.
title: The drama, a poem:

text: BRERETON has person, is not void of grace, But wants the energy of voice and face; In gay description, or in polish'd ease, His taste and judgment never fail to please.
author: Downman, Hugh, 1740-1809.
title: The drama, a poem:

text: If music's voice, the throbbing breast can move, Or melting softness, wake the soul to love; If mild expression, beaming from a face, Where sweetness revels with resistless grace, Can cold attention into rapture warm, Behold in BADD'LY ev'ry pow'r to charm.
author: Downman, Hugh, 1740-1809.
title: The drama, a poem:

text: And the Young and Able Lightermen hide and withdraw from their Employments, until the Preſs is over, which makes Wages very dear, obſtructs Trade, and raiſes the price of Proviſion, Fewel, &c. which tends to the prejudice of all, eſpecially the poorer ſort.
author: Watermen and Lightermen of the River Thames (Guild)
title: The watermens case, in relation to the bill for increase and encouragement of seamen

text: It's therefore Humbly ſubmitted to the great Wiſdom of this preſent Parliament, Whether it might not highly conduce towards the Furniſhing the Navy with great Numbers of Able Men, and thereby better promote the good purpoſes of the deſigned Regiſtring of Seamen.
author: Watermen and Lightermen of the River Thames (Guild)
title: The watermens case, in relation to the bill for increase and encouragement of seamen

text: Whereby a more Exact and full Liſt of all Watermen may be more ſpeedily had, and with leſs Charge than others can procure, that do not know or are converſant amongſt the Watermen.
author: Watermen and Lightermen of the River Thames (Guild)
title: The watermens case, in relation to the bill for increase and encouragement of seamen

text: Whereas the ſaid Company now is one of the beſt Seminaries for Breeding up Youth to the Sea, and is computed to have afforded above 4000 Voluntiers and Preſſed Men for the Navy, ſince His Majeſty's Happy Acceſſion to the Crown.
author: Watermen and Lightermen of the River Thames (Guild)
title: The watermens case, in relation to the bill for increase and encouragement of seamen

text: For the Barges now leave their luſty and able Men at Kingston, &c. and are brought from thence to London with Old Men only.
author: Watermen and Lightermen of the River Thames (Guild)
title: The watermens case, in relation to the bill for increase and encouragement of seamen

text: And ſeveral Thouſands of Stout and Able Men, as Lightermen, Bargemen, &c. will be added, and made forth coming, more than the Regiſtring Bill comprehends, or ſeems to have any notice of.
author: Watermen and Lightermen of the River Thames (Guild)
title: The watermens case, in relation to the bill for increase and encouragement of seamen

text: THE disappointment which Cajanus met with in his love-adventure, was soon spread over the town of Oulo, and the neighbouring villages; that he became the jest of all the young people of those parts, to whom this amour was well known.
author: Boreman, Thomas, fl. 1730-1743.
title: The history of Cajanus: the Swedish giant, from his birth to the present time. By the author of the Gigantick histories.

text: How Giant Puff was afraid he had made a compact with the Devil, by what be had done: and how his master deliver'd him from such terrible apprehensions.
author: Boreman, Thomas, fl. 1730-1743.
title: The history of Cajanus: the Swedish giant, from his birth to the present time. By the author of the Gigantick histories.

text: The perfections of this fair maid had taken deep root in our Giant's heart, so that in her center'd all his happiness.
author: Boreman, Thomas, fl. 1730-1743.
title: The history of Cajanus: the Swedish giant, from his birth to the present time. By the author of the Gigantick histories.

text: He likewise brought him up to industry, to work in the garden with the spade, &c. and to labour in the field in husbandry affairs, and in short, to get his bread by the sweat of his brow.
author: Boreman, Thomas, fl. 1730-1743.
title: The history of Cajanus: the Swedish giant, from his birth to the present time. By the author of the Gigantick histories.

text: Dolla Rucina has this day received a strict charge from her parents, no longer to entertain thee on any other terms than that of a friend.
author: Boreman, Thomas, fl. 1730-1743.
title: The history of Cajanus: the Swedish giant, from his birth to the present time. By the author of the Gigantick histories.

text: THIS Swedish Giant was born at Oulo, or Ula. a port town situated on the east side of the Botnick Bay in Finland, bordering on Russia, in the year 1709.
author: Boreman, Thomas, fl. 1730-1743.
title: The history of Cajanus: the Swedish giant, from his birth to the present time. By the author of the Gigantick histories.

text: I should have told my readers, that Dolla Rucina was now married to a young farmer, whose father was lately dead, and had left him in possession of a rich farm.
author: Boreman, Thomas, fl. 1730-1743.
title: The history of Cajanus: the Swedish giant, from his birth to the present time. By the author of the Gigantick histories.

text: However, in some little time he began to recollect himself; to walk, talk, and use his reason.
author: Boreman, Thomas, fl. 1730-1743.
title: The history of Cajanus: the Swedish giant, from his birth to the present time. By the author of the Gigantick histories.

text: He had read of persons selling themselves, and making such compacts for a term of years, at the end of which they were fetcht away: the thoughts hereof terribly frighted this mighty Christian Goliah.
author: Boreman, Thomas, fl. 1730-1743.
title: The history of Cajanus: the Swedish giant, from his birth to the present time. By the author of the Gigantick histories.

text: She at this time reach'd but a little above Cajanus's waste, and was of an agreeable size, and not likely to be taller.
author: Boreman, Thomas, fl. 1730-1743.
title: The history of Cajanus: the Swedish giant, from his birth to the present time. By the author of the Gigantick histories.

text: That they should inform Cajanus, at his next visit, that they could not approve of a match so unequal; that they were sorry they had not broke it off sooner; and advised their daughter no longer to entertain thoughts of marrying a man whose size exceeded all reason.
author: Boreman, Thomas, fl. 1730-1743.
title: The history of Cajanus: the Swedish giant, from his birth to the present time. By the author of the Gigantick histories.

text: And before his departure they regaled him with curds, cream, and other country fare, as usual; which Cajanus was a dear lover of, and fed pretty cheerfully upon.
author: Boreman, Thomas, fl. 1730-1743.
title: The history of Cajanus: the Swedish giant, from his birth to the present time. By the author of the Gigantick histories.

text: He suffered Love's flame to smother a long time in his breast, before he dared to undertake this adventure.
author: Boreman, Thomas, fl. 1730-1743.
title: The history of Cajanus: the Swedish giant, from his birth to the present time. By the author of the Gigantick histories.

text: Ye Waters, who at his Command, whose Voice First call'd ye forth from Nothing, left disclos'd The World's Foundations, now again return, And at his Bidding in your Channel flow.
author: Hawkesworth, John, 1715?-1773.
title: The fall of Egypt; an oratorio. As it is performed at the Theatre Royal in Drury-lane. Written by the late John Hawkesworth LL.D. and set to musick by John Stanley:

text: Now let us fly; What now forbids, that, careless of his Will Whom Darkness binds, and Hunger must destroy, We quit for ever this detested Land, And seek the promis'd Heritage of Heav'n?
author: Hawkesworth, John, 1715?-1773.
title: The fall of Egypt; an oratorio. As it is performed at the Theatre Royal in Drury-lane. Written by the late John Hawkesworth LL.D. and set to musick by John Stanley:

text: So, when the transient Storm is past, The sudden Gloom, and driving Show'r, The sweetest Sunshine is the last, The lov'liest, is the Evening Hour.
author: Hawkesworth, John, 1715?-1773.
title: The fall of Egypt; an oratorio. As it is performed at the Theatre Royal in Drury-lane. Written by the late John Hawkesworth LL.D. and set to musick by John Stanley:

text: The Way grows sleep; ascending from th' Abyss Behold the Thousands that pass on before us; A moving Column, rising Rank o'er Rank, Swarm on th' Ascent, and quicken all the Way!
author: Hawkesworth, John, 1715?-1773.
title: The fall of Egypt; an oratorio. As it is performed at the Theatre Royal in Drury-lane. Written by the late John Hawkesworth LL.D. and set to musick by John Stanley:

text: Fear not the Hosts that now enrag'd pursue; Though now ye see them, ye shall see no more.
author: Hawkesworth, John, 1715?-1773.
title: The fall of Egypt; an oratorio. As it is performed at the Theatre Royal in Drury-lane. Written by the late John Hawkesworth LL.D. and set to musick by John Stanley:

text: I am again myself, and scorn the Fears, The vain fantastic Fears, that Darkness breeds; Let the loud Trumpets sound, that if the Sun Still combats with a Foe not yet subdu'd, The Sound may lend him Aid, and let your Song Conjure the Pow'rs of Darkness from the Sky.
author: Hawkesworth, John, 1715?-1773.
title: The fall of Egypt; an oratorio. As it is performed at the Theatre Royal in Drury-lane. Written by the late John Hawkesworth LL.D. and set to musick by John Stanley:

text: But he whose sad Reward is Pain, Whom Sorrow meets at his Return, Can ne'er the Load of Life sustain, To hide his Anguish ne'er can learn.
author: Hawkesworth, John, 1715?-1773.
title: The fall of Egypt; an oratorio. As it is performed at the Theatre Royal in Drury-lane. Written by the late John Hawkesworth LL.D. and set to musick by John Stanley:

text: O! that untroubled by deccitful Hopes Content still sweeten'd Toil, and welcome Rest Still crown'd our Evening when the Day was past!
author: Hawkesworth, John, 1715?-1773.
title: The fall of Egypt; an oratorio. As it is performed at the Theatre Royal in Drury-lane. Written by the late John Hawkesworth LL.D. and set to musick by John Stanley:

text: Accursed Sorcerer!—But in vain I curse him; I am myself the Murderer of my Child!— Why did I fear to take a forfeit Life!
author: Hawkesworth, John, 1715?-1773.
title: The fall of Egypt; an oratorio. As it is performed at the Theatre Royal in Drury-lane. Written by the late John Hawkesworth LL.D. and set to musick by John Stanley:

text: We hear thee, and with Transport trust, Thy Rod shall make the Tyrant just, And all our Wrongs atone; Where'er the circling Sun displays His rising or his setting Rays, Our Triumph shall be known.
author: Hawkesworth, John, 1715?-1773.
title: The fall of Egypt; an oratorio. As it is performed at the Theatre Royal in Drury-lane. Written by the late John Hawkesworth LL.D. and set to musick by John Stanley:

text: That this is certain, let the Signs attest, Which he who speaks by me, by me has wrought.
author: Hawkesworth, John, 1715?-1773.
title: The fall of Egypt; an oratorio. As it is performed at the Theatre Royal in Drury-lane. Written by the late John Hawkesworth LL.D. and set to musick by John Stanley:

text: Ah! not so— Revenge will then make Tyranny more dreadful; Waste not the Lives one Day's Delay may cost, Nor add one Day to Bondage worse than Death!
author: Hawkesworth, John, 1715?-1773.

text: Thus publick happiness our care But for our own peculiar share: While sons their father's schemes traduce; And here all patriotism abuse.

title: Epistles philosophical and moral:

text: Disdaining at the lamp to pore, That lights us to the classick lore, The half-taught deist thus exclaims At texts rever'd and hallow'd names, Damning profane or sacred writ, That squares not with his shallow wit.
author: Kenrick, W. (William), 1725?-1779.
title: Epistles philosophical and moral:

text: For not a son of Adam's race Innate conviction can efface The highland loon, the lowland lout, Wild Irish fierce, and Cambrian stout, The boor that Rhynland's polder drains, Tho' reason slumber in his brains, All, all, like premises in view, The like conclusions ever drew.
author: Kenrick, W. (William), 1725?-1779.
title: Epistles philosophical and moral:

text: Tho' plung'd by zeal in errour deep, While common-sense lies fast asleep, Their faith rash bigots strangely boast; The strongest his who's cheated most; Who least for truth presumes to search; But headlong runs into the church.
author: Kenrick, W. (William), 1725?-1779.
title: Epistles philosophical and moral:

text: Since gospel witnesses in form were tried, Their valid evidence I ne'er denied; Ne'er intermeddled with the jury's quest, Nor contradicted Littleton or West.

text: What tho' without an obvious cause We see inverted custom's laws, Must we immediately infer That nature from itself can err?

text: No proofs of being objects bring, Whose essence ever on the wing, Flown from their forms, ere yet defin'd, Leaves no identity behind.
author: Kenrick, W. (William), 1725?-1779.
title: Epistles philosophical and moral:

text: Yet custom's rules caprice hath broke, And turn'd her statutes into joke; Nor boast her laws, however old, Resistance to the pow'r of gold.
author: Kenrick, W. (William), 1725?-1779.
title: Epistles philosophical and moral:

text: The diff'rence plain 'twixt bliss and woe, Whate'er we feel we surely know: What state can, then, be ever thine Which sense nor science can define.
author: Kenrick, W. (William), 1725?-1779.

text: A Court debauch'd, a Theatre profane, Were all the Blessings of that virtuous Reign: Poets themselves by Lewdness then did raise, By servile Flatt'ry, and by fulsom Praise; He then wrote best, that made the lewdest Plays.
author: Blackmore, Richard, Sir, d. 1729.
title: An Epistle to Sr. Richard Blackmore occasion'd by the new session of the poets.

text: Both for their Counsel and their Justice fear'd, No vicious Kings or Potentates they spar'd: To future Times they did the Truth declare, Which were the Lewd, and which the Virtuous were.
author: Blackmore, Richard, Sir, d. 1729.
title: An Epistle to Sr. Richard Blackmore occasion'd by the new session of the poets.

text: The Poet now the self-same method takes, His Reason, Virtue, and his God forsakes, Declines Instructions of the Good and Wise, By Vanity and Vice attempts to rise; Some Packhorse for a Pegasus he strides, And stumbles on Preferment as he rides.
author: Blackmore, Richard, Sir, d. 1729.
title: An Epistle to Sr. Richard Blackmore occasion'd by the new session of the poets.

text: Tho he attempts the Regions of the Sky, Flutters o'er Earth, nor can ascend on high; His Pinions broken, and his Lute unstrung, He sings a horrid and confounded Song.
author: Blackmore, Richard, Sir, d. 1729.
title: An Epistle to Sr. Richard Blackmore occasion'd by the new session of the poets.

text: 'Tis true, your Genius was by Fate design'd To shew us Virtue and exalted Mind; And those blest Paths, alas! we seldom find.
author: Blackmore, Richard, Sir, d. 1729.
title: An Epistle to Sr. Richard Blackmore occasion'd by the new session of the poets.

text: No matter how unfurnish'd be his Scull, Be he a Sot, incorrigibly dull: If some lewd Courtier he can meanly praise, He never fails of Honour and the Bays.
author: Blackmore, Richard, Sir, d. 1729.
title: An Epistle to Sr. Richard Blackmore occasion'd by the new session of the poets.

text: Of all your Foes, the Rhymer of most note Is he who the new Session lately wrote, Who, that his Lines may better pass for Wit, Has stamp'd with Honour all the stuff he writ.
author: Blackmore, Richard, Sir, d. 1729.
title: An Epistle to Sr. Richard Blackmore occasion'd by the new session of the poets.

text: This, Sir's your Fate, curs'd Criticks you oppose, The most Tyrannical and cruel Foes: Dr—n their Huntsman dead, no more he wounds, But now you must engage his Pack of Hounds.
author: Blackmore, Richard, Sir, d. 1729.
title: An Epistle to Sr. Richard Blackmore occasion'd by the new session of the poets.

text: So much we now decline from Virtue's ways, The Poet works his Labours into Plays; Each Bard is grown a Mimick or Buffoon, And what was Satyr once, is now Lampoon: They meanly flatter for the Bread they eat, And not by Virtue, but by Crimes grow great.
author: Blackmore, Richard, Sir, d. 1729.
title: An Epistle to Sr. Richard Blackmore occasion'd by the new session of the poets.

text: If we mistrust him, we are not to blame, Who shews his Honour, but conceals his Name; No Suit of Scandal can we undergo, His mighty Honour being incognito.
author: Blackmore, Richard, Sir, d. 1729.
title: An Epistle to Sr. Richard Blackmore occasion'd by the new session of the poets.

text: When e'er we see a Comet in the Sky, We strait conclude some Potentate will die; So when the stormy Winds come puffing on, Disturb the Waters of smooth Helicon, This Mountain Poet does bring forth a Mouse, Larger and bigger than a Souldiers Louse.
author: Blackmore, Richard, Sir, d. 1729.
title: An Epistle to Sr. Richard Blackmore occasion'd by the new session of the poets.

text: Great M—ue, the wonder of the Nation, Only a Poet is by Imputation, And others Works of Supererrogation.

text: NOT that you need Assistance in your Wars, Or have receiv'd dishonourable Scars, By Criticks worried, as by Beasts of Prey, Men void of Sense, and full as wild as they; Who against Wit Infernal Batt'ries raise, And tear with Envy what they ought to praise.
author: Blackmore, Richard, Sir, d. 1729.

text: Beware your Pupils tender Age Imbibe no superstitious Rage, Which Fools Religion call; Such narrow Principles remove, Inculcate universal Love, And Charity to all.

text: The Law of Nature let them know, Instruct their Bosoms how to glow And pant for honest Fame; Make it their Bus'ness and Delight To vindicate the native Right, Which free-born Britons claim.

text: Our Fathers wisely dar'd to raise Their Fabric on the triple Base Of COMMONS, LORDS, and KING; And hence BRITANNIA's happy Fate, Hence all the Music of our State, Hence all our Blessings spring.

text: Yet shun the furious Zeal of such Who act the Patriot overmuch, And Monarchy invade; Who mindless of their Laws at home, Would copy those of Greece and Rome, Where Commonwealths-men sway'd.

text: Rash daring Muse, resign the Lyre; For Shame! be not so bold; Nor useless Hints to Him impart, Who knows so well to cast the Heart In VIRTUE's genuine Mould.

text: Bid them assert their Country's Cause, Teach them our Government and Laws, All servile Precepts shun, Such as, contriv'd by holy Knaves, Persuade us, Subjects are but Slaves, And All were made for One.

text: Not less absurd may I be thought, Who bred, from Colleges remote, In honest simple Truth; Ne'er study'd Science at the Schools, And yet presume to give You Rules For educating Youth.

text: Yet if the Maxims I advance May be of Use, or right by chance, They cannot give Offence: Forgive me then, for Reason's sake; For Reason dictates what I speak, And says, 'tis Common Sense.

text: So shall your SCHOOL increase each Day, And flourish like the verdant Bay, Or branching Vine in Spring; Your Youth be virtuously inclin'd, Be real PATRIOTS of Mankind, And loyal to their KING.

text: As VIRTUE shall her Charms display, (Charms! which increasing ev'ry Day, Shall make her more approv'd) Your Pupils shall adore the Dame, Shall court her with a Lover's Flame, As worthiest to be lov'd.

text: Who in diſdain of all the Scoffing Crew, Doth ſtill his Duty, giving all their due, In ſpight of Spight it ſelf, and all that Jeer'd, Tho' much deſpiſed, Heaven-ward he Stear'd His Courſe with patience onwards ſtill he goes, Arriving there in ſpight of all his Foes.

text: But if you Guilty be of ſome, or all, By cauſing his Credit thereby to fall, By Slander, Railing, or by ill report, Unto the Injur'd Party then reſort, Begging his Pardon, if you can reſtore To him the ſame Good Name he had before.

text: Worldly Men indeed think they have built themſelves and their Enjoyments upon a Rock, when it proves only a Bog or Foundation of Sand, which adverſe Winds and Flouds of Affliction ſoon beat down or waſh away.

text: Our Saviour tells us, Thoſe who mourn now ſhall be comforted, Mat. 5.4. and St. Paul reckons the heavieſt afflictions light, becauſe they are but for a moment, 2 Cor. 4.17.

text: If the Time of Worldly Proſperity be ſhort, we muſt not confide, rely upon, or place our Happineſs in it.

text: Riches, when we think we have them in ſafe keeping, make themſelves Wings and fly away, Prov. 23.5.

text: The Time is ſhort; it remaineth therefore, that they that weep be as though they wept not; and they that rejoyce, as though they rejoyced not; —and they that uſe this World, as not abuſing it: for the faſhion of this World paſſeth away.

text: The Inference from it, That we ſhould moderate our Affections and Paſſions, ſo as not to be overwhelmed with Grief under Afflictions, nor too much tranſported with Joy in Proſperity.

text: That we have not had time to go through and experience the ſeveral ſorts of Evils that are in the World?

text: Stop here, my Muſe, no more thy Office boaſt, This drop of Praiſe is in an Ocean loſt; His Works alone are Trumpets of his Fame, And every Line will Chronicle his Name.
author: Manley, Mrs. (Mary de la Rivière), 1663-1724.
title: The Nine muses, or, Poems written by nine several ladies upon the death of the late famous John Dryden, Esq.

text: Cromwel's great Genius here was greater ſhewn, Well might ſuch Vertues for one Vice attone; If vaſt Ambition can be reckon'd Vice, Which to great Jove gave the Imperial Skies.
author: Manley, Mrs. (Mary de la Rivière), 1663-1724.
title: The Nine muses, or, Poems written by nine several ladies upon the death of the late famous John Dryden, Esq.

text: With Virgil, Chaucer ſings Great Dryden's Name, Who gave new luſter to his darkned Fame; Diſpel'd the Clouds by which he was conceal'd, And to his native Iſle the Bard reveal'd; Not bleſt enough in his own glorious State, Till he to them a part Communicate.
author: Manley, Mrs. (Mary de la Rivière), 1663-1724.
title: The Nine muses, or, Poems written by nine several ladies upon the death of the late famous John Dryden, Esq.

text: With a Superior and victorious Grace The Sacred Place, He did almoſt unenvy'd aſſume, I, pleas'd to ſee the Branches ſpread O're his triumphant Head, From th' Helicon Spring Did Water bring, Sprinkled them oft that they might ever bloom.
author: Manley, Mrs. (Mary de la Rivière), 1663-1724.
title: The Nine muses, or, Poems written by nine several ladies upon the death of the late famous John Dryden, Esq.

text: I taught Him all the ſofter Airs of Love, And Anthems ſo divine; he'll find the ſame above.
author: Manley, Mrs. (Mary de la Rivière), 1663-1724.
title: The Nine muses, or, Poems written by nine several ladies upon the death of the late famous John Dryden, Esq.

text: You have been pleaſed already to ſhew Your Reſpect to his Memory, in contributing ſo largely towards His Burial notwithſtanding He had that unhappineſs of Conduct, when alive, to give you Cauſe to Diſclaim the Protection of Him.
author: Manley, Mrs. (Mary de la Rivière), 1663-1724.
title: The Nine muses, or, Poems written by nine several ladies upon the death of the late famous John Dryden, Esq.

text: I with profoundeſt Cauſe, and Sorrow mourn, Over my Dryden's ſacred Urn: He was my greateſt Glory, only boaſt, Through him I let ungrateful Mankind know, What mighty Wonders I could do, But now, like him, to the inferior World I'm loſt.
author: Manley, Mrs. (Mary de la Rivière), 1663-1724.
title: The Nine muses, or, Poems written by nine several ladies upon the death of the late famous John Dryden, Esq.

text: With an auſpicious Pride I did diſpence My mighty Favours, when He did implore, From my pregnant unexhauſted Store, Of tuneful Fancies, and harmonious Sence.
author: Manley, Mrs. (Mary de la Rivière), 1663-1724.
title: The Nine muses, or, Poems written by nine several ladies upon the death of the late famous John Dryden, Esq.

text: When Cleopatra's paſſion he adorns, How nobly Anthony the Empire ſcorns, Diſſolv'd in her kind Arms tranſported lay, For Love's ſoft Joys gave the rough Crown away.
author: Manley, Mrs. (Mary de la Rivière), 1663-1724.
title: The Nine muses, or, Poems written by nine several ladies upon the death of the late famous John Dryden, Esq.

text: Poetry's not th' effect of Art, or Wine, or Love, Tho' They ſometimes the Gift improve, Nor is the warmth that Poets does inſpire, Vinum Daemonum, but Celeſtial Fire.
author: Manley, Mrs. (Mary de la Rivière), 1663-1724.
title: The Nine muses, or, Poems written by nine several ladies upon the death of the late famous John Dryden, Esq.

text: But who on Earth can Boaſt of true Repoſe, Pale Envy from her Snaky Bed aroſe, In thouſand Shapes his Merit to oppoſe.
author: Manley, Mrs. (Mary de la Rivière), 1663-1724.
title: The Nine muses, or, Poems written by nine several ladies upon the death of the late famous John Dryden, Esq.

text: COME all my Siſters now in Conſort join, Each weep her Favrite's loſs with Tears Divine: Fill all the Space with your immortal Sighs, The vaulted Heavens return your louder Cries.
author: Manley, Mrs. (Mary de la Rivière), 1663-1724.
title: The Nine muses, or, Poems written by nine several ladies upon the death of the late famous John Dryden, Esq.

author: Manley, Mrs. (Mary de la Rivière), 1663-1724.

text: And I verily thought, that this was the man, for whose supposed murder I suffered so much in England, and the thought being strong in my head, I could not sleep all night.

title: The life and adventures of Ambrose Gwinett: well known to the public, as the lame beggar-man, ...

text: As soon as they came up to the house, they stopt and one of them lighting, suddenly seized me by the collar, crying, You are King's prisoner.

text: In a word, a warrant was produced, and I was carried back to Deal attended by the three men; my brother with another friend accompanying us, who knew not what to say for, nor how to comfort me.

title: The life and adventures of Ambrose Gwinett: well known to the public, as the lame beggar-man, ...

text: Not with more care shall H-me avoid his wife, Not C-pe fly swifter, lashing for his life; Than I to leave the meagre fiend behind.
author: Smollett, Tobias George, 1721-1771.
title: Advice: a satire:

text: What! join the Crew that pilfer one another, Betray my friend, and persecute my brother: Turn usurer, o'er cent. per cent. to brood, Or quack, to feed like fleas, on human blood?
author: Smollett, Tobias George, 1721-1771.
title: Advice: a satire:

text: Sooner, in hopeless anguish would I mourn, Than owe my fortune to the man I scorn!— What new Resourse?
author: Smollett, Tobias George, 1721-1771.
title: Advice: a satire:

text: No! petrify'd by dulness and disdain, Beyond the feeling of another's pain; The tear of pity ne'er bedew'd his eye, Nor his lewd bosom felt the social sigh!
author: Smollett, Tobias George, 1721-1771.
title: Advice: a satire:

text: Th' Hesperian dragon not more fierce of old, By ev'ry charm unmov'd, but that of gold: Thus at hell gates th' affrighted shade must drop For ev'ry mouth of Cerberus, a sop.
author: Smollett, Tobias George, 1721-1771.
title: Advice: a satire:

text: 'Tis he, that lures th' unpractis'd mind astray, Then leaves the wretch to misery, a prey; Perverts the race of virtue just begun, And stabs the publick in its ruin'd son.
author: Smollett, Tobias George, 1721-1771.
title: Advice: a satire:

text: Exert your Talents; Nature, ever kind, Enough for happiness, bestows on all; 'Tis sloth or pride that finds her gifts too small— Why sleeps the muse?—is there no room for praise, When such bright names in constellation blaze?
author: Smollett, Tobias George, 1721-1771.
title: Advice: a satire:

text: No;—thanks to discord, war shall be my friend; And moral rage, heroic courage lend To pierce the gleaming squadron of the foe, And win renown by some distinguish'd blow.
author: Smollett, Tobias George, 1721-1771.
title: Advice: a satire:

text: From the pale hag, O teach me to get loose; Divorc'd! all hell shall not retie the noose!
author: Smollett, Tobias George, 1721-1771.
title: Advice: a satire:

text: But one thing more,—how loud must I repeat, To gain th'ingag'd attention of the Great, Amus'd, perhaps, with C---'s prolific bum, Or rapt amidst the transports of a drum; While the grim porter watches ev'ry door, Stern foe to tradesmen, poets, and the poor.
author: Smollett, Tobias George, 1721-1771.
title: Advice: a satire:

text: These sons of sloth that by profusion thrive, His pride inveigled from the public hive; And numbers pine in solitary woe, That furnish'd out this phantasie of shew.
author: Smollett, Tobias George, 1721-1771.
title: Advice: a satire:

text: 'Tis well;—enjoy that petulance of stile, And, like an evious adder, lick the file: What 'tho' success will not attend on all?
author: Smollett, Tobias George, 1721-1771.
title: Advice: a satire:

text: ENough, enough; all this we knew before: 'Tis infamous, I grant it, to be poor: And who so much to sense and glory lost, Will hug the curse that not one joy can boast?
author: Smollett, Tobias George, 1721-1771.
title: Advice: a satire:

text: This is all I think fit to ſay of this matter, I chuſe to addreſs it to you Zenobio, for the conſtant friendſhip I have ever entertained with you, and formerly with your deceaſed Father, the companion of my Studies, and ornament of our City.

title: Nicholas Machiavel's letter to Zanobius Buondelmontius in vindication of himself and his writings..

text: The word Clergy is a term, wholly unknown to the Scriptures, otherwiſe than in this ſence; a peculiar People or Gods lot, uſed often for the whole Jewiſh Nation, who are likewiſe called a Kingdom of Prieſts in ſome places.

title: Nicholas Machiavel's letter to Zanobius Buondelmontius in vindication of himself and his writings..

text: And how can any man pretend to write concerning Policy, who deſtroyes the moſt eſſential part of it, which is obedience to all Governments.

title: Nicholas Machiavel's letter to Zanobius Buondelmontius in vindication of himself and his writings..

text: Now If it ſhall appear, that as the luſts of our firſt Parents did at that time diſappoint the good intention of GOD, in making a pure World, and brought in by their diſobedience the corruptions that are now in it.
author: Neville, Henry, 1620-1694.
title: Nicholas Machiavel's letter to Zanobius Buondelmontius in vindication of himself and his writings..

text: If I remember well, the exceptions that are taken to theſe poor things I have publiſhed, are reducible to three.

title: Nicholas Machiavel's letter to Zanobius Buondelmontius in vindication of himself and his writings..

text: I ſhall anſwer ſomething to every one of theſe; and that I may obſerve a right method, will begin with the firſt.

title: Nicholas Machiavel's letter to Zanobius Buondelmontius in vindication of himself and his writings..

text: CHRIST tells us, his Kingdom is not of this World; And, if any will be the greateſt amongſt his Diſciples, that he muſt be ſervant to the reſt, which ſhews that his Followers were to be great in Sanctity and Humility, and not in worldly power.
author: Neville, Henry, 1620-1694.
title: Nicholas Machiavel's letter to Zanobius Buondelmontius in vindication of himself and his writings..

text: Was I not Born, Bred, and imployed in a City, which being at the time I write, under that form of Government, did owe all wealth and greatneſs, and all proſperity to it?
author: Neville, Henry, 1620-1694.
title: Nicholas Machiavel's letter to Zanobius Buondelmontius in vindication of himself and his writings..
