title: An heroic answer, from Richard Twiss, Esq: F.R.S. at Rotterdam, to Donna Teresa Pinna Ruiz, of Murica.

text: A thousand tongues from stage to stage pursu'd, And fresh disgrace th' unwearied gibe renew'd: Thus down the chimney some poor sparrow strays, And roams the parlour with a wild amaze; Dogs, cats, and children, a malignant crew, The hapless stranger round the room pursue.
author: MacNally, Leonard, 1752-1820.
title: An heroic answer, from Richard Twiss, Esq: F.R.S. at Rotterdam, to Donna Teresa Pinna Ruiz, of Murica.

text: "But soon, the victim of ill-manners, fell; "A youth of Galway hurl'd me down to hell: "Chang'd to a goat, to travel mountains sent, "What was my pastime, is my punishment.
author: MacNally, Leonard, 1752-1820.
title: An heroic answer, from Richard Twiss, Esq: F.R.S. at Rotterdam, to Donna Teresa Pinna Ruiz, of Murica.

text: Too well, my love, thou know'st the guilty shore, And "perils such as never errant bore."
author: MacNally, Leonard, 1752-1820.
title: An heroic answer, from Richard Twiss, Esq: F.R.S. at Rotterdam, to Donna Teresa Pinna Ruiz, of Murica.

text: Revenge inspires them in Apollo's spite; A Twiss provokes; and well, or ill, they write.
author: MacNally, Leonard, 1752-1820.
title: An heroic answer, from Richard Twiss, Esq: F.R.S. at Rotterdam, to Donna Teresa Pinna Ruiz, of Murica.

text: Rail, write, and rage; I prize the sordid cry Less than the hummings of the smallest fly.

text: Some back to back, some side by side are plac'd, The ravish'd maid by panting youth embrac'd. By dozens thus, full many a Sunday morn, With dangling legs the jovial croud is borne; Clontarf they seek, or Howth's aspiring brow, Or Leixlip, smiling on the stream below.
author: MacNally, Leonard, 1752-1820.
title: An heroic answer, from Richard Twiss, Esq: F.R.S. at Rotterdam, to Donna Teresa Pinna Ruiz, of Murica.

text: To serpents, teeth; to scorpions gave a tail; To me, my printer, and my leaden flail; Hibernian dames are train'd to cuff and kick, And nature arm'd them,—for their legs are thick.
author: MacNally, Leonard, 1752-1820.
title: An heroic answer, from Richard Twiss, Esq: F.R.S. at Rotterdam, to Donna Teresa Pinna Ruiz, of Murica.

text: (A mighty stink-pot in his hand appear'd, And ass's ears were on his temples rear'd) "Once, like thyself, I travel'd, lied, and wrote, "An author then, tho' now a mountain goat.
author: MacNally, Leonard, 1752-1820.
title: An heroic answer, from Richard Twiss, Esq: F.R.S. at Rotterdam, to Donna Teresa Pinna Ruiz, of Murica.

text: Of fish they talk'd with gizzard like a bird: I went, by doubtful, faint emotions, stir'd. Heavens! have I caught it! rapture fires my mind!
author: MacNally, Leonard, 1752-1820.
title: An heroic answer, from Richard Twiss, Esq: F.R.S. at Rotterdam, to Donna Teresa Pinna Ruiz, of Murica.

text: Hast thou not seen a vase of antique mold, Of Parian marble, or Barbaric gold, Doom'd to enshrine some lovers cold remains, Or pour libations at some mystic fanes?
author: MacNally, Leonard, 1752-1820.
title: An heroic answer, from Richard Twiss, Esq: F.R.S. at Rotterdam, to Donna Teresa Pinna Ruiz, of Murica.

text: But why, my Pinna, kill me with thy tears, Thy causeless sorrows, and thy idle fears?
author: MacNally, Leonard, 1752-1820.
title: An heroic answer, from Richard Twiss, Esq: F.R.S. at Rotterdam, to Donna Teresa Pinna Ruiz, of Murica.

text: Yet still in dreams th' ideal terrours rise, Stain all my cloaths, and seal my blacken'd eyes; And oaken cudgels whistle in the wind, And sharp-toed shoes assail me from behind.

title: An heroic answer, from Richard Twiss, Esq: F.R.S. at Rotterdam, to Donna Teresa Pinna Ruiz, of Murica.

text: Thus shall each Belle a lovely L'ENCLOS prove, Drive Boys of future Cent'ries mad with love; The Marriage Table its degrees extend, And to our great, great Grandmother ascend.
author: Darwin, Erasmus, 1731-1802.
title: The golden age, a poetical epistle: from Erasmus D-n, M.D. to Thomas Beddoes, M.D.

text: Despis'd, detested, all shall wing their flight, And sink, no more to rise, in endless night!
author: Darwin, Erasmus, 1731-1802.
title: The golden age, a poetical epistle: from Erasmus D-n, M.D. to Thomas Beddoes, M.D.

text: While fluids, which a wondrous change betray, Ooze from the vernal bud, the summer spray, Differing from animals alone in name, (As Botanists already half exclaim).
author: Darwin, Erasmus, 1731-1802.
title: The golden age, a poetical epistle: from Erasmus D-n, M.D. to Thomas Beddoes, M.D.

text: No more the Despot view, whose mighty nods Shook nature, and proclaim'd him God of Gods; Drunk with applause who rais'd his rolling Eyes, And seem'd, whene'er he mov'd, to tread the skies!
author: Darwin, Erasmus, 1731-1802.
title: The golden age, a poetical epistle: from Erasmus D-n, M.D. to Thomas Beddoes, M.D.

text: View them like us inclin'd to watch or sleep, Like us to smile, and, ah! like us to weep!
author: Darwin, Erasmus, 1731-1802.
title: The golden age, a poetical epistle: from Erasmus D-n, M.D. to Thomas Beddoes, M.D.

text: No more the lazy Ox shall gormandize, And swell with fattening grass his monstrous size; No more trot round and round the groaning field, But tons of Beef our loaded Thickets yield!
author: Darwin, Erasmus, 1731-1802.
title: The golden age, a poetical epistle: from Erasmus D-n, M.D. to Thomas Beddoes, M.D.

text: The time may come When many a pious King in Christendom, Dash'd from his throne, and made Dame Fortune's Fool, Shall envy little Capet's cobbling stool!
author: Darwin, Erasmus, 1731-1802.
title: The golden age, a poetical epistle: from Erasmus D-n, M.D. to Thomas Beddoes, M.D.

text: See reverend Thames, who God of Rivers reigns, And winds meand'ring through our richest plains, To treat the Cits, that many a sixpence give Once in a week like Gentlemen to live, Resign his majesty of mud, and stream O'er strawberry beds in deluges of Cream!
author: Darwin, Erasmus, 1731-1802.
title: The golden age, a poetical epistle: from Erasmus D-n, M.D. to Thomas Beddoes, M.D.

text: No more immers'd in many a foreign dye Shall British wool be taught to blush and lie; But all our pastures glow with purple Rams, With scarlet Lambkins, and their yellow Dams!
author: Darwin, Erasmus, 1731-1802.
title: The golden age, a poetical epistle: from Erasmus D-n, M.D. to Thomas Beddoes, M.D.

text: Soon shall we view no more the glittering Things Bestarr'd, begarter'd, and befool'd by Kings; The pretty Twinklers that so sweetly shone, And deem'd their lovely lustre all their own!
author: Darwin, Erasmus, 1731-1802.
title: The golden age, a poetical epistle: from Erasmus D-n, M.D. to Thomas Beddoes, M.D.

text: No circling Gold his royal brow surrounds, A Yard of Room his sphere of Action bounds; His sole ambition and his prime pursuit, With skill a Shoe to patch, to stitch a Boot!
author: Darwin, Erasmus, 1731-1802.
title: The golden age, a poetical epistle: from Erasmus D-n, M.D. to Thomas Beddoes, M.D.

text: The sottish Jews, who in a God believ'd, And sometimes blessings, oftener plagues receiv'd, Shouted a Miracle, when on the ground Their boasted bread the greedy grumblers found: By no dry crusts shall Infidels be fed, Our soil producing Butter to our Bread!
author: Darwin, Erasmus, 1731-1802.
title: The golden age, a poetical epistle: from Erasmus D-n, M.D. to Thomas Beddoes, M.D.

text: Happy the Poet's lot, who can prolong, Till time shall be no more, his deathless song; And live himself to see his swelling name Roll, like a Snowball, gathering all its fame!
author: Darwin, Erasmus, 1731-1802.
title: The golden age, a poetical epistle: from Erasmus D-n, M.D. to Thomas Beddoes, M.D.

text: You Artists of the Aesculapian Tribe, Wou'd you, like Aesculapius's Self, Prescribe, Cure Maladies, and Maladies prevent?— Receive this Plant from your own Phoebus sent; Whence Life's nice Lamp in Temper is maintain'd, When Dim, Recruited; when too fierce, restrain'd.
author: Tate, Nahum, 1652-1715.
title: Panacea, a poem upon tea in two canto's [sic] / by N. Tate ...

text: You Statesmen, who in Storms the Publick Helm Wou'd Guide with Skill, and Save a sinking Realm, TEA, your Minerva, shall suggest such Sense, Such safe and sudden Turns of Thought dispense, That you, like her Ulysses, may Advise, And start Designs that shall the World surprise.
author: Tate, Nahum, 1652-1715.
title: Panacea, a poem upon tea in two canto's [sic] / by N. Tate ...

text: You that to Isis's Bank, or Cam retreat, Wou'd you prove worthy Sons of either Seat, And All in Learning's Commonwealth be Great?
author: Tate, Nahum, 1652-1715.
title: Panacea, a poem upon tea in two canto's [sic] / by N. Tate ...

text: The Wretches now to ev'ry Temple press In sighing Crowds, not to implore Redress, But own the Justice of their Doom, and crave The Favour only of a speedy Grave.
author: Tate, Nahum, 1652-1715.
title: Panacea, a poem upon tea in two canto's [sic] / by N. Tate ...

text: This Revolution, on the Wings of Fame, To the Fantastick Lovers Palace came; Whose Fairy-Joys transform'd to dismal Fright, They quit their Mansion of perpetual Light, To sculk in Caves and thickest shades of Night.
author: Tate, Nahum, 1652-1715.
title: Panacea, a poem upon tea in two canto's [sic] / by N. Tate ...

text: "When, deep in Briny Cells, my Nymphs and I "The Business of your Ocean-Empire ply, "Gods!
author: Tate, Nahum, 1652-1715.
title: Panacea, a poem upon tea in two canto's [sic] / by N. Tate ...

text: This strange Discov'ry both surpris'd the Gods, And set the Goddesses again at Odds; Whilst, to secure the Quiet of the Skies, The Thunderer once more was forc'd to rise.
author: Tate, Nahum, 1652-1715.
title: Panacea, a poem upon tea in two canto's [sic] / by N. Tate ...

text: But ah! this Eastern Glory to allay, The changing Scene must frantick Vice display; Such Pomp of Luxury as ne'er was seen 'Twixt rev'ling Anthony and Egypt's Queen.
author: Tate, Nahum, 1652-1715.
title: Panacea, a poem upon tea in two canto's [sic] / by N. Tate ...

text: The Delicacy of the Subject oblig'd me to treat it with some Gayety and Embellishment of Fancy, but especially with Decency, to make the Poem (like the Nepenthe on which 'tis writ) an Entertainment for the Ladies.
author: Tate, Nahum, 1652-1715.
title: Panacea, a poem upon tea in two canto's [sic] / by N. Tate ...

text: The Reader must pardon me this Trifling, 'tis paying Nonsense in its Own Coin; and if you would have better from me, you must stay till Wit comes in— as then you may depend on me, sufficient Authors (City Security) having vouch'd for my Honesty.
author: Tate, Nahum, 1652-1715.
title: Panacea, a poem upon tea in two canto's [sic] / by N. Tate ...

text: Now Banquets, Musick, Masques and Mimick Sport Are all the Business of th' Imperial Court; From which the Monarch never did remove, But to the dearer Solaces of Love.
author: Tate, Nahum, 1652-1715.
title: Panacea, a poem upon tea in two canto's [sic] / by N. Tate ...

text: Or, with Promethean Boldness, wou'd aspire To catch a Spark of that Celestial Fire That Crown'd the Royal Conquest, and could raise Juverne's Boyn above Scamander's Praise?
author: Tate, Nahum, 1652-1715.
title: Panacea, a poem upon tea in two canto's [sic] / by N. Tate ...

text: Quintilian was a musty old Pedant, and would have been pos'd with our new Figures of Speech—Iustness without Fire—Slavery to Sense, &c.
author: Tate, Nahum, 1652-1715.
title: Panacea, a poem upon tea in two canto's [sic] / by N. Tate ...

text: To do all this, at leaſt ſuch a part of them as can be begun with, a ſmall Sum will ſerve, and He ought to have Hopes of it, and of the Command.
author: Melfort, John Drummond, Earl of, 1649-1715.
title: A letter directed to the Right Honourable the Earl of Perth, governour to the Prince

text: That Mr. Carrell is qualified no man doubts, but in Society with the other, theſe who muſt be Inſtrumental will not truſt him as he ought, ſo that ſo long as the other is within diſtance of penetrating the Affairs, they will never think themſelves ſecure.
author: Melfort, John Drummond, Earl of, 1649-1715.
title: A letter directed to the Right Honourable the Earl of Perth, governour to the Prince

text: For ſince even in it, there is ſuch a Struggle againſt the Government, what would there be in a Free Parliament, which the P. of O. durſt never hazard to call.
author: Melfort, John Drummond, Earl of, 1649-1715.
title: A letter directed to the Right Honourable the Earl of Perth, governour to the Prince

text: So that the Diſaffection to the Government will encreaſe, and one may judge of the Nation in general, which is of an other Temper than this pretended Parliament, or rather Presbiterian Rabble, ill repreſenting the Nation.
author: Melfort, John Drummond, Earl of, 1649-1715.
title: A letter directed to the Right Honourable the Earl of Perth, governour to the Prince

text: Nothing is ſo dangerous as firſt to Determine what one will do, and then hear Reaſons againſt it, and immitate the deaf Adder who hearkens not to the Voice of the Charmer, let him Charm never ſo ſweatly.
author: Melfort, John Drummond, Earl of, 1649-1715.
title: A letter directed to the Right Honourable the Earl of Perth, governour to the Prince

text: The Places of Strength would be ſecured, and ſuch as can be put in Defence (without Expences) fortified.
author: Melfort, John Drummond, Earl of, 1649-1715.
title: A letter directed to the Right Honourable the Earl of Perth, governour to the Prince

text: Theſe being only Heads to be diſcourſed of, and much to be ſaid of every part, it is not to be thought that this Letter can carry a final Concluſion; for it may be upon Diſcourſe, I might change my Mind, or be more confirmed in, and ſee further.
author: Melfort, John Drummond, Earl of, 1649-1715.
title: A letter directed to the Right Honourable the Earl of Perth, governour to the Prince

text: This makes me inſiſt again to you, upon two things as appearing to me abſolutely neceſſary to put things upon a right foot.
author: Melfort, John Drummond, Earl of, 1649-1715.
title: A letter directed to the Right Honourable the Earl of Perth, governour to the Prince

text: And the Second is of the laſt Uſe, both to their Majeſties and the Prince, which is the Eſtabliſhing of ſuch a Number, under no Qualification, to talk of their Affairs in their Majeſties Preſence, with whom we can freely converſe and propoſe what may be for their Majeſties Service.
author: Melfort, John Drummond, Earl of, 1649-1715.
title: A letter directed to the Right Honourable the Earl of Perth, governour to the Prince

text: SInce I promiſt to put in Writing what we had not time to talk fully of, I am ſet down to it in the Morning, that my Letter may be ready for the Meſſenger if any call.
author: Melfort, John Drummond, Earl of, 1649-1715.
title: A letter directed to the Right Honourable the Earl of Perth, governour to the Prince

text: If ſo I ſhall ſhew what I think to be done in it, if otherwiſe I ſhall ſave the Pains.
author: Melfort, John Drummond, Earl of, 1649-1715.
title: A letter directed to the Right Honourable the Earl of Perth, governour to the Prince

text: The Army who are and ever were well-affected, are to be gained by Money, and a little goes a great way with them.
author: Melfort, John Drummond, Earl of, 1649-1715.
title: A letter directed to the Right Honourable the Earl of Perth, governour to the Prince

text: The Firſt is the removing of all Impediments out of the way, and ſending all Suſpected Perſons to Champagne or Burgundy, according to their Gouſt.
author: Melfort, John Drummond, Earl of, 1649-1715.
title: A letter directed to the Right Honourable the Earl of Perth, governour to the Prince

text: Be quick, or else thou'lt spend thy Breath in vain; Old Age is cross—thou must not him detain.
title: The chase: a pastoral drama of two acts:

text: Nay, hold thee there—don't fancy she is thine— My Right is best, because I sung the last.
title: The chase: a pastoral drama of two acts:

text: Yes: I was seized with a sudden Chill, And, fearful of some Danger, left the Chase— But, praise the Gods! my Health returns apace.
title: The chase: a pastoral drama of two acts:

text: No such Thing; Besides, the Mare's with Foal—thou can'st not go— Get thee to work.
title: The chase: a pastoral drama of two acts:

text: "Tho' Sorrow for awhile disturbs thy Peace, "Submit to Patience, and thy Pains shall cease."
title: The chase: a pastoral drama of two acts:

text: Away, away, No more Delay, The Hounds are on the Scent: Mount, mount your Steeds, Actaeon speeds, And gains the steep Ascent.
title: The chase: a pastoral drama of two acts:

text: Submit to Care, And ne'er despair, All Pains shall have an End; The virtuous Mind Shall ever find In Heav'n a tender Friend.
title: The chase: a pastoral drama of two acts:

text: How his Eyes Are fix'd on mine—what strange Commotions rise Within me—ev'ry Word he utters shakes My wond'ring Soul!
title: The chase: a pastoral drama of two acts:

text: Thief, hold thy Tongue—or I can something blab— I can—that will thy Reputation stab.
title: The chase: a pastoral drama of two acts:

text: Oh! did the tim'rous Fair One know The rending Pangs I feel, With Love her frozen Heart wou'd glow, And ev'ry Anguish heal.
title: The chase: a pastoral drama of two acts:

text: I will not trouble thee—If 'tis not far The Walk may be of Service to me—Hah!
title: The chase: a pastoral drama of two acts:

text: Little Cupids, hear my Pray'r, Commis'rate Woes that know no Cure; To the beauteous Maid repair, Relate the Pangs that I endure: Tell her, in the softest Sighs, It is to her I owe them all: Gently whisper, "Mopsus dies!"
title: The chase: a pastoral drama of two acts:

text: The same which forc'd Tibistheus to the Act, Forc'd also me—but Heav'n chose to retract Her former Blessings to revenge the Deed.
title: The chase: a pastoral drama of two acts:

text: Meanwhile all pale th' expiring poet laid, And sunk his awful head, While vocal shadows pleasing dreams prolong; For so, his sick'ning spirits to release, They pour'd the balm of visionary peace.
author: Mason, William, 1725-1797.
title: Musæus: a monody to the memory of Mr. Pope: in imitation of Milton's Lycidas.

text: But now dun clouds the welkin 'gan to streak; And now down-dropt the larks, and ceas'd their strain: They ceas'd, and with them ceas'd the shepherd swain.
author: Mason, William, 1725-1797.
title: Musæus: a monody to the memory of Mr. Pope: in imitation of Milton's Lycidas.

text: "Various this peaceful scene; this mineral roof; "This 'semblage meet of coral, ore, and shell; "These pointed crystals fair, mid each obscure "Bright glist'ring; all these slowly-dripping rills, "That tinkling stray amid the cooly cave.
author: Mason, William, 1725-1797.
title: Musæus: a monody to the memory of Mr. Pope: in imitation of Milton's Lycidas.

text: "Accept this gratulation: may it chear "Thy sinking soul; nor these corporeal ills "Ought daunt thee, or appall.
author: Mason, William, 1725-1797.
title: Musæus: a monody to the memory of Mr. Pope: in imitation of Milton's Lycidas.

text: Or have they deign'd to play, Where Camus winds along his broider'd vale, Feeding each white pink, and each daisie pied, That mingling paint his rushy-fringed side?
author: Mason, William, 1725-1797.
title: Musæus: a monody to the memory of Mr. Pope: in imitation of Milton's Lycidas.

text: But ah! my Muse, how will thy voice express Th' immortal strain, harmonious, as it flow'd?
author: Mason, William, 1725-1797.
title: Musæus: a monody to the memory of Mr. Pope: in imitation of Milton's Lycidas.

text: "O! in that strain, if all of wit had flow'd, "All music warbled, and all beauty glow'd; "Had liveliest nature, happiest art combin'd; "That lent each grace, and This each grace refin'd, "Alas! how little were my proudest boast!
author: Mason, William, 1725-1797.
title: Musæus: a monody to the memory of Mr. Pope: in imitation of Milton's Lycidas.

text: I meanwhile, "To sooth thee in these irksome hours of pain, "Approach thy visitant, with mortal laud "To praise thee mortal.
author: Mason, William, 1725-1797.
title: Musæus: a monody to the memory of Mr. Pope: in imitation of Milton's Lycidas.

text: Forego each vain excuse, And haste to Thames's shores; for Thames shall join Our sad society, and passing mourn, Letting cold tears bedew his silver urn.
author: Mason, William, 1725-1797.
title: Musæus: a monody to the memory of Mr. Pope: in imitation of Milton's Lycidas.

text: Such tribute paid, again ye may repair To what lov'd haunt you whilom did elect; Whether Lycaeus, or that mountain fair Trim Maenalus, with piny verdure deckt.
author: Mason, William, 1725-1797.
title: Musæus: a monody to the memory of Mr. Pope: in imitation of Milton's Lycidas.

text: "Yet rede aright, and if this friendly lay "Thou nathless judgest all too slight and vain, "Let my well-meaning mend my ill essay: "So may I greet thee with a nobler strain, "When soon we meet for aye, in yon star-sprinkled plain."
author: Mason, William, 1725-1797.
title: Musæus: a monody to the memory of Mr. Pope: in imitation of Milton's Lycidas.

text: How, midst yon grot, each silver trickling spring Wander'd the shelly channels all among; While as the coral roof did softly ring, Responsive to their sweetly-doleful song.
author: Mason, William, 1725-1797.
title: Musæus: a monody to the memory of Mr. Pope: in imitation of Milton's Lycidas.

text: Poet, in whom conjoin'd "All that to ear, or heart, or head, could yield "Rapture; harmonious, manly, clear, sublime.
author: Mason, William, 1725-1797.
title: Musæus: a monody to the memory of Mr. Pope: in imitation of Milton's Lycidas.

text: Thou, O God, art Righteous, but we have done exceeding wickedly in following the imaginations of our fooliſh Hearts, to offend againſt thy holy Laws: We have provoked moſt juſtly thy Wrath and Indignation by our wicked Works; and have moſt grievouſly ſinned againſt our own Souls.
author: Raymond, George, A.M.
title: A short and plain account of religion for the instruction of families, by being often read in them : recommended especially to those under his charge / by Geo. Raymond ...

text: When through the neglect of God, and abuſe of themſelves, Men had depraved this Religion, by wicked Lives and Idolatrous Worſhip; they became Reprobate in their Minds, and vile in their Affections; and ſunk into a degenerate and forlorn Eſtate; that was as Wretched as it was Sinful.
author: Raymond, George, A.M.
title: A short and plain account of religion for the instruction of families, by being often read in them : recommended especially to those under his charge / by Geo. Raymond ...

text: For we are his off ſpring, and his eternal power and God-head are ſeen from the Creation of the World, ſo that we are without excuſe.
author: Raymond, George, A.M.
title: A short and plain account of religion for the instruction of families, by being often read in them : recommended especially to those under his charge / by Geo. Raymond ...

text: We can neither blame the Doctrine, nor refute the Proofs of it; but Men become unbelievers by being reſolvedly wicked; for they being Enemies to the Truth, will not receive it.
author: Raymond, George, A.M.
title: A short and plain account of religion for the instruction of families, by being often read in them : recommended especially to those under his charge / by Geo. Raymond ...

text: For Men by Virtue improve their Capacity of future Happineſs: but Vice lays a Foundation only for Miſery and Wretchedneſs.
author: Raymond, George, A.M.
title: A short and plain account of religion for the instruction of families, by being often read in them : recommended especially to those under his charge / by Geo. Raymond ...

text: If we thus think of God our Maker, and of our ſelves his Creatures, we muſt ſee the Reaſon and neceſſity of keeping the Laws of our Creation; which require us to be and do what is right and meet, towards God, to our fellow Creatures, and to our ſelves.
author: Raymond, George, A.M.
title: A short and plain account of religion for the instruction of families, by being often read in them : recommended especially to those under his charge / by Geo. Raymond ...

text: YOƲ have here laid before you a Scheme of Religion, or the Subſtance of thoſe things which the Miniſters of Chriſt are continually inculcating; and in the Method you are wont to hear them from me.
author: Raymond, George, A.M.
title: A short and plain account of religion for the instruction of families, by being often read in them : recommended especially to those under his charge / by Geo. Raymond ...

text: By the one, Baptiſm, we are made Diſciples of Chriſt, to learn that Religion which God the Father Taught by his Son, and confirmed by the holy Ghoſt: and oblige our ſelves to the Study, Profeſſion, and Practice thereof.
author: Raymond, George, A.M.
title: A short and plain account of religion for the instruction of families, by being often read in them : recommended especially to those under his charge / by Geo. Raymond ...

text: That we ought to ſtudy the Divine Nature, and meditate upon the Excellencies thereof, and to acknowledge them by ſuitable affections of Reverence, Love and Truſt; to give unto God ſupream Honour and Worſhip; and to ſubmit our ſelves to his moſt wiſe and holy Will.
author: Raymond, George, A.M.
title: A short and plain account of religion for the instruction of families, by being often read in them : recommended especially to those under his charge / by Geo. Raymond ...

text: O God the Father Almighty Maker of Heaven and Earth, we thy Creatures fall down with all humility to Worſhip thee; in whoſe Hands our Breath is, and before whom are all our Ways.
author: Raymond, George, A.M.
title: A short and plain account of religion for the instruction of families, by being often read in them : recommended especially to those under his charge / by Geo. Raymond ...

text: And what is more fit and juſt both in it ſelf, and in order to ſo great an end, than that the Righteous Will of God be heartily done by us?
author: Raymond, George, A.M.
title: A short and plain account of religion for the instruction of families, by being often read in them : recommended especially to those under his charge / by Geo. Raymond ...

text: That we be content with our Condition of Life, and bear with an even and calm Spirit the Viciſſitudes, Misfortunes, and Afflictions which are common to Men, fearing more to do than to ſuffer evil, and ſtudying to adorn every Lot, which is Fortitude and Patience.
author: Raymond, George, A.M.
title: A short and plain account of religion for the instruction of families, by being often read in them : recommended especially to those under his charge / by Geo. Raymond ...

text: Every one in his turn needeth forbearance and forgiveneſs; and all Men commend in others, and expect from them, Candour, and Gentleneſs, and Kindneſs, and other ſuch like Fruits of Sincere Benevolence.
author: Raymond, George, A.M.
title: A short and plain account of religion for the instruction of families, by being often read in them : recommended especially to those under his charge / by Geo. Raymond ...

text: Let the Birth be in the Seventh Hour of Night, add to that the Twelve Hours of the Day, and that Seventh Hour will be the Nineteenth, from the Suns Riſing: Then add, multiply, and work, as in the former Method.
author: Manilius, Marcus.
title: The five books of Mr. Manilius containing a system of the ancient astronomy and astrology : together with the philosophy of the Stoicks / done into English verse with notes by Mr. Tho. Creech.

text: For who can think that when the 10 Sun doth riſe He's born anew, or when He ſets He dies?
author: Manilius, Marcus.
title: The five books of Mr. Manilius containing a system of the ancient astronomy and astrology : together with the philosophy of the Stoicks / done into English verse with notes by Mr. Tho. Creech.

text: And to his Births the World oblig'd ſhall owe Spheres, Cycles, Orbs, and turn new Skies below.
author: Manilius, Marcus.
title: The five books of Mr. Manilius containing a system of the ancient astronomy and astrology : together with the philosophy of the Stoicks / done into English verse with notes by Mr. Tho. Creech.

text: So that begin with Piſces, and then you find two Day Signs together, and then two Night Signs, and ſo in Order.
author: Manilius, Marcus.
title: The five books of Mr. Manilius containing a system of the ancient astronomy and astrology : together with the philosophy of the Stoicks / done into English verse with notes by Mr. Tho. Creech.

text: Oppos'd to Aries, Libra's Stars appear With the like power to ſway the rouling Year, She equals Day and Night: But ſoon the Scale O'repois'd by Darkneſs, lets the Night prevail; And Day, that lengthned in the Summer's height, Shortens 'till Winter, and is loſt in Night.
author: Manilius, Marcus.
title: The five books of Mr. Manilius containing a system of the ancient astronomy and astrology : together with the philosophy of the Stoicks / done into English verse with notes by Mr. Tho. Creech.

text: The ſecond Forty Courſes of the Sun, And two beſtows, and when that term is done, The Man goes off, e're half his race be run.
author: Manilius, Marcus.
title: The five books of Mr. Manilius containing a system of the ancient astronomy and astrology : together with the philosophy of the Stoicks / done into English verse with notes by Mr. Tho. Creech.

text: How pale thy Look? and how thy Spirit fled In a deep ſigh, and hover'd round thy Head?
author: Manilius, Marcus.
title: The five books of Mr. Manilius containing a system of the ancient astronomy and astrology : together with the philosophy of the Stoicks / done into English verse with notes by Mr. Tho. Creech.

text: Whilſt Brothers poyſon, with a ſmiling Face They mix the Cup, and kill where they embrace: No place is ſafe, no Temple yields Defence Againſt ſecret Stabs, or open Violence; And many a ſlaughter'd Prieſt profanely dies On the ſame Altar with his Sacrifice.
author: Manilius, Marcus.
title: The five books of Mr. Manilius containing a system of the ancient astronomy and astrology : together with the philosophy of the Stoicks / done into English verse with notes by Mr. Tho. Creech.

text: And yet how often from the Piles retire, E'en 14 fly themſelves, and wander thro' the Fire?
author: Manilius, Marcus.
title: The five books of Mr. Manilius containing a system of the ancient astronomy and astrology : together with the philosophy of the Stoicks / done into English verse with notes by Mr. Tho. Creech.

text: To him the Flouds in ſpacious windings turn, One Fountain flows from cold Aquarius Urn; And meets the other where they joyn their Streams One Chanel keep, and mix the Starry Beams.
author: Manilius, Marcus.
title: The five books of Mr. Manilius containing a system of the ancient astronomy and astrology : together with the philosophy of the Stoicks / done into English verse with notes by Mr. Tho. Creech.

text: In his vaſt Head immerſt in boundleſs ſpheres Three Stars leſs bright, but yet as great, he bears.
author: Manilius, Marcus.
title: The five books of Mr. Manilius containing a system of the ancient astronomy and astrology : together with the philosophy of the Stoicks / done into English verse with notes by Mr. Tho. Creech.

text: For one appearance in another lies, Conceals its Powers, and Acts in diſguiſe; And that which Lurks, and ſubtly interferes Hath different Powers from that which then appears.
author: Manilius, Marcus.
title: The five books of Mr. Manilius containing a system of the ancient astronomy and astrology : together with the philosophy of the Stoicks / done into English verse with notes by Mr. Tho. Creech.

text: Succeſsleſs Vertue ſinks whilſt Vice prevails, And Folly wins the Prize when Prudence fails: He argues ill that from the Fortune draws The goodneſs or the badneſs of a Cauſe: Succeſs or Merit do not always Crown, Midſt good and bad Men they are blindly thrown, Without Reſpect, ſixt fatally on One.
author: Manilius, Marcus.
title: The five books of Mr. Manilius containing a system of the ancient astronomy and astrology : together with the philosophy of the Stoicks / done into English verse with notes by Mr. Tho. Creech.

title: An epistle from a lady in England: to a gentleman at Avignon.

text: The Pope himself, surrounded with Alarms, To France his Bulls, to Corfu sends his Arms, And though He hears his Darling Son's Complaint, Can hardly spare one Tutelary Saint, But lists them all to guard his own Abodes, And into Ready Money coyns his Gods.
author: Tickell, Mr. (Thomas), 1686-1740.
title: An epistle from a lady in England: to a gentleman at Avignon.

text: Should blinded Friends thy doubtful Conduct blame, Great Brunswick's Virtues will secure thy Fame: Say, these invite thee to approach his Throne, And own the Monarch, Heav'n vouchsafes to own.
author: Tickell, Mr. (Thomas), 1686-1740.
title: An epistle from a lady in England: to a gentleman at Avignon.

text: TO Thee, dear Rover, and thy vanquish'd Friends, The Health, she wants, thy gentle Chloe sends: Though much You suffer, think I suffer more, Worse than an Exile on my Native Shore.
author: Tickell, Mr. (Thomas), 1686-1740.
title: An epistle from a lady in England: to a gentleman at Avignon.

text: Companions in your Master's Flight you roame, Unenvy'd by your haughty Foes at home; For-ever near the Royal Outlaw's side You share his Fortunes, and his Hopes divide, On glorious Schemes, and Thoughts of Empire dwell, And with Imaginary Titles swell.
author: Tickell, Mr. (Thomas), 1686-1740.
title: An epistle from a lady in England: to a gentleman at Avignon.

text: Then mourn not, hapless Prince, thy Kingdoms lost, A Crown, tho' late, thy sacred Brow may boast; Heav'n seems through Us thy Empire to decree, Those who Win Hearts, have giv'n their Hearts to Thee.
author: Tickell, Mr. (Thomas), 1686-1740.
title: An epistle from a lady in England: to a gentleman at Avignon.

text: The Fate of James with pitying Eyes I view, And wish my Homage were not Brunswick's Due: To James my Passions and my Weakness guide, But Reason sways me to the Victor's Side.
author: Tickell, Mr. (Thomas), 1686-1740.
title: An epistle from a lady in England: to a gentleman at Avignon.

text: The World, convinc'd, thy Reasons will approve, Say this to Them; but swear to Me 'twas Love.
author: Tickell, Mr. (Thomas), 1686-1740.
title: An epistle from a lady in England: to a gentleman at Avignon.

text: Or wilt not Thou, for thy lov'd Chloe's sake, Tir'd out at length, submit to Fate's Decree?

title: Poetæ Britannici a poem satyrical and panegyrical.

title: Poetæ Britannici a poem satyrical and panegyrical.

text: For these, if well observ'd, can strictly shew, In charming Numbers what is false, what true, And Teach more good than Hobbs or Locke can do.

text: Our HOGARTH here a grand improver shines, And nobly on the gen'ral plan refines; He, like himself, o'erleaps the servile bound; Worth is his mark, wherever Worth is found.
author: Churchill, Charles, 1731-1764.
title: An epistle to William Hogarth: By C. Churchill.

text: With so much merit, and so much success, With so much pow'r to curse, so much to bless, Would He have been Man's friend, instead of foe, HOGARTH had been a little God below.
author: Churchill, Charles, 1731-1764.
title: An epistle to William Hogarth: By C. Churchill.

text: Why then, like savage Giants, fam'd of old, Of whom in Scripture Story we are told, Dost Thou in cruelty that strength employ, Which Nature meant to save, not to destroy, Why dost Thou, all in horrid pomp array'd, Sit grinning o'er the ruins Thou hast made?
author: Churchill, Charles, 1731-1764.
title: An epistle to William Hogarth: By C. Churchill.

text: But, when the work was finish'd, could thy mind So partial be, and to herself so blind, What with contempt All view'd, to view with awe, Nor see those faults which ev'ry Blockhead saw?
author: Churchill, Charles, 1731-1764.
title: An epistle to William Hogarth: By C. Churchill.

text: Hence, Dotard, to thy closet, shut thee in, By deep repentance wash away thy sin, From haunts of men to shame and sorrow fly; And, on the verge of death, learn how to die.
author: Churchill, Charles, 1731-1764.
title: An epistle to William Hogarth: By C. Churchill.

text: But if thy spirit, resolute in ill, Once having err'd, persists in error still, Go on at large, no longer worth my care, And freely vent those blasphemies in air, Which I would stamp as false, tho' on the tongue Of Angels, the injurious slander hung.
author: Churchill, Charles, 1731-1764.
title: An epistle to William Hogarth: By C. Churchill.

text: O! that I here could that rare Virtue mean Which scorns the rule of Envy, Pride and Spleen, Which springs not from the labour'd Works of Art, But hath its rise from Nature in the heart, Which in itself with happiness is crown'd, And spreads with joy the blessing all around!
author: Churchill, Charles, 1731-1764.
title: An epistle to William Hogarth: By C. Churchill.

text: On this foundation shalt thou stand or fall— Prove that in One, which you have charg'd on All.
author: Churchill, Charles, 1731-1764.
title: An epistle to William Hogarth: By C. Churchill.

text: Loud as the Drum, which spreading terrour round From emptiness acquires the pow'r of sound, Doth not the voice of NORTON strike thy ear, And the pale MANSFIELD chill thy soul with fear?
author: Churchill, Charles, 1731-1764.
title: An epistle to William Hogarth: By C. Churchill.

text: None but the damn'd, and amongst them the worst, Those who for double guilt are doubly curs'd, Can be so lost; nor can the worst of all At once into such deep damnation fall; By painful slow degrees they reach this crime, Which e'en in Hell must be a work of time.
author: Churchill, Charles, 1731-1764.
title: An epistle to William Hogarth: By C. Churchill.

text: SURE 'tis a curse which angry Fates impose, To mortify man's arrogance, that Those Who're fashion'd of some better sort of clay, Much sooner than the common herd decay.
author: Churchill, Charles, 1731-1764.
title: An epistle to William Hogarth: By C. Churchill.

text: Might this be true, had we so far fill'd up The measure of our crimes, and from the cup Of guilt so deeply drank, as not to find, Thirsting for sin, one drop, one dreg behind, Quick ruin must involve this flaming ball, And Providence in Justice crush us all.
author: Churchill, Charles, 1731-1764.
title: An epistle to William Hogarth: By C. Churchill.

text: But let not Youth, to insolence allied, In heat of blood, in full career of pride, Possess'd of GENIUS, with unhallow'd rage Mock the infirmities of rev'rend age.
author: Churchill, Charles, 1731-1764.
title: An epistle to William Hogarth: By C. Churchill.

text: And tho' the Voice be not Audible, nor the Direction always Perceptable (or Diſcernable) to Senſe; yet it is equally as Real as if a Man heard the Voice ſaying, This is the Way, walk in it.

text: But yet in theſe Diſorders ſomething lies, That's worth thy Notice, out of which the Wiſe May trace and find that Juſt and Powerful HAND, That Secretly, but Surely, doth Command; And manage theſe Diſtempers with that Skill; That while they ſeem to Croſs they Act HIS Will.
author: Hale, Matthew, Sir, 1609-1676.
title: Some necessary and important considerations, (to be consider'd of by all sorts of people) Taken out of (that late worthy and renowned judge) Sr Matthew Hale's account of The good steward. By J.P.

text: Let not my Life, or Name, be known unto The Grandees of the Times; Toſs'd to and fro, By Cenſures or Applauſe: But let my Age Slide gently By, not Over-thwart the Stage Of Publick Action; Unheard, Unſeen, And Unconcern'd, as if I ne'er had been.
author: Hale, Matthew, Sir, 1609-1676.
title: Some necessary and important considerations, (to be consider'd of by all sorts of people) Taken out of (that late worthy and renowned judge) Sr Matthew Hale's account of The good steward. By J.P.

text: In Actions to be Done or Omitted, I have always Adviſed with It, and taken Its Advice; I have neither Stifled, nor Forced, nor Bribed It; but gave It a free Liberty to Adviſe and Speak out, and a free Subjection of my Will, Purpoſes, and Actions to It.
author: Hale, Matthew, Sir, 1609-1676.
title: Some necessary and important considerations, (to be consider'd of by all sorts of people) Taken out of (that late worthy and renowned judge) Sr Matthew Hale's account of The good steward. By J.P.

text: When She was Pleaſed, and gave me Good Words, I was Glad; for I eſteemed Her as a Glaſs that repreſented to my Soul the Favour or Diſpleaſure of GOD Himſelf, and how HE ſtood affected towards me.
author: Hale, Matthew, Sir, 1609-1676.
title: Some necessary and important considerations, (to be consider'd of by all sorts of people) Taken out of (that late worthy and renowned judge) Sr Matthew Hale's account of The good steward. By J.P.

text: And the very ſame Conſideration hath always gone a long with me, in reference to the Labour of THY Creatures.
author: Hale, Matthew, Sir, 1609-1676.
title: Some necessary and important considerations, (to be consider'd of by all sorts of people) Taken out of (that late worthy and renowned judge) Sr Matthew Hale's account of The good steward. By J.P.

text: Makes thee to ſet an Equal Eſtimate On this Uncertain World; and a Juſt Rate On that to Come: It bids thee Wait and Stay, Until thy MASTER Calls; And then with Joy To entertain it: Such a Change as this, Renders thy Loſs, thy Gain; Improves thy Bliſs.
author: Hale, Matthew, Sir, 1609-1676.
title: Some necessary and important considerations, (to be consider'd of by all sorts of people) Taken out of (that late worthy and renowned judge) Sr Matthew Hale's account of The good steward. By J.P.

text: Give me ſome mean obſcure Receſs; a Sphere Out of the Road of Bus'neſs, or the Fear Of Falling Lower; where I ſweetly may My Self, and dear Retirement, ſtill Enjoy.

title: Some necessary and important considerations, (to be consider'd of by all sorts of people) Taken out of (that late worthy and renowned judge) Sr Matthew Hale's account of The good steward. By J.P.

text: I have not only looked upon THY Bleſſings and Bounty, in Lending me THY own Creatures for my Uſe; but I have ſought unto THEE for a Bleſſing upon them, in my Uſe of them.
author: Hale, Matthew, Sir, 1609-1676.
title: Some necessary and important considerations, (to be consider'd of by all sorts of people) Taken out of (that late worthy and renowned judge) Sr Matthew Hale's account of The good steward. By J.P.

text: Obſerve that Silver Thread, that ſteers and bends The worſt of all Diſorders to ſuch Ends, That ſpeak HIS Juſtice, Goodneſs, Providence, Who cloſely guides it by HIS Influence.
author: Hale, Matthew, Sir, 1609-1676.
title: Some necessary and important considerations, (to be consider'd of by all sorts of people) Taken out of (that late worthy and renowned judge) Sr Matthew Hale's account of The good steward. By J.P.

text: I can call my own Experience to witneſs, That even in the External Actions of my whole Life, I was never diſappointed of the beſt Guidance and Direction, when I have, in Humility and Sincerity, implored the Secret Direction, and Guidance, of the Divine Wiſdom.
author: Hale, Matthew, Sir, 1609-1676.
title: Some necessary and important considerations, (to be consider'd of by all sorts of people) Taken out of (that late worthy and renowned judge) Sr Matthew Hale's account of The good steward. By J.P.

text: LET him that will, Aſcend the Tottering Seat Of Courtly Grandeur, and become as Great As are his Mounting Wiſhes: As for me, Let ſweet Repoſe and Reſt, my Portion be.
author: Hale, Matthew, Sir, 1609-1676.
title: Some necessary and important considerations, (to be consider'd of by all sorts of people) Taken out of (that late worthy and renowned judge) Sr Matthew Hale's account of The good steward. By J.P.

text: And thus, whilſt I ſhall paſs my Silent Days In Shady Privacy, free from the Noiſe And Buſtles of the World: Then, then ſhall I A Good, Old, Innocent Plebeian, dye.
author: Hale, Matthew, Sir, 1609-1676.

text: But certainly there is a Way left to give to God that Honour which is due to Him; otherwise, it were to little purpose to say, Them that honour me I will honour.

text: But there are other Sins, as Profaneness and Contempt of God and Religion, Hypocrisy, Idolatry, &c. and of such which Work as Moral Causes, God himself is the only Judge, when the Measure of their Iniquity is filled up.

text: But there are others (I wish I could only say there had been) who are Profane out of Principles; who not only Neglect Religion, but Despise it; and Affront and Ridicule it, as far as they dare with regard to their own Safety.

title: Reformation of manners the true way of honouring God with the necessity of putting the laws in execution against vice and profaneness : in a sermon preached at White-hall / by the late Right Reverend

text: And so it implies, that the Welfare and Reputation, and flourishing Condition of such, depends upon their Zeal and Concernment for God and Religion.

text: The People of the Plantations have very calmly ſubmitted to the Duties laid upon them by the Government here, tho they have no Repreſentatives in Parliament, which is directly againſt the Engliſh Conſtitution.

text: The Anſwer is ready: It was Money raiſed by the Inhabitants of Barbadoes for their own Uſe; but has been ever ſince it was raiſed taken from them.

text: But when they raiſe Money in the Colonies for their own Defence, and for their own Uſe; to have that tranſmitted from them to England, ſeems to be very hard, and altogether repugnant to the Freedom that every Engliſhman is born to.
title: A letter to S C.M. a member of Parliament from an inhabitant of the island of Barbadoes.

text: Sir, I lay theſe things before you, that as they are all certain Truths, and upon Enquiry will be found ſo, you will be pleaſed to give your helping Hand for the Removal of ſuch Grievances, when they come to be complained of in a proper Place.
title: A letter to S C.M. a member of Parliament from an inhabitant of the island of Barbadoes.

text: This then would not only render Barbadoes impregnable, but would be a great Security for the reſt of the Sugar Iſlands, which otherwiſe may be in great danger; and if the Plantation.

text: Sir, your coming in with your Intereſt to ſave a People under ſuch Hardſhips, and in danger upon ſo many Accounts, in which good Work all Impartial and Juſt Men will join with you, will carry its Reward with it, and will be very acceptable to all good Men, eſpecially thoſe concerned.

text: "Oh, if we seize with Skill the coming Hour, "And re-invest us with the Robe of Pow'r, "Rule while we live!
author: Bentley, R. (Richard), 1708-1782.
title: Patriotism, a mock-heroic. In five cantos:

text: "Our empty Niches know us all no more; "Still the State Truncheon flys our eager Grasp, "And Calumny is at its latest Gasp.
author: Bentley, R. (Richard), 1708-1782.
title: Patriotism, a mock-heroic. In five cantos:

text: Up the steep Height an Iron Causeway tends, And at the Footstool of the Monarch ends; Here FOLLY pass'd, and as she climb'd the Mound, Hollow and loud her shuffling Steps resound.
author: Bentley, R. (Richard), 1708-1782.
title: Patriotism, a mock-heroic. In five cantos:

text: And now in general Discourse they join, So tipsy with the Healths, not with the Wine, That Custom, Reason, Fact, are chang'd and chopp'd, To all that Modern Patriots adopt.
author: Bentley, R. (Richard), 1708-1782.
title: Patriotism, a mock-heroic. In five cantos:

text: "'Twere needless here to tell, what yet you see "Draws its conceal'd, dim, Origin from me— "The Rage of Faction, when each Nerve it moves, "He who does not disclaim, be sure approves.
author: Bentley, R. (Richard), 1708-1782.
title: Patriotism, a mock-heroic. In five cantos:

text: On ev'ry Side, and scatter'd ev'ry Way, Her finish'd Labours in wild Parcels lay Unrang'd by their Importance, equal here The Loss of Battles, or at Whist appear; A Statesman chang'd, or Lodging newly lett, Empires transferr'd, or Fashions out of Date.
author: Bentley, R. (Richard), 1708-1782.
title: Patriotism, a mock-heroic. In five cantos:

text: "Thus far, indeed, Success has crown'd our Arms, "BUTE quits; nor shaken with our fierce Alarms, "For who our Roar and Riot would regard, "That in his Conscience seeks for his Reward?
author: Bentley, R. (Richard), 1708-1782.
title: Patriotism, a mock-heroic. In five cantos:

text: "Here then we stick; but still of Hope a Gleam "Points thro' the dusky Thought its trembling Beam, "The Deities, from Heav'n self-exil'd, meet "At a grand Council, and a grander Treat, "To-morrow.
author: Bentley, R. (Richard), 1708-1782.
title: Patriotism, a mock-heroic. In five cantos:

text: To please the Mob, our Fleets their Canvas strain, And Expeditions hide the wond'ring Main, The Main more wond'ring wafts us back, alas!
author: Bentley, R. (Richard), 1708-1782.
title: Patriotism, a mock-heroic. In five cantos:

text: The Goddess, no Confusion to create, Impatient as she was, thought fit to wait: Civilities are ne'er so duly paid To any Folks, as when we want their Aid.
author: Bentley, R. (Richard), 1708-1782.
title: Patriotism, a mock-heroic. In five cantos:

text: There round a Chariot, thro' the parted Throng, In Bronze the threat'ning Bruisers march'd along; The decent Mob, such Fear within them dwelt, Retire to Distance, and forbear to pelt.
author: Bentley, R. (Richard), 1708-1782.
title: Patriotism, a mock-heroic. In five cantos:

text: Tribunes, and Ephori, and Demagogues, By Men call'd Patriots, but by Gods plain Rogues; Such as, provided they themselves grew great, Had no Objection to subvert a State.

title: Creüsa, Queen of Athens: A tragedy. As it is acted at the Theatre Royal in Drury-Lane by His Majesty's servants. Written by Mr. William Whitehead.

text: Had I known Nicander was your Lord, by Earth and Heaven, I would have rais'd all Athens in his Cause,; Nay, been a Rebel to the best of Masters, Ere the dear Pledge of your unspotted Loves Should thus have fallen untimely.
author: Whitehead, William, 1715-1785.
title: Creüsa, Queen of Athens: A tragedy. As it is acted at the Theatre Royal in Drury-Lane by His Majesty's servants. Written by Mr. William Whitehead.

text: Bred up in Shades, poor Youth, He never knew the Arts of base Mankind, Nor should he share their Punishment.
author: Whitehead, William, 1715-1785.
title: Creüsa, Queen of Athens: A tragedy. As it is acted at the Theatre Royal in Drury-Lane by His Majesty's servants. Written by Mr. William Whitehead.

text: In secret she assuag'd My piercing Pangs, and to Nicander's Arms In secret she convey'd the wretched Infant.
author: Whitehead, William, 1715-1785.
title: Creüsa, Queen of Athens: A tragedy. As it is acted at the Theatre Royal in Drury-Lane by His Majesty's servants. Written by Mr. William Whitehead.

text: In Sport he spake, but at his Words a Glow Of sudden Joy spread o'er her Face, her Tongue Forgot Restraint, and in his Praise grew lavish: Then stopp'd again, and hesitating strove To check its Zeal, as fearful to betray Some hidden Transport.
author: Whitehead, William, 1715-1785.
title: Creüsa, Queen of Athens: A tragedy. As it is acted at the Theatre Royal in Drury-Lane by His Majesty's servants. Written by Mr. William Whitehead.

text: These were the Lessons of thy private Life, This I have told thee oft, but my fond Tongue Runs o'er its former Precepts, and forgets Thou now must mount a Throne; a larger Scene Of Duty opens.
author: Whitehead, William, 1715-1785.
title: Creüsa, Queen of Athens: A tragedy. As it is acted at the Theatre Royal in Drury-Lane by His Majesty's servants. Written by Mr. William Whitehead.

text: How has he been beset, and how escap'd! —Where is my Boy, for I may own him now, And clasp him to my Breast, no more Aletes, The sage Instructor of a Youth unknown, But the dear Father weeping o'er his Child.
author: Whitehead, William, 1715-1785.
title: Creüsa, Queen of Athens: A tragedy. As it is acted at the Theatre Royal in Drury-Lane by His Majesty's servants. Written by Mr. William Whitehead.

text: I see thou shudder'st at it: but, great Queen, Hear but the cogent Reasons I shall offer And thou wilt think as I do.
author: Whitehead, William, 1715-1785.
title: Creüsa, Queen of Athens: A tragedy. As it is acted at the Theatre Royal in Drury-Lane by His Majesty's servants. Written by Mr. William Whitehead.

text: The good Priests And pious Priestess, who with Care sustain'd My helpless Infancy, left not my Youth Without Instruction.
author: Whitehead, William, 1715-1785.
title: Creüsa, Queen of Athens: A tragedy. As it is acted at the Theatre Royal in Drury-Lane by His Majesty's servants. Written by Mr. William Whitehead.

text: Be gone.—Insulting Tyrant, Touch but a Wreath that's sacred to Nicander, And by pale Hecate's awful Rites I swear Thy Life shall pay the Forfeit; nay the Lives Of thy whole dastard Race.—Plebeian Grave!
author: Whitehead, William, 1715-1785.
title: Creüsa, Queen of Athens: A tragedy. As it is acted at the Theatre Royal in Drury-Lane by His Majesty's servants. Written by Mr. William Whitehead.

author: Pollexfen, John, b. ca. 1638.

text: Trades that have ſo good a foundation ſhould be promoted; becauſe not ſo difficult to judge what Trades are good by the Exportation, as what are bad by Importation.
author: Pollexfen, John, b. ca. 1638.
title: Of trade 1. In general. 2. In particular. 3. Domestick. 4. Foreign. 5. The East-India. 6. The African. 7. The Turky. 8. The Spanish. 9. The Hamburgh. 10. The Portugal. 11. The Italian. 12. The Dutch.

text: If all Trades ſhould be left to take their courſe till they mend themſelves, we may be reduced to a low ebb before that may happen; for in moſt Caſes, nothing but our Poverty and Inability, longer to ſupport a bad Trade, like to occaſion any ſuch change.
author: Pollexfen, John, b. ca. 1638.
title: Of trade 1. In general. 2. In particular. 3. Domestick. 4. Foreign. 5. The East-India. 6. The African. 7. The Turky. 8. The Spanish. 9. The Hamburgh. 10. The Portugal. 11. The Italian. 12. The Dutch.

author: Pollexfen, John, b. ca. 1638.

text: As we ought to make a Reformation in our Courſe of Living, ſo ſuch alterations in our Trades as before mentioned, or ſuch as may be propoſed by thoſe who have better Judgments.

author: Pollexfen, John, b. ca. 1638.

text: Ay, who indeed;—but I ha no vine Cloaths to go to Court in tho', what mun I do for that now?
author: Centlivre, Susanna, 1667?-1723.
title: The Gotham election: a farce. By Mrs. Centlivre.

text: I, I found your Husband a Man for my Business, I have a Husband as fit for Business as yours;—and tho' I zay it, that shou'd not zay it, there is not a better Workman in the Parish.
author: Centlivre, Susanna, 1667?-1723.
title: The Gotham election: a farce. By Mrs. Centlivre.

text: Ay, and he and his Family has represented this zame Burrough of Gotham these Vorty Years, and yet I believe he will lose it now, I am sorry vor't, vor he's a very honest Gentleman.
author: Centlivre, Susanna, 1667?-1723.
title: The Gotham election: a farce. By Mrs. Centlivre.

text: We began to dispair of your Company Sir, we have Christen'd the Child,—but we got one to stand in your Place, Squire.
author: Centlivre, Susanna, 1667?-1723.
title: The Gotham election: a farce. By Mrs. Centlivre.

text: If they had gone thro' a legal Course of Theatrical Justice, tho' it might have been partial, yet I should have submitted to it, as others had done before me; but to be prejudg'd and condemn'd unheard, was harder Measure than any body else meets with at this time a Day.
author: Centlivre, Susanna, 1667?-1723.
title: The Gotham election: a farce. By Mrs. Centlivre.

text: When my Neighbour Washball, and I zaw that, we wou'd have had the Mayor made his Mittimuss, and zent him to Gaol.
author: Centlivre, Susanna, 1667?-1723.
title: The Gotham election: a farce. By Mrs. Centlivre.

text: My third Son is a Bookseller, a notable Fellow, he lives in London; he is a kind of a Wit; too, they say, and makes Verses; then he has an admirable Knack at quacking Titles.
author: Centlivre, Susanna, 1667?-1723.
title: The Gotham election: a farce. By Mrs. Centlivre.

text: He shall do it, your Husband shall be his Tailor, and you shall be dresser to his Queen.
author: Centlivre, Susanna, 1667?-1723.
title: The Gotham election: a farce. By Mrs. Centlivre.

text: Ha, ha, ha, I'll send my Servant to receive the Money immediately, I think I have paid them in their own Coin.
author: Centlivre, Susanna, 1667?-1723.
title: The Gotham election: a farce. By Mrs. Centlivre.

text: A fine Child indeed,— Here Sirrah, here's a Cup for you, and besure you drink my Health out of it as soon as you can speak, do you hear.—Which is the Father.
author: Centlivre, Susanna, 1667?-1723.
title: The Gotham election: a farce. By Mrs. Centlivre.

text: You are witty upon my Name, Mr. Mallet; but no matter for that, what will you lay I don't carry't?
author: Centlivre, Susanna, 1667?-1723.
title: The Gotham election: a farce. By Mrs. Centlivre.

text: Excellent Contrivance!—we'll about it this Moment.—I can but laugh to think how I shall chouse the young Jade into her Happiness.
author: Centlivre, Susanna, 1667?-1723.
title: The Gotham election: a farce. By Mrs. Centlivre.

text: Why his Worship is a huge Admiror of the French; Nay 'tis whisper'd by zome, that his Zon is with the Knight of the Dragon, for he has never been zeen zince the Duke of what d'e call him went away.
author: Centlivre, Susanna, 1667?-1723.
title: The Gotham election: a farce. By Mrs. Centlivre.

text: But consider, I'm a man of consequence, principal store-keeper to his Majesty's yard, here at Portsmouth, and know all the King's secrets; and let me tell you, if the French should come, they'll take your wives away from you: think of that.
author: Andrews, Miles Peter, d. 1814.
title: Fire and water!: A comic opera: in two acts. Performed at the Theatre-Royal in the Hay-Market. By Miles Peter Andrews.

text: I'll tell you what, child; I'm a man of consequence, and I could wish you to think no more of that midshipman, that Frederick; so mark my words, I'm a man of consequence.
author: Andrews, Miles Peter, d. 1814.
title: Fire and water!: A comic opera: in two acts. Performed at the Theatre-Royal in the Hay-Market. By Miles Peter Andrews.

text: Though I practise the science of arms, Yet, trust me, I think it an evil; And fighting, for me, has such charms, That I'd rather shake hands with the devil.
author: Andrews, Miles Peter, d. 1814.
title: Fire and water!: A comic opera: in two acts. Performed at the Theatre-Royal in the Hay-Market. By Miles Peter Andrews.

text: That's right, my boys, always sing while you work; a song, in my mind, makes labour easy, in spite of mine and his Majesty's enemies.
author: Andrews, Miles Peter, d. 1814.
title: Fire and water!: A comic opera: in two acts. Performed at the Theatre-Royal in the Hay-Market. By Miles Peter Andrews.

text: So it had need, master Launch; for we have enough of it: these cursed French Monsieurs find us constant employment.
author: Andrews, Miles Peter, d. 1814.
title: Fire and water!: A comic opera: in two acts. Performed at the Theatre-Royal in the Hay-Market. By Miles Peter Andrews.

text: Besides, isn't he a republican tallowchandler, who sells candles to the mob, and forces us to light up for liberty? and am not I on the other side the question? and don't wish to have any hand in such stuff.
author: Andrews, Miles Peter, d. 1814.
title: Fire and water!: A comic opera: in two acts. Performed at the Theatre-Royal in the Hay-Market. By Miles Peter Andrews.

text: Aye, I have it under his own hand; here is the infernal scroll; I shou'dn't wonder if it was to flash in his face!
author: Andrews, Miles Peter, d. 1814.
title: Fire and water!: A comic opera: in two acts. Performed at the Theatre-Royal in the Hay-Market. By Miles Peter Andrews.

text: 'Psha! my dear father, never fear the French; they may talk of invading us, but, believe me, they will never do it effectually but with their vices.
author: Andrews, Miles Peter, d. 1814.
title: Fire and water!: A comic opera: in two acts. Performed at the Theatre-Royal in the Hay-Market. By Miles Peter Andrews.

text: Why yes; but if you and Madame Commode would take upon you to recollect that it was not mauvaise, why I would take upon me to forget the Bob-major, the Three Chickens, and the Twopenny Ordinary.
author: Andrews, Miles Peter, d. 1814.
title: Fire and water!: A comic opera: in two acts. Performed at the Theatre-Royal in the Hay-Market. By Miles Peter Andrews.

text: But sure, sir, my Frederick is not to answer for his father's folly; he is himself a slave to no party; and is he not bravely venturing his life in the service of his King?
author: Andrews, Miles Peter, d. 1814.
title: Fire and water!: A comic opera: in two acts. Performed at the Theatre-Royal in the Hay-Market. By Miles Peter Andrews.

text: What then, have you really forgotten your old friend Ambuscade, who was fellow-apprentice with you in Fleet-ditch, at the sign of the Bob-Major, and that used to dine with you every day at the Twopenny Ordinary, where they chain down the knives and forks?
author: Andrews, Miles Peter, d. 1814.
title: Fire and water!: A comic opera: in two acts. Performed at the Theatre-Royal in the Hay-Market. By Miles Peter Andrews.

text: I wish I had not forgot that letter tho'; however, they'll be hanged, I shall be married, and all will be settled, and my poor rival too.
author: Andrews, Miles Peter, d. 1814.
title: Fire and water!: A comic opera: in two acts. Performed at the Theatre-Royal in the Hay-Market. By Miles Peter Andrews.

text: Winds and waves now bear him far, Far from Nancy doom'd to rove; Where amidst the din of war, He perhaps forgets his love.
author: Andrews, Miles Peter, d. 1814.
title: Fire and water!: A comic opera: in two acts. Performed at the Theatre-Royal in the Hay-Market. By Miles Peter Andrews.

text: Did we reflect how Good, how Juſt he was, We ſhould Lament th' Irreparable Loſs; And not as common Mourners uſe, With well Diſſembl'd Sorrow Grace the Funeral.
author: W. B. (William Browne)
title: An ode on the death of William, Duke of Gloucester by W.B. of St. John's, Oxon.

text: Aſſiſt me, all you Mighty Nine, All your United Forces joyn; Fill my Soul with Noble Heat, Thoughts ſublimely Elevate: And let your Inſpiration be Divine, Leſt I ſhould Deviate from the Noble Theme, Or ſomething Write Unworthy Him.
author: W. B. (William Browne)
title: An ode on the death of William, Duke of Gloucester by W.B. of St. John's, Oxon.

text: A greater Reaſon may be ſhown Why a Veil o'er You be thrown, Your Mourning Beauty, ſo Tranſplendent bright, Wou'd dazle the great Artiſt's Sight, While Your ſad Griefs and Sufferings pierce his Heart.
author: W. B. (William Browne)
title: An ode on the death of William, Duke of Gloucester by W.B. of St. John's, Oxon.

text: Here I'm reminded of great William's Name, Tho' mention'd Laſt, the Firſt in Fame: How ſhall I ſtop the Muſes Horſe?
author: W. B. (William Browne)
title: An ode on the death of William, Duke of Gloucester by W.B. of St. John's, Oxon.

text: So when rapid Whirl-winds blow; When Billows roar, and Tempeſts toſs, The Pilot's Art is at a loſs.
author: W. B. (William Browne)
title: An ode on the death of William, Duke of Gloucester by W.B. of St. John's, Oxon.

text: But Fate, alas! does our vain Wiſh reject: For Naſſau's Self, who can command Even all our Powers, cannot Deaths Power withſtand, But muſt reſign his Triumph up to His all-Conquering Hand?
author: W. B. (William Browne)
title: An ode on the death of William, Duke of Gloucester by W.B. of St. John's, Oxon.

text: And tho' his Soul can never die, Which fill'd with Heavenly Fire, In Bliſs muſt Reign among his Kindred of the Sky, Yet muſt his Mortal part Expire; And a Third Heroine ſit upon the Throne, To which by Virtue ſhe has Right, and not by Blood alone.
author: W. B. (William Browne)
title: An ode on the death of William, Duke of Gloucester by W.B. of St. John's, Oxon.

text: Deſcriptions force is uſeleſs here, Where I ſhou'd Court the Readers Ear, With Sound of Horrent Arms, and all the Glorious din of War.
author: W. B. (William Browne)
title: An ode on the death of William, Duke of Gloucester by W.B. of St. John's, Oxon.

text: Not the Old alone ſuffice, But Fate is Deaf to Tender Infants Cries Tho' Floods of Tears do fall from the ſad Parents Eyes.
author: W. B. (William Browne)
title: An ode on the death of William, Duke of Gloucester by W.B. of St. John's, Oxon.

text: He wou'd not from his Wiſdom derogate ſo far, To infringe the Laws himſelf had made, But gave him power to wage perpetual War, And all the World Invade.
author: W. B. (William Browne)
title: An ode on the death of William, Duke of Gloucester by W.B. of St. John's, Oxon.

text: Had the God-like Prince we now bemoan, Liv'd to Succeed, and Wear the Brittiſh Crown, What might we not expect?
author: W. B. (William Browne)
title: An ode on the death of William, Duke of Gloucester by W.B. of St. John's, Oxon.

text: Horatius gain'd a vaſt Eſteem, A Never-dying Fame; He plung'd in Tyber's rapid Stream, To avoid a Conquering Foe: How then can we beſtow, On Great Naſſau his Praiſes due, Who waded thro' the Boyn, the Conquer'd to purſue?
author: W. B. (William Browne)
title: An ode on the death of William, Duke of Gloucester by W.B. of St. John's, Oxon.

text: How ſhall we Celebrate his Name; WHo kept his Neighbouring Foes in Awe, And gave Proud France a Law; And forc'd their King reſign the Forts he did unjuſtly claim?
author: W. B. (William Browne)
title: An ode on the death of William, Duke of Gloucester by W.B. of St. John's, Oxon.
