text: What am I—What I was—From whence I came, Are Thoughts can't leave me long without a Theme.
author: Duck, Stephen, 1705-1756.
title: Royal benevolence. A poem. Most humbly address'd to Her Majesty Queen Caroline: As it was presented to the said Queen's Majesty, by the author, on Friday, the 2d of October, 1730. at Windsor-Castle. T

text: She talk'd, like Woman, guided by a Will, Who nothing knew of real Good or Ill: But when she had the Course of Things survey'd, She own'd, what all must own, Heaven sends its Aid.
author: Duck, Stephen, 1705-1756.
title: Royal benevolence. A poem. Most humbly address'd to Her Majesty Queen Caroline: As it was presented to the said Queen's Majesty, by the author, on Friday, the 2d of October, 1730. at Windsor-Castle. T

text: As on our Parents Labour was intail'd, I work'd, and fallen State of Man bewail'd: I pray'd for Ease, from Sorrow, Want and Pain, And labour'd, my poor Offspring to maintain.
author: Duck, Stephen, 1705-1756.
title: Royal benevolence. A poem. Most humbly address'd to Her Majesty Queen Caroline: As it was presented to the said Queen's Majesty, by the author, on Friday, the 2d of October, 1730. at Windsor-Castle. T

text: One Shilling goes for this, and one for that, And still the Flail went patt and patt a-patt.
author: Duck, Stephen, 1705-1756.
title: Royal benevolence. A poem. Most humbly address'd to Her Majesty Queen Caroline: As it was presented to the said Queen's Majesty, by the author, on Friday, the 2d of October, 1730. at Windsor-Castle. T

text: I, who have labour'd for a trifling Sum, Was pleas'd, to think the time of Pay was come.
author: Duck, Stephen, 1705-1756.
title: Royal benevolence. A poem. Most humbly address'd to Her Majesty Queen Caroline: As it was presented to the said Queen's Majesty, by the author, on Friday, the 2d of October, 1730. at Windsor-Castle. T

text: Nay, some have strove their Poverty to hide, Through Shame, or what should shame, remaining Pride.
author: Duck, Stephen, 1705-1756.
title: Royal benevolence. A poem. Most humbly address'd to Her Majesty Queen Caroline: As it was presented to the said Queen's Majesty, by the author, on Friday, the 2d of October, 1730. at Windsor-Castle. T

text: I bid her look on Birds in Bushes there, And see the little silly Insect here; Behold the Order of the Universe, And ask the Hen and Chickens for a Purse.
author: Duck, Stephen, 1705-1756.
title: Royal benevolence. A poem. Most humbly address'd to Her Majesty Queen Caroline: As it was presented to the said Queen's Majesty, by the author, on Friday, the 2d of October, 1730. at Windsor-Castle. T

text: Now, as I've leisure Fancy to display, My Pen shall ever grateful Homage pay: For sure no Wretch can e're so stupid prove, As to be blind to such abundant Love.
author: Duck, Stephen, 1705-1756.
title: Royal benevolence. A poem. Most humbly address'd to Her Majesty Queen Caroline: As it was presented to the said Queen's Majesty, by the author, on Friday, the 2d of October, 1730. at Windsor-Castle. T

text: MOST bounteous QUEEN, my grateful Thanks I pay, Which scarcely for the Dress of Words will stay: Your ROYAL MAJESTY a Muck-worm took From Labour, pleas'd with his mean trifling Book: And now the Reptile at your Foot-stool lays In humble Strains, to sing your worthy Praise.
author: Duck, Stephen, 1705-1756.
title: Royal benevolence. A poem. Most humbly address'd to Her Majesty Queen Caroline: As it was presented to the said Queen's Majesty, by the author, on Friday, the 2d of October, 1730. at Windsor-Castle. T

text: Th'Almighty seeing so much Christian Grace, And how, on Earth, she ran the heavenly Race; Has constituted ROYAL CAROLINE His Agent here, to make his Glory shine.
author: Duck, Stephen, 1705-1756.
title: Royal benevolence. A poem. Most humbly address'd to Her Majesty Queen Caroline: As it was presented to the said Queen's Majesty, by the author, on Friday, the 2d of October, 1730. at Windsor-Castle. T

text: No Meadow green, or Stack or Cock of Hay, But where I view will furnish an Essay: And then the Objects of my Praise will be, The mighty Lord, and her great Majesty.
author: Duck, Stephen, 1705-1756.
title: Royal benevolence. A poem. Most humbly address'd to Her Majesty Queen Caroline: As it was presented to the said Queen's Majesty, by the author, on Friday, the 2d of October, 1730. at Windsor-Castle. T

text: Your Royal Goodness o're my Cottage shone, With brighter Beams, than did the rising Sun: And from a Barn Companion to the Mice, Plac'd me at Ease, and in a Paradice.
author: Duck, Stephen, 1705-1756.
title: Royal benevolence. A poem. Most humbly address'd to Her Majesty Queen Caroline: As it was presented to the said Queen's Majesty, by the author, on Friday, the 2d of October, 1730. at Windsor-Castle. T

text: But I need no such Phantoms to inspire; Your Royal Bounty sets my Soul on fire; And what I lov'd before, I now admire.
author: Duck, Stephen, 1705-1756.
title: Royal benevolence. A poem. Most humbly address'd to Her Majesty Queen Caroline: As it was presented to the said Queen's Majesty, by the author, on Friday, the 2d of October, 1730. at Windsor-Castle. T

text: If then, your gracious Queen, tho' few her Days, Has practis'd ev'ry Virtue worthy Praise, Worthy immortal Bliss: What can she more, Tho' Heav'n again her former Health restore?
author: Duck, Stephen, 1705-1756.
title: The vision. A poem on the death of Her Most Gracious Majesty Queen Caroline. By Stephen Duck:

text: Few are the Years to Mortal Man assign'd, Ah! let not Her—to fewer be confin'd: But stop thy threat'ning Arm, and spare awhile Her sacred Life, so precious to my Isle."
author: Duck, Stephen, 1705-1756.
title: The vision. A poem on the death of Her Most Gracious Majesty Queen Caroline. By Stephen Duck:

text: " BRITANNIA, cease thy fruitless Tears, and know, One certain Day is fix'd for all below: That Day permit to Heav'n; for Heav'n alone Knows when the noble Work of Virtue's done.
author: Duck, Stephen, 1705-1756.
title: The vision. A poem on the death of Her Most Gracious Majesty Queen Caroline. By Stephen Duck:

text: Few are the Years, you say, of human Kind; But Years add nothing to the perfect Mind.
author: Duck, Stephen, 1705-1756.
title: The vision. A poem on the death of Her Most Gracious Majesty Queen Caroline. By Stephen Duck:

text: Heav'n's greatest Lord, that over All presides; Who rules that Sun, and all his Motions guides; In Length of Years an Equal ne'er survey'd; But is not therefore worshipp'd, or obey'd: His Goodness only claims that Tribute due; His Goodness, not his Age, tho' ever New.
author: Duck, Stephen, 1705-1756.
title: The vision. A poem on the death of Her Most Gracious Majesty Queen Caroline. By Stephen Duck:

text: A Cloud of Glory shone before my Face, Which shed refulgent Rays around the Place, And scatter'd Colours, various to behold, Here blushing Rubies, there the burnish'd Gold.
author: Duck, Stephen, 1705-1756.
title: The vision. A poem on the death of Her Most Gracious Majesty Queen Caroline. By Stephen Duck:

text: Suppose the Sun, that chears your earthly Clime, Should run his destin'd Course in half the Time, Performing all the Offices of Light, Of Heat, of circling Seasons, Day and Night: Say, Could you think his Race too swiftly run?
author: Duck, Stephen, 1705-1756.
title: The vision. A poem on the death of Her Most Gracious Majesty Queen Caroline. By Stephen Duck:

text: But That, alas! is not to Mortals giv'n; Yet surely This is in the Grant of Heav'n: Increase her Days, restore her native Bloom, Nor crop the Royal Fruit till Autumn come.
author: Duck, Stephen, 1705-1756.
title: The vision. A poem on the death of Her Most Gracious Majesty Queen Caroline. By Stephen Duck:

text: " ALMIGHTY Father! whose Commanding Pow'r, Can hasten, or adjourn, the fatal Hour; Can lengthen, or contract, a Monarch's Reign, Or raise the silent Dead to Life again: Oh! stop thy threat'ning Arm, and spare awhile One sacred Life, so precious to my Isle.
author: Duck, Stephen, 1705-1756.
title: The vision. A poem on the death of Her Most Gracious Majesty Queen Caroline. By Stephen Duck:

text: NOR fewer Charms adorn her private Life, The tend'rest Mother, most submissive Wife; Who never yet her Consort disobey'd, By Honour, Duty, Love, and Virtue sway'd: In Virtue's Path she constantly proceeds, By Virtue's Rule she measures all her Deeds.
author: Duck, Stephen, 1705-1756.
title: The vision. A poem on the death of Her Most Gracious Majesty Queen Caroline. By Stephen Duck:

text: When strait I hear Complaints from ev'ry Tongue, On ev'ry Face a Cloud of Sorrow hung: Sad Sighs and Floods of fruitless Tears bemoan The Noblest Queen that ever grac'd a Throne.
author: Duck, Stephen, 1705-1756.
title: The vision. A poem on the death of Her Most Gracious Majesty Queen Caroline. By Stephen Duck:

text: Oh! were She like Thee more in ev'ry State; Oh! were She, were She, like Thee, free from Fate!
author: Duck, Stephen, 1705-1756.
title: The vision. A poem on the death of Her Most Gracious Majesty Queen Caroline. By Stephen Duck:

text: For Royal CAROLINA'S Health I sue, The best of Sov'reigns, and of Subjects too; In ev'ry State her Goodness has been prov'd, When rul'd, obedient; and when ruling, lov'd. Securely blest, beneath her gentle Sway, 'Tis Happiness to serve, and Pleasure to obey.
author: Duck, Stephen, 1705-1756.
title: The vision. A poem on the death of Her Most Gracious Majesty Queen Caroline. By Stephen Duck:

text: I wish, with all my heart I could make your's. The Countess of Crambo insists on the best places for the first night of performance.
author: Colman, George, 1762-1836.
title: New hay at the old market: an occassional drama, in one act: written by George Colman, (the younger, ) on opening the Hay-Market Theatre. On the 9th of June, 1795.

text: Oh, faith, you need not tell me that:—I trust I have always been found to work willingly—and at present I have a double motive to activity, in serving the town, and assisting an old friend, who ventures largely for its amusement.
author: Colman, George, 1762-1836.
title: New hay at the old market: an occassional drama, in one act: written by George Colman, (the younger, ) on opening the Hay-Market Theatre. On the 9th of June, 1795.

text: They are given as Portraits, not as Caricatures; and the Publick has pronounced them to be strong, but unexaggerated likenesses of originals, whom its discernment has long patronised and admired.
author: Colman, George, 1762-1836.
title: New hay at the old market: an occassional drama, in one act: written by George Colman, (the younger, ) on opening the Hay-Market Theatre. On the 9th of June, 1795.

text: Damn'd bad indeed, Sir—The Dunstable Company:—where I have eight shillings a week, four bits of candle, one wife, three shirts, and nine children.
author: Colman, George, 1762-1836.
title: New hay at the old market: an occassional drama, in one act: written by George Colman, (the younger, ) on opening the Hay-Market Theatre. On the 9th of June, 1795.

text: Egad, if you were at my lodgings, you should have that, and a bottle of wine too.
author: Colman, George, 1762-1836.
title: New hay at the old market: an occassional drama, in one act: written by George Colman, (the younger, ) on opening the Hay-Market Theatre. On the 9th of June, 1795.

text: Ise warrant me, now, if I was to ax the Carpenter, he would not have any dejection.
author: Colman, George, 1762-1836.
title: New hay at the old market: an occassional drama, in one act: written by George Colman, (the younger, ) on opening the Hay-Market Theatre. On the 9th of June, 1795.

text: Well, friend, you'll let your master know Mr. Fustian is here, when the two gentlemen have left him at leisure.
author: Colman, George, 1762-1836.
title: New hay at the old market: an occassional drama, in one act: written by George Colman, (the younger, ) on opening the Hay-Market Theatre. On the 9th of June, 1795.

text: Now I desire you'll hold your tongue, for if you talk you'll put me out —These gardens which are now the admiration of the larned and curish, &c. &c.
author: Colman, George, 1762-1836.
title: New hay at the old market: an occassional drama, in one act: written by George Colman, (the younger, ) on opening the Hay-Market Theatre. On the 9th of June, 1795.

text: I am so loth to disturb him, poor gentleman, that I never wake him till a full half hour after my master is gone out.
author: Colman, George, 1762-1836.
title: New hay at the old market: an occassional drama, in one act: written by George Colman, (the younger, ) on opening the Hay-Market Theatre. On the 9th of June, 1795.

text: In my travels, I had soon the happiness of forming a romantick attachment with the present Mrs. Daggerwood— wife to Sylvester Daggerwood, your humble servant to command, whose benefit is fixed for the eleventh of June, by the particular desire of several persons of distinction.
author: Colman, George, 1762-1836.
title: New hay at the old market: an occassional drama, in one act: written by George Colman, (the younger, ) on opening the Hay-Market Theatre. On the 9th of June, 1795.

text: Pretty treatment! pretty treatment truly! to be kept here, half the morning, kicking my heels in a Manager's anti-room, shut up with a mad Dunstable actor.
author: Colman, George, 1762-1836.
title: New hay at the old market: an occassional drama, in one act: written by George Colman, (the younger, ) on opening the Hay-Market Theatre. On the 9th of June, 1795.

text: The Theatre opens this Evening—and Mr. Bannister Jun. and Mr. Suett, are to meet him there, on particular business.
author: Colman, George, 1762-1836.
title: New hay at the old market: an occassional drama, in one act: written by George Colman, (the younger, ) on opening the Hay-Market Theatre. On the 9th of June, 1795.

text: Yes, mother—but, as we have a little bit leisure, as you do say, there be one thing I wish to ax you to do for me.
author: Colman, George, 1762-1836.
title: New hay at the old market: an occassional drama, in one act: written by George Colman, (the younger, ) on opening the Hay-Market Theatre. On the 9th of June, 1795.

text: Whate'er bold Trojan arm'd his daring Hands Against the sable Ships with flaming Brands, So well the Chief his Naval Weapon sped, The luckless Warrior at his Stern lay dead: Full twelve, the boldest, in a Moment fell, Sent by great Ajax to the Shades of Hell.
author: Homer.
title: The Iliad: of Homer. Translated by Mr. Pope. [pt.4]

text: Not thus I burn'd for either Theban Dame, (Bacchus from this, from that Alcides came) Not Phoenix' Daughter, beautiful and young, Whence godlike Rhadamanth and Minos sprung.
author: Homer.
title: The Iliad: of Homer. Translated by Mr. Pope. [pt.4]

text: It is very probable that these Priests by this hard living had a mind to attract the Admiration and Confidence of a People who lov'd Luxury and Delicacy so much.
author: Homer.
title: The Iliad: of Homer. Translated by Mr. Pope. [pt.4]

text: Agamemnon proposes to make their Escape by Night, which Ulysses withstands; to which Diomed adds his Advice, that, wounded as they were, they should go forth and encourage the Army with their Presence; which Advice is pursued.
author: Homer.
title: The Iliad: of Homer. Translated by Mr. Pope. [pt.4]

text: For this, behold! in horrid Arms I shine, And urge thy Soul to rival Acts with mine: Together let us battel on the Plain; Two, not the worst; nor ev'n this Succour vain.
author: Homer.
title: The Iliad: of Homer. Translated by Mr. Pope. [pt.4]

text: But lest new Wounds on Wounds o'erpower us quite, Beyond the missile Javelin's sounding Flight, Safe let us stand; and from the Tumult far, Inspire the Ranks, and rule the distant War.
author: Homer.
title: The Iliad: of Homer. Translated by Mr. Pope. [pt.4]

text: But the Answer is very obvious; Homer intends to paint a Man in Passion; the Wishes and Schemes of such an one are seldom conformable to Reason; and the Manners are preserv'd the better, the less they are represented to be so.
author: Homer.
title: The Iliad: of Homer. Translated by Mr. Pope. [pt.4]

text: 'Tis a merry Conceit of Eustathius, that Pedasus is only said to be mortal, because of the three Horses he only was a Gelding.
author: Homer.
title: The Iliad: of Homer. Translated by Mr. Pope. [pt.4]

text: Glaucus, be bold; thy Task be first to dare The glorious Dangers of destructive War, To lead my Troops, to combate at their Head, Incite the Living, and supply the Dead.
author: Homer.
title: The Iliad: of Homer. Translated by Mr. Pope. [pt.4]

text: This noble Life is ended with a Death as glorious; for in his last Moments he has no other Concern, but for the Honour of his Friends, and the Event of the Day.
author: Homer.
title: The Iliad: of Homer. Translated by Mr. Pope. [pt.4]

text: There are not only Replies, but Rejoinders in Homer, a thing scarce ever to be found in Virgil; the Consequence whereof is, that there must be in the Iliad many continued Conversations (such as this of our two Heroes) a little resembling common Chit-chat.
author: Homer.
title: The Iliad: of Homer. Translated by Mr. Pope. [pt.4]

text: Disarm'd, he mingled in the Trojan Crew; But Merion's Spear o'ertook him as he flew, Deep in the Belly's Rim an Entrance found, Where sharp the Pang, and mortal is the Wound.
author: Homer.
title: The Iliad: of Homer. Translated by Mr. Pope. [pt.4]

text: The Circumstance of Sleep's sitting in Likeness of a Bird on the Fir-Tree upon Mount Ida, is alluded to in his 4th Book, where Satan sits in Likeness of a Cormorant on the Tree of Life.
author: Homer.
title: The Iliad: of Homer. Translated by Mr. Pope. [pt.4]

text: Pitt—s had to the God his Honours done, But knowing well Tom's Case, and his, were one, Just as he rose, as decently sate down.
author: Person of honour.
title: A new session of the poets occasion'd by the death of Mr. Dryden / by a person of honour.

text: Of Plays, and Poems Cr—n produc'd a load, And all the Lumber laid before the God.
author: Person of honour.
title: A new session of the poets occasion'd by the death of Mr. Dryden / by a person of honour.

text: How can you from those Bards expect the Bays, Who him that wore 'em, could so sadly praise?
author: Person of honour.
title: A new session of the poets occasion'd by the death of Mr. Dryden / by a person of honour.

text: The Gaudy God, did soon Himself proclaim; To whom in Troops, the Airy-Sons of Fame, From humble Elegy, to Epick, came.
author: Person of honour.
title: A new session of the poets occasion'd by the death of Mr. Dryden / by a person of honour.

text: E're at the Wreath you reach, all else excell: You write correct, but Southern writes as well.
author: Person of honour.
title: A new session of the poets occasion'd by the death of Mr. Dryden / by a person of honour.

text: The God soon told him he had gain'd the Bays, Had he contented been t'have wrote three Plays: But since he knew not when he he'd Glory won, 'Twas just that Capua's Fate should prove his own.
author: Person of honour.
title: A new session of the poets occasion'd by the death of Mr. Dryden / by a person of honour.

text: Some come from Will's, and some from Rouse's come; Some wondrous warm, extreamly Sober some; Some out of gloomy Cellars, upwards bend; From Garrets some, Six Stories down, descend: Each left his known, or else unknown Abode, And all obey'd the Summons of the God.
author: Person of honour.
title: A new session of the poets occasion'd by the death of Mr. Dryden / by a person of honour.

text: And you, audacious Mortal, tell me why You dare my Fav'rite Waller's Faults descry, And yet expose your own vile Elegy?
author: Person of honour.
title: A new session of the poets occasion'd by the death of Mr. Dryden / by a person of honour.

text: An Author can't in French, or Spanish prate, But you must make the Sot speak English straight!
author: Person of honour.
title: A new session of the poets occasion'd by the death of Mr. Dryden / by a person of honour.

text: Stiff, as his Works, th' elab'rate Cong—ve came, Who could so soon Preferment get, and Fame.
author: Person of honour.
title: A new session of the poets occasion'd by the death of Mr. Dryden / by a person of honour.

text: For whatsoe're was scandalously writ, No Author known, Tom's Carcass paid for it: Who pray'd Apollo to reward his Lays, And to much Birch to add a little Bays, Oh Heav'ns, cry'd out Apollo, grant me patience!
author: Person of honour.
title: A new session of the poets occasion'd by the death of Mr. Dryden / by a person of honour.

text: Appollo, who from High beheld their Jarrs, And all the Tuneful Tribe at Civil Wars, Upon a Ray of his own Light slid down, To find among the Crowd some wondrous One, That well again the Sacred Wreath might wear, And the departed Dryden justly Heir.
author: Person of honour.
title: A new session of the poets occasion'd by the death of Mr. Dryden / by a person of honour.

text: Then told him, that he did not now Translate, As heretofore, for Glory, but to Eat: That Bards should never offer at the Bays, That often Dine but once in twice two days.
author: Person of honour.
title: A new session of the poets occasion'd by the death of Mr. Dryden / by a person of honour.

text: Fair Mourner rise—Thus far thou hast prevail'd, If, to attone for all I have endur'd, For all thy cold Neglect, thy Arts, Delays, For all my Years of anxious Expectation, This Night thou give thy Beauties to my Arms; This Night!
author: Rowe, Nicholas, 1674-1718.
title: Ulysses: a tragedy. As it is acted at the Queen's Theatre in the Hay-Market. By Her Majesty's sworn servants. Written by N. Rowe, Esq;.

text: Why was this Mass ta'ne from the Heap of Matter, Where innocent and senseless it had rested, To be indu'd with Form, and vext with Motion?
author: Rowe, Nicholas, 1674-1718.
title: Ulysses: a tragedy. As it is acted at the Queen's Theatre in the Hay-Market. By Her Majesty's sworn servants. Written by N. Rowe, Esq;.

text: Come to my Aid!—Be calm but for a Moment, And wait to see what Wonders it will shew thee.
author: Rowe, Nicholas, 1674-1718.
title: Ulysses: a tragedy. As it is acted at the Queen's Theatre in the Hay-Market. By Her Majesty's sworn servants. Written by N. Rowe, Esq;.

text: E'er the Mid-hour of rowling Night approach, Remember well to plant thee at that Door, Thou know'st it opens to the Queen's Apartment.
author: Rowe, Nicholas, 1674-1718.
title: Ulysses: a tragedy. As it is acted at the Queen's Theatre in the Hay-Market. By Her Majesty's sworn servants. Written by N. Rowe, Esq;.

text: To find those Wishes then, those fond Desires, To trace the fulsome Haunts of wanton Appetite, She must be try'd.
author: Rowe, Nicholas, 1674-1718.
title: Ulysses: a tragedy. As it is acted at the Queen's Theatre in the Hay-Market. By Her Majesty's sworn servants. Written by N. Rowe, Esq;.

text: Telemachus—why is thy King and Father Stretch'd on the Earth a cold and lifeless Coarse, Inglorious and forgotten—Oh!
author: Rowe, Nicholas, 1674-1718.
title: Ulysses: a tragedy. As it is acted at the Queen's Theatre in the Hay-Market. By Her Majesty's sworn servants. Written by N. Rowe, Esq;.

text: Far from my Lips within my Breast I'll keep it, Nor breathe it softly to my self alone, Lest some officious murmuring Wind should tell it, And babbling Eccho's catch the feeble Sound.
author: Rowe, Nicholas, 1674-1718.
title: Ulysses: a tragedy. As it is acted at the Queen's Theatre in the Hay-Market. By Her Majesty's sworn servants. Written by N. Rowe, Esq;.

text: I cannot Court you with a silken Tale, With easie ambling Speeches, fram'd on Purpose, Made to be spoke in Tune—But be my Queen, And leave my plain spoke Love to prove its Merit.
author: Rowe, Nicholas, 1674-1718.
title: Ulysses: a tragedy. As it is acted at the Queen's Theatre in the Hay-Market. By Her Majesty's sworn servants. Written by N. Rowe, Esq;.

text: Whate'er those Orders were, I have my Reasons To think my self excepted:—And whoe'er Brought you the Message, through officious Haste Mistook the Queen, and has inform'd you wrong.
author: Rowe, Nicholas, 1674-1718.
title: Ulysses: a tragedy. As it is acted at the Queen's Theatre in the Hay-Market. By Her Majesty's sworn servants. Written by N. Rowe, Esq;.

text: Ye valiant Samian Chiefs, ye faithful Followers Of your unhappy King, justly perform Your pious Office to his sacred Relicks, Bear to your Fleet his pale, his bloody Coarse, Nor let his discontented Ghost repine, To think his injur'd Ashes shall be mixt With the detested Earth of cruel Ithaca.
author: Rowe, Nicholas, 1674-1718.
title: Ulysses: a tragedy. As it is acted at the Queen's Theatre in the Hay-Market. By Her Majesty's sworn servants. Written by N. Rowe, Esq;.

text: Did not her Soul resent the Violation, And spight of all the Wrongs she labour'd under, Dash his Ambition and presumptuous Love?
author: Rowe, Nicholas, 1674-1718.
title: Ulysses: a tragedy. As it is acted at the Queen's Theatre in the Hay-Market. By Her Majesty's sworn servants. Written by N. Rowe, Esq;.

text: Our Daughter once was wont to share your Thoughts, Believe me, she has Reason to complain, If you prefer your Solitude to her; While here you stay, disconsolate and musing, Lonely she sits, the tender-hearted Maid, And kindly thinks of you, and mourns your Absence.
author: Rowe, Nicholas, 1674-1718.
title: Ulysses: a tragedy. As it is acted at the Queen's Theatre in the Hay-Market. By Her Majesty's sworn servants. Written by N. Rowe, Esq;.

text: Behold it there! behold the Love thou bear'st me; Behold that! that!—more dreadful than Medusa, It drives my Soul back to her inmost Seats, And freezes every stiff'ning Limb to Marble.
author: Rowe, Nicholas, 1674-1718.
title: Ulysses: a tragedy. As it is acted at the Queen's Theatre in the Hay-Market. By Her Majesty's sworn servants. Written by N. Rowe, Esq;.

text: The Stings of Falshood Those shall try, And hard Unkindness' alter'd Eye, That mocks the Tear it forc'd to flow; And keen Remorse with Blood defil'd, And moody Madness laughing wild Amid severest Woe.
author: Gray, Thomas, 1716-1771.
title: An ode on a distant prospect of Eton College:

text: To each his Suff'rings: all are Men, Condemn'd alike to groan, The Tender for another's Pain; Th' Unfeeling for his own.
author: Gray, Thomas, 1716-1771.
title: An ode on a distant prospect of Eton College:

text: No Sense have they of Ills to come, Nor Care beyond to-day: Yet see how all around 'em wait The Ministers of human Fate, And black Misfortune's baleful Train!
author: Gray, Thomas, 1716-1771.
title: An ode on a distant prospect of Eton College:

text: Say, Father Thames, for thou hast seen Full many a sprightly Race Disporting on thy Margent green The Paths of Pleasure trace, Who foremost now delight to cleave With pliant Arm thy glassy Wave?
author: Gray, Thomas, 1716-1771.
title: An ode on a distant prospect of Eton College:

text: I feel the Gales, that from ye blow, A momentary Bliss bestow, As waving fresh their gladsome Wing, My weary Soul they seem to sooth, And, redolent of Joy and Youth, To breathe a second Spring.
author: Gray, Thomas, 1716-1771.
title: An ode on a distant prospect of Eton College:

text: Ambition This shall tempt to rise, Then whirl the Wretch from high, To bitter Scorn a Sacrifice, And grinning Infamy.

text: "No more, my son, the rural reed employ, Nor trill the trifling strain of empty joy; No more thy love-resounding sonnets suit To notes of past'ral pipe, or oaten flute.

title: The triumph of Isis: a poem. Occasioned by Isis, an elegy.

text: Let GR—boast the patrons of her name, Each pompous fool of fortune and of fame; Still of preferment let her shine the queen, Prolific parent of each bowing Dean!
author: Warton, Thomas, 1728-1790.
title: The triumph of Isis: a poem. Occasioned by Isis, an elegy.

text: While arms like these my stedfast sages wield, While mine is Truth's impenetrable shield; Say, shall the PUNY CHAMPION fondly dare, To wage with force like this scholastic war?
author: Warton, Thomas, 1728-1790.
title: The triumph of Isis: a poem. Occasioned by Isis, an elegy.

text: Tho' rude the dome, and humble the retreat, Where first his pious care ordain'd her seat, Lo! now on high she dwells in Attic bow'rs, And proudly lifts to heav'n her hundred tow'rs.
author: Warton, Thomas, 1728-1790.
title: The triumph of Isis: a poem. Occasioned by Isis, an elegy.

text: Be her's each Pr—te of the pamper'd cheek, Each courtly Chaplain sanctify'd and sleek: Still let the Drones of her exhaustless hive On fat pluralities supinely thrive.
author: Warton, Thomas, 1728-1790.
title: The triumph of Isis: a poem. Occasioned by Isis, an elegy.

text: These from thy source the fires of Freedom caught: How well thy sons by their example taught; While in each breast th' hereditary flame Still blazes unextinguish'd and the same!
author: Warton, Thomas, 1728-1790.
title: The triumph of Isis: a poem. Occasioned by Isis, an elegy.

text: Yet the laws are despised, and discover their impotence most, when they attempt to exert their greatest force.
author: Gerard, Alexander, 1728-1795.
title: The influence of piety on the public good. A sermon, preached in the High Church of Edinburgh, May 31. 1761, ... By Alexander Gerard,:

text: They can execute the laws against others; but themselves have many advantages for eluding the force of the laws, from their rank, their authority, and power.
author: Gerard, Alexander, 1728-1795.
title: The influence of piety on the public good. A sermon, preached in the High Church of Edinburgh, May 31. 1761, ... By Alexander Gerard,:

text: We consider those alone as intitled to the character of piety, who are possessed of a greater regard to religion than the generality of mankind.
author: Gerard, Alexander, 1728-1795.
title: The influence of piety on the public good. A sermon, preached in the High Church of Edinburgh, May 31. 1761, ... By Alexander Gerard,:

text: Let all the earth, therefore, fear the Lord; let all the inhabitants of the world stand in awe of him.
author: Gerard, Alexander, 1728-1795.
title: The influence of piety on the public good. A sermon, preached in the High Church of Edinburgh, May 31. 1761, ... By Alexander Gerard,:

text: All men have some imperfect sense of religion, which renders them much fitter for the duties of society than they could be without it.
author: Gerard, Alexander, 1728-1795.
title: The influence of piety on the public good. A sermon, preached in the High Church of Edinburgh, May 31. 1761, ... By Alexander Gerard,:

text: Without religion, this would be the state of every nation: nothing could make the laws to be revered but the most dreadful tortures.
author: Gerard, Alexander, 1728-1795.
title: The influence of piety on the public good. A sermon, preached in the High Church of Edinburgh, May 31. 1761, ... By Alexander Gerard,:

text: Civil laws control only our external actions; but the laws of religion kill the seeds of those principles, which, when they are cherished, spring up slowly and gradually into crimes.
author: Gerard, Alexander, 1728-1795.
title: The influence of piety on the public good. A sermon, preached in the High Church of Edinburgh, May 31. 1761, ... By Alexander Gerard,:

text: They cannot exert themselves in this character, if they be either indifferent about religion, or averse from it.
author: Gerard, Alexander, 1728-1795.
title: The influence of piety on the public good. A sermon, preached in the High Church of Edinburgh, May 31. 1761, ... By Alexander Gerard,:

text: The Christian religion represents the character of God as in the highest degree worthy of all our pious regards, by assuring us that he is God our saviour, by informing us of the stupendous dispensation of grace for the redemption of the apostate world, which he has carried on.
author: Gerard, Alexander, 1728-1795.
title: The influence of piety on the public good. A sermon, preached in the High Church of Edinburgh, May 31. 1761, ... By Alexander Gerard,:

text: It is chiefly religion that supports those connections of individuals, which bestow order on society, which distinguish a regular polity from a confused multitude, and which produce public peace, prosperity, and power.
author: Gerard, Alexander, 1728-1795.
title: The influence of piety on the public good. A sermon, preached in the High Church of Edinburgh, May 31. 1761, ... By Alexander Gerard,:

text: But if religion had not considerable power even over the generality of mankind, it would be necessary, and perhaps insufficient likewise, to inflict the most exquisite tortures on every criminal.
author: Gerard, Alexander, 1728-1795.
title: The influence of piety on the public good. A sermon, preached in the High Church of Edinburgh, May 31. 1761, ... By Alexander Gerard,:

text: True piety is to every nation, like the sun to this earth; it alone can enlighten, warm, cherish, or invigorate all its inhabitants.
author: Gerard, Alexander, 1728-1795.
title: The influence of piety on the public good. A sermon, preached in the High Church of Edinburgh, May 31. 1761, ... By Alexander Gerard,:

text: Can any person be insensible, how valuable a blessing it is to society, that mild and moderate punishments are sufficient to preserve its peace?
author: Gerard, Alexander, 1728-1795.
title: The influence of piety on the public good. A sermon, preached in the High Church of Edinburgh, May 31. 1761, ... By Alexander Gerard,:

text: It was, perhaps, with-held thro' an indolent, or wilful Neglect, 'till those, who lingered in the Want of it, grew almost past the Sense of Comfort.
author: Savage, Richard, d. 1743.
title: The wanderer: a poem. In five canto's. By Richard Savage, ...

text: He scoops the stubborn Alps, and, still employ'd, Fills with soft, fertile Mold the steril Void; Slop'd up white Rocks, small, yellow Harvests grow, And, green on terrass'd Stages, Vineyards blow!
author: Savage, Richard, d. 1743.
title: The wanderer: a poem. In five canto's. By Richard Savage, ...

text: This Cave!—Yon Walks!—But e'er I more unfold, What artful Scenes, thy Eyes shall here behold, Think Subjects of my Toil: nor wond'ring gaze!
author: Savage, Richard, d. 1743.
title: The wanderer: a poem. In five canto's. By Richard Savage, ...

text: If wailing Worth can gen'rous Warmth excite, If Verse can gild Instruction with Delight, Inspire his honest Muse with orient Flame, To rise, to dare, to reach the noblest Aim!
author: Savage, Richard, d. 1743.
title: The wanderer: a poem. In five canto's. By Richard Savage, ...

text: Straight heard the Furies, and with Envy glar'd, And to precipitate his Fall prepar'd: First Av'rice came.
author: Savage, Richard, d. 1743.
title: The wanderer: a poem. In five canto's. By Richard Savage, ...

text: When, lo! the Mendicant, so late behind, Strange View! now journeying in our Front we find!
author: Savage, Richard, d. 1743.
title: The wanderer: a poem. In five canto's. By Richard Savage, ...

text: If Rains, redundant, flood the abject Ground, Mountains are but supplied, when Vales are drown'd; If, with soft Moisture swell'd, the Vale looks gay, The Verdure of the Mountain fades away.
author: Savage, Richard, d. 1743.
title: The wanderer: a poem. In five canto's. By Richard Savage, ...

text: Pinch'd, pierc'd, and torn, enflam'd, and unassuag'd, They smart, and swell, and throb, and shoot enrag'd!
author: Savage, Richard, d. 1743.
title: The wanderer: a poem. In five canto's. By Richard Savage, ...

text: When first we met, how soon you seem'd to know My Bosom, lab'ring with the Throbs of Woe!
author: Savage, Richard, d. 1743.
title: The wanderer: a poem. In five canto's. By Richard Savage, ...

text: I heard, obey'd; nor more of Fate complain'd; Long Seas I measur'd, and this Mountain gain'd. Soon to a yawning Rift, Chance turn'd my Way; A Den it prov'd, where a huge Serpent lay!
author: Savage, Richard, d. 1743.
title: The wanderer: a poem. In five canto's. By Richard Savage, ...

text: When worship'd Woman we entranc'd behold, We praise the Maker in his fairest Mold; The Pride of Nature, Harmony combin'd, And Light immortal to the Soul refin'd!
author: Savage, Richard, d. 1743.
title: The wanderer: a poem. In five canto's. By Richard Savage, ...

text: Bright It collects the Beams, which, trembling All, Back from the God, a show'ry Radiance, fall, Light'ning the Scene beneath! a Scene divine!
author: Savage, Richard, d. 1743.
title: The wanderer: a poem. In five canto's. By Richard Savage, ...

text: The Roof is now the Daw's, or Raven's Haunt, And loathsome Toads in the dark Entrance pant; Or Snakes, that lurk to snap the heedless Fly, And fated Bird, that oft comes flutt'ring by.
author: Savage, Richard, d. 1743.
title: The wanderer: a poem. In five canto's. By Richard Savage, ...

text: For, if a cherub in the shape of woman Should walk this world, yet defamation would, Like a vile cur, bark at the angel's train— To-day the baron started at your tears.
author: Home, John, 1722-1808.
title: Douglas: a tragedy. As it is acted at the Theatre-Royal in Covent-Garden.

text: Hath fill'd his bosom with that sacred fire, Which in the breasts of his forefathers burn'd: Set him on high like them, that he may shine The star and glory of his native land!
author: Home, John, 1722-1808.
title: Douglas: a tragedy. As it is acted at the Theatre-Royal in Covent-Garden.

text: Whoe'er thou art, thy spirit is ennobled By the great King of Kings! thou art ordain'd And stampt a hero by the sovereign hand Of nature! blush not, flower of modesty As well as valour, to declare thy birth.
author: Home, John, 1722-1808.
title: Douglas: a tragedy. As it is acted at the Theatre-Royal in Covent-Garden.

text: Had some good angel op'd to me the book Of providence, and let me read my life, My heart had broke, when I beheld the sum Of ills, which one by one I have endur'd.
author: Home, John, 1722-1808.
title: Douglas: a tragedy. As it is acted at the Theatre-Royal in Covent-Garden.

text: I know not: But since my words have made my mistress tremble, I will speak so no more; but silent mix My tears with hers.
author: Home, John, 1722-1808.
title: Douglas: a tragedy. As it is acted at the Theatre-Royal in Covent-Garden.

text: Yet I am not safe: By love, or something like it, stung, inflam'd, Madly I blabb'd my passion to his wife, And she has threaten'd to acquaint him of it.
author: Home, John, 1722-1808.
title: Douglas: a tragedy. As it is acted at the Theatre-Royal in Covent-Garden.

text: This night once more Within these walls I rest; my tent I pitch To-morrow in the field.
author: Home, John, 1722-1808.
title: Douglas: a tragedy. As it is acted at the Theatre-Royal in Covent-Garden.

text: I am resolv'd. I'll go Straight to the battle, where the man that makes Me turn aside must threaten worse than death.
author: Home, John, 1722-1808.
title: Douglas: a tragedy. As it is acted at the Theatre-Royal in Covent-Garden.

text: Yet I incline to think her stormy virtue Is lull'd awhile: 'tis her alone I fear: Whilst she and RANDOLPH live, and live in faith And amity, uncertain is my tenure.
author: Home, John, 1722-1808.
title: Douglas: a tragedy. As it is acted at the Theatre-Royal in Covent-Garden.

text: This billet must to blooming NORVAL go: At the next turn awaits my trusty spy; I'll give it him refitted for his master.
author: Home, John, 1722-1808.
title: Douglas: a tragedy. As it is acted at the Theatre-Royal in Covent-Garden.

text: The deed's a doing now, that makes me lord Of these rich valleys, and a chief of power.
author: Home, John, 1722-1808.
title: Douglas: a tragedy. As it is acted at the Theatre-Royal in Covent-Garden.

text: Three weeks, three little weeks, with wings of down, Had o'er us flown, when my lov'd lord was call'd To fight his father's battles; and with him, In spite of all my tears, did MALCOLM go.
author: Home, John, 1722-1808.
title: Douglas: a tragedy. As it is acted at the Theatre-Royal in Covent-Garden.

text: Thou speak'st a woman's, hear a warrior's wish: Right from their native land, the stormy north, May the wind blow, till every keel is fix'd Immoveable in Caledonia's strand!
author: Home, John, 1722-1808.
title: Douglas: a tragedy. As it is acted at the Theatre-Royal in Covent-Garden.

text: Thestor wants power to work upon the king; That power I'll quickly furnish; play the son An engine on his sire.
author: Delap, J. (John), 1725-1812.
title: The royal suppliants. A tragedy: As performed at the Theatre-Royal in Drury-Lane.

text: True, sacred seer; Thy word's the word of heaven; as heaven thou heed'st, Oh, holy Demophon! hear and obey.
author: Delap, J. (John), 1725-1812.
title: The royal suppliants. A tragedy: As performed at the Theatre-Royal in Drury-Lane.

text: From Alcander, lady, A letter to Eurystheus was dispatched, To storm th' Athenian camp, while Acamas Was prisoner.
author: Delap, J. (John), 1725-1812.
title: The royal suppliants. A tragedy: As performed at the Theatre-Royal in Drury-Lane.

text: Alas, too noble!—let me gaze thee o'er; Let me find where that godlike spirit dwells, That lifts thee thus aloft.
author: Delap, J. (John), 1725-1812.
title: The royal suppliants. A tragedy: As performed at the Theatre-Royal in Drury-Lane.

text: When thus burst forth the awful voice:—"No steer, "No blood of bulls will now propitiate heaven "To grant success.
author: Delap, J. (John), 1725-1812.
title: The royal suppliants. A tragedy: As performed at the Theatre-Royal in Drury-Lane.

text: Summon all thy powers, For thou need'st all, at this tremendous trial, Unhappy queen!—that sacrilegious villain Dispatched a ruffian, with a secret dagger, T' assassinate thy Hyllus.
author: Delap, J. (John), 1725-1812.
title: The royal suppliants. A tragedy: As performed at the Theatre-Royal in Drury-Lane.

text: Let no thought, Ill-omen'd look, or word, this place profane; With solemn silence all ye priests of heaven Attend.
author: Delap, J. (John), 1725-1812.
title: The royal suppliants. A tragedy: As performed at the Theatre-Royal in Drury-Lane.

text: A little longer, balmy sleep, Spread thy still pinions; in oblivious dews Her senses steep a little longer yet; Grief soon enough will rouse them.
author: Delap, J. (John), 1725-1812.
title: The royal suppliants. A tragedy: As performed at the Theatre-Royal in Drury-Lane.

text: Ah, more of horror yet, Unhappy queen, remains! much horror more, To wound a mother's, and a sister's breast!
author: Delap, J. (John), 1725-1812.
title: The royal suppliants. A tragedy: As performed at the Theatre-Royal in Drury-Lane.

text: May it check Eurystheus' impious rage; and, like a tower, Baffle the bloody tyrant, who from Argos Exiles the royal race; and now forbids Each state to shelter our distress.
author: Delap, J. (John), 1725-1812.
title: The royal suppliants. A tragedy: As performed at the Theatre-Royal in Drury-Lane.

text: And if war e'er was just, and heaven approved, 'Tis now; when Deianira and Macaria, By a vile tyrant exiled, suppliants come To thee, and to the God whom thy religion Doth venerate in that shrine; which scarce protects them From the brute outrage of a haughty herald.
author: Delap, J. (John), 1725-1812.
title: The royal suppliants. A tragedy: As performed at the Theatre-Royal in Drury-Lane.

text: Far as the eye From yonder tower can reach, a cloud of dust Darkens the air; while thro' it break by fits Bright transient flashes; such as to the sun Glitter from pikes and helmed heads: it seems Hitherward moving.
author: Delap, J. (John), 1725-1812.
title: The royal suppliants. A tragedy: As performed at the Theatre-Royal in Drury-Lane.

text: Her voice, her mien!—such the bright blaze of beauty That burst on me at Argos!—What rude hand Could injure that fair form; which my heart worship'd, When my enchanted eyes first gazed upon thee?
author: Delap, J. (John), 1725-1812.
title: The royal suppliants. A tragedy: As performed at the Theatre-Royal in Drury-Lane.

text: And I the rather encline to this Conclusion, because it is agreeable to the Promise and Prediction of our Saviour himself, while he was upon Earth.
author: Hayley, William, 1657-1715.
title: A sermon preach'd in Lambeth-chapel, at the consecration of ... John Lord Bishop of Bangor, on Sunday, Jan. 4th 1701/2. By William Hayley,:

text: And that particularly Philip, who was one of the Seven Deacons, and is called the Evangelist, went down to Samaria, and preached Christ to them. v. 5.
author: Hayley, William, 1657-1715.
title: A sermon preach'd in Lambeth-chapel, at the consecration of ... John Lord Bishop of Bangor, on Sunday, Jan. 4th 1701/2. By William Hayley,:

text: The Priesthood was a natural right of Primogeniture at first, and God by a particular Command order'd the First-Born to be Sanctified to his Service; and 'tis no question but these are the Priests which we read of before the giving of the Law.
author: Hayley, William, 1657-1715.
title: A sermon preach'd in Lambeth-chapel, at the consecration of ... John Lord Bishop of Bangor, on Sunday, Jan. 4th 1701/2. By William Hayley,:

text: We are then in the next place to consider the different Employments of these Three Orders, and the different Powers that enabled them to discharge the same.
author: Hayley, William, 1657-1715.
title: A sermon preach'd in Lambeth-chapel, at the consecration of ... John Lord Bishop of Bangor, on Sunday, Jan. 4th 1701/2. By William Hayley,:

text: The Lord said unto Moses go down, charge the People least they break through unto the Lord, to gaze and many of them perish; and let the Priests also which come near to the Lord, Sanctify themselves, least the Lord break forth among them.
author: Hayley, William, 1657-1715.
title: A sermon preach'd in Lambeth-chapel, at the consecration of ... John Lord Bishop of Bangor, on Sunday, Jan. 4th 1701/2. By William Hayley,:

text: We must therefore hasten to the Third thing to be considered, the end and design of this Dispensation, in these Words.
author: Hayley, William, 1657-1715.
title: A sermon preach'd in Lambeth-chapel, at the consecration of ... John Lord Bishop of Bangor, on Sunday, Jan. 4th 1701/2. By William Hayley,:

text: Till we all come in the Ʋnity of the Faith, and of the Knowledge of the Son of God unto a perfect Man, unto the measure of the Stature of the fulness of Christ.
author: Hayley, William, 1657-1715.
title: A sermon preach'd in Lambeth-chapel, at the consecration of ... John Lord Bishop of Bangor, on Sunday, Jan. 4th 1701/2. By William Hayley,:

text: Thus our Lord Jesus when he had conquered Satan and Sin, and Hell and Death, and made his Triumphant Entry into Heaven, distributed the different Gifts of his holy Spirit, in such kinds and such proportions as the Persons and Offices required to which they were conveyed. v. 8.
author: Hayley, William, 1657-1715.
title: A sermon preach'd in Lambeth-chapel, at the consecration of ... John Lord Bishop of Bangor, on Sunday, Jan. 4th 1701/2. By William Hayley,:

text: That so Imitating the Apostolical Churches in Doctrine, Practice and Discipline, we may be an Exemplary Part of the Church Militant in this World, and a Glorious Part of the Church Triumphant in a Future.
author: Hayley, William, 1657-1715.
title: A sermon preach'd in Lambeth-chapel, at the consecration of ... John Lord Bishop of Bangor, on Sunday, Jan. 4th 1701/2. By William Hayley,:

text: Behold I send to you Prophets, and Wise men, and Scribes, and some of them you shall kill and crucify, &c. Where there are only these Three Orders promis'd; the Second of which though here first placed, are called by the same name as in the Text, Prophets.
author: Hayley, William, 1657-1715.
title: A sermon preach'd in Lambeth-chapel, at the consecration of ... John Lord Bishop of Bangor, on Sunday, Jan. 4th 1701/2. By William Hayley,:

text: And that this is the Faith here mentioned is evident from what follows, which is an enumeration of some of the great Powers of this Faith.
author: Hayley, William, 1657-1715.
title: A sermon preach'd in Lambeth-chapel, at the consecration of ... John Lord Bishop of Bangor, on Sunday, Jan. 4th 1701/2. By William Hayley,:

text: And this is consonant to what the Apostle says upon the same occasion, 1 Cor. 12. 25.
author: Hayley, William, 1657-1715.
title: A sermon preach'd in Lambeth-chapel, at the consecration of ... John Lord Bishop of Bangor, on Sunday, Jan. 4th 1701/2. By William Hayley,:

text: By Knowledge, the gift of Christian Prophets, seems to be meant the Understanding of the Scripture and the Mysteries of the Gospel; how they were foretold in the Prophecies of old, and how accomplish'd in our Saviour Jesus; and therefore St. Paul joyns these things together 1 Cor. 13. 2.
author: Hayley, William, 1657-1715.
title: A sermon preach'd in Lambeth-chapel, at the consecration of ... John Lord Bishop of Bangor, on Sunday, Jan. 4th 1701/2. By William Hayley,:

text: Just Heaven! if e'er The Wretched's Prayer I hear'd, and eas'd his Pain; Now in return, Let me not mourn, Nor ask Relief in vain.
author: Lillo, George, 1693-1739.
title: Britannia and Batavia: a masque. Written on the marriage of the Princess Royal with his Highness the Prince of Orange. By the late Mr. Lillo.

text: Europe sees few so great, and none so blest: Freedom, and Wealth and Power are in your Hand.
author: Lillo, George, 1693-1739.
title: Britannia and Batavia: a masque. Written on the marriage of the Princess Royal with his Highness the Prince of Orange. By the late Mr. Lillo.

text: You Terror of Britannia's Foes, Whose Valour does maintain Her Power, where'er the Ocean flows, Or stormy Tempests reign; For Liberty restor'd, Now let your Joys o'erflow: As on the Shore The Billows roar, When the stormy Winds do blow.
author: Lillo, George, 1693-1739.
title: Britannia and Batavia: a masque. Written on the marriage of the Princess Royal with his Highness the Prince of Orange. By the late Mr. Lillo.

text: Consult not Reason, close the Eye of Sense; So shall you judge aright, and see the better.
author: Lillo, George, 1693-1739.
title: Britannia and Batavia: a masque. Written on the marriage of the Princess Royal with his Highness the Prince of Orange. By the late Mr. Lillo.

text: Just Heaven! if e'er The Wretched's Prayer I hear'd, and eas'd his Pain; Now in return, Let me not mourn, Nor ask Relief in vain.
author: Lillo, George, 1693-1739.
title: Britannia and Batavia: a masque. Written on the marriage of the Princess Royal with his Highness the Prince of Orange. By the late Mr. Lillo.

text: Taste of this Cup, and be enlighten'd: Thou hast lost no Freedom, Except the fatal Liberty to err; And Riches are but Snares; Those we'll remove: But in return the Church Shall pour forth all her Benedictions on thee: Thou shalt abound in Grace.
author: Lillo, George, 1693-1739.
title: Britannia and Batavia: a masque. Written on the marriage of the Princess Royal with his Highness the Prince of Orange. By the late Mr. Lillo.

text: Not so, bright Chief; Unable to defend her From proud Hispania's fierce and cruel Power, I've brought her here, To seek Protection from Britannia's Arms.
author: Lillo, George, 1693-1739.
title: Britannia and Batavia: a masque. Written on the marriage of the Princess Royal with his Highness the Prince of Orange. By the late Mr. Lillo.

text: Distinguish'd as thou art, Prudent, and brave, and of approv'd Integrity, Thou can'st not doubt thy Welcome: Yet let me wonder, high and friendly Guest, Why thou hast left thy Charge.
author: Lillo, George, 1693-1739.
title: Britannia and Batavia: a masque. Written on the marriage of the Princess Royal with his Highness the Prince of Orange. By the late Mr. Lillo.

text: Those gentler Methods, May first be tried; If these shou'd seem too mild, You must impute it to our tender Mercy.
author: Lillo, George, 1693-1739.
title: Britannia and Batavia: a masque. Written on the marriage of the Princess Royal with his Highness the Prince of Orange. By the late Mr. Lillo.

text: Rest is the Recompence of Toil, The noblest Fruit of Conquest, Peace; Learn but Content, high-favour'd Isle, And nothing can your Bliss increase.
author: Lillo, George, 1693-1739.
title: Britannia and Batavia: a masque. Written on the marriage of the Princess Royal with his Highness the Prince of Orange. By the late Mr. Lillo.

text: Thou great and just Defender of th'opprest, See at your Feet poor and distrest Batavia: Her Cities ras'd, her sacred Rights destroy'd, Her Nobles slaughter'd, and her Sons enslav'd. O whither shall I turn me, whither fly, If you refuse your Aid?
author: Lillo, George, 1693-1739.
title: Britannia and Batavia: a masque. Written on the marriage of the Princess Royal with his Highness the Prince of Orange. By the late Mr. Lillo.

text: While Heaven refers to you the Fate Of Europe; while you hold the Scale, And may dispense the casting Weight, Justice and Virtue must prevail.
author: Lillo, George, 1693-1739.
title: Britannia and Batavia: a masque. Written on the marriage of the Princess Royal with his Highness the Prince of Orange. By the late Mr. Lillo.

text: SLEEP, fair Britannia, sleep secure; Thy own Ithuriel, happy in his Charge, Thy Guardian Angel wakes.
author: Lillo, George, 1693-1739.
title: Britannia and Batavia: a masque. Written on the marriage of the Princess Royal with his Highness the Prince of Orange. By the late Mr. Lillo.

text: Such a tendency has the slave-trade to debauch men's minds, and harden them to every feeling of humanity!
author: Equiano, Olaudah, b. 1745.
title: The interesting narrative of the life of Olaudah Equiano: or Gustavus Vassa, the African. Written by himself. [pt.1]

text: We soon got loaded again, and returned to Montserrat; and there, amongst the rest of the islands, I sold my goods well; and in this manner I continued trading during the year 1764; meeting with various scenes of imposition, as usual.
author: Equiano, Olaudah, b. 1745.
title: The interesting narrative of the life of Olaudah Equiano: or Gustavus Vassa, the African. Written by himself. [pt.1]

text: After staying here some time till our vessel was loaded, and I had bought in my little traffic, we sailed from this agreeable spot for Montserrat, once more to encounter the raging surfs.
author: Equiano, Olaudah, b. 1745.
title: The interesting narrative of the life of Olaudah Equiano: or Gustavus Vassa, the African. Written by himself. [pt.1]

text: When we got ready, we joined a very large fleet at Spithead, commanded by Commodore Keppel, which was destined against Belle-Isle, and with a number of transport ships with troops on board to make a descent on the place, we sailed once more in quest of fame.
author: Equiano, Olaudah, b. 1745.

text: O horrible Abuse and Blasphemy against God and his Word! and even all Men are deluded and deceived thereby: Verily, verily, they deserve the Name they give to others, of denying the Word of God.
author: Richardson, Samuel, fl. 1643-1658.
title: Of the torments of Hell: the foundation and pillars thereof discovered, searched, shaken, and removed. ...

title: Of the torments of Hell: the foundation and pillars thereof discovered, searched, shaken, and removed. ...

text: Have they a plentiful Eſtate? they do not ſpend it in making proviſion for the Fleſh; nor do they covetouſly hoard it up, but imploy a conſiderable part of it in ſupporting the Worſhip of God, propagating the Goſpel of Chriſt, and relieving thoſe that are in diſtreſs.
author: Harrison, Thomas, fl. 1700.
title: A funeral sermon on Mordecai Abbott Esq. preach'd at Lorimers Hall, April the 7th, 1700 / by Thomas Harrison.

text: Their Souls ſhall be perfectly conform'd to his human Soul, in Purity and Felicity, and their Bodies ſhall be faſhion'd into the likeneſs of his glorious Body.
author: Harrison, Thomas, fl. 1700.
title: A funeral sermon on Mordecai Abbott Esq. preach'd at Lorimers Hall, April the 7th, 1700 / by Thomas Harrison.

text: The Soul muſt needs have a great Affection for its Body, and when ſeparate from it, deſires a reunion.
author: Harrison, Thomas, fl. 1700.
title: A funeral sermon on Mordecai Abbott Esq. preach'd at Lorimers Hall, April the 7th, 1700 / by Thomas Harrison.

text: Since this is a matter of everlaſting importance, how ſtrict ſhould we be in the examination of our ſelves, that we may come to a due reſult in our own Minds about it?
author: Harrison, Thomas, fl. 1700.
title: A funeral sermon on Mordecai Abbott Esq. preach'd at Lorimers Hall, April the 7th, 1700 / by Thomas Harrison.

text: Nothing ſhort of an Inveſtiture with Chriſt's perfect Righteouſneſs can render our Perſons acceptable to the moſt High; and till they become ſo, our moſt ſplendid Services will be abominable in his ſight.
author: Harrison, Thomas, fl. 1700.
title: A funeral sermon on Mordecai Abbott Esq. preach'd at Lorimers Hall, April the 7th, 1700 / by Thomas Harrison.

text: Then ſhall Men return and diſcern between the righteous and the wicked; between him that ſerveth God, and him that ſerveth him not.
author: Harrison, Thomas, fl. 1700.
title: A funeral sermon on Mordecai Abbott Esq. preach'd at Lorimers Hall, April the 7th, 1700 / by Thomas Harrison.

text: I. I am to deſcribe the faithful Servants of Chriſt, who they are that ſhall be own'd as ſuch by the Supreme Lord, when he comes to Judgment.
author: Harrison, Thomas, fl. 1700.
title: A funeral sermon on Mordecai Abbott Esq. preach'd at Lorimers Hall, April the 7th, 1700 / by Thomas Harrison.

text: But he is gone, his place ſhall know him no more: having ſerv'd his own Generation by the Will of God, he is fallen aſleep; God hath call'd him away in the midſt of his days, when many unprofitable Servants are left behind.
author: Harrison, Thomas, fl. 1700.
title: A funeral sermon on Mordecai Abbott Esq. preach'd at Lorimers Hall, April the 7th, 1700 / by Thomas Harrison.

text: But I conceive our Lord chiefly reſpects the General Judgment, when the Trial will be public, the Sentence pronounc'd with the moſt awful Solemnity; and the Happineſs or Miſery of every Man compleated.
author: Harrison, Thomas, fl. 1700.
title: A funeral sermon on Mordecai Abbott Esq. preach'd at Lorimers Hall, April the 7th, 1700 / by Thomas Harrison.

text: THO I readily comply'd with Your deſire in preaching the following Sermon, I could not without ſome reluctancy conſent to the printing of it: But my great Obligations both to Your deceas'd Husband, and Your ſelf, gave Your Requeſt the force of a Command.
author: Harrison, Thomas, fl. 1700.
title: A funeral sermon on Mordecai Abbott Esq. preach'd at Lorimers Hall, April the 7th, 1700 / by Thomas Harrison.

text: Their Perſons cannot therefore their Actions cannot; becauſe they are the Products of a Nature at variance with him, a Nature that is not, nor cannot be ſubject to his Law.
author: Harrison, Thomas, fl. 1700.
title: A funeral sermon on Mordecai Abbott Esq. preach'd at Lorimers Hall, April the 7th, 1700 / by Thomas Harrison.

text: When we enter into the other World, we ſhall be freed from all ſorrowful, and from all ſinful Evils.
author: Harrison, Thomas, fl. 1700.
title: A funeral sermon on Mordecai Abbott Esq. preach'd at Lorimers Hall, April the 7th, 1700 / by Thomas Harrison.

text: This is expreſt by Joy, becauſe the fruition of it will produce a triumphant and unſpeakable Joy in thoſe that enter into it.
author: Harrison, Thomas, fl. 1700.
title: A funeral sermon on Mordecai Abbott Esq. preach'd at Lorimers Hall, April the 7th, 1700 / by Thomas Harrison.

text: The Duke of Braganza reflecting on theſe high Marks of Confidence; and how little agreeable this was to the uſual Conduct of that Miniſter, began to ſuſpect the Sincerity of his Intentions, which, in the end, caus'd the Author to fall into that Snare which he laid for another.
author: Vertot, abbé de, 1655-1735.
title: The history of the revolution in Portugal in the year, 1640, or, An account of their revolt from Spain and setting the crown on the head of Don John of Braganza, father to Don Pedro, the present king

text: That the chief Conſpirators being of ſeveral of the firſt Houſes of the Kingdom, their Kindred would be ſo many ſecret Enemies of the Government, and the deſire to revenge their Death, would be the unhappy ſource of perpetual Plots.
author: Vertot, abbé de, 1655-1735.
title: The history of the revolution in Portugal in the year, 1640, or, An account of their revolt from Spain and setting the crown on the head of Don John of Braganza, father to Don Pedro, the present king

text: That the Death of Count Egmont in Flanders, and of the Guiſes in France, had both fatal Conſequences; that to Pardon ſome, and inflict a leſs ſevere Puniſhment than Death, would win the Hearts of all Perſons, and oblige them, their Relations and Friends, to act by motives of Gratitude.
author: Vertot, abbé de, 1655-1735.
title: The history of the revolution in Portugal in the year, 1640, or, An account of their revolt from Spain and setting the crown on the head of Don John of Braganza, father to Don Pedro, the present king

text: The Great Men of the Kingdom could not ſee his Elevation without a ſecret Envy, and moſt of the Nobility, (who had no ſhare in the Conſpiracy) were ſilent, waiting for the Iſſue before they would declare their Sentiments.
author: Vertot, abbé de, 1655-1735.
title: The history of the revolution in Portugal in the year, 1640, or, An account of their revolt from Spain and setting the crown on the head of Don John of Braganza, father to Don Pedro, the present king

text: He knew very well the Ancient and Natural Antipathy of theſe Neighbouring Nations muſt needs render the Spaniſh Government hateful to the Portugueſe; and that Nation could never tamely ſee all Places in the State fill'd with Strangers, or Fellows of mean Extraction, whoſe only Merit was their entire Devotion to the Court.
author: Vertot, abbé de, 1655-1735.
title: The history of the revolution in Portugal in the year, 1640, or, An account of their revolt from Spain and setting the crown on the head of Don John of Braganza, father to Don Pedro, the present king

text: Thus finding every one firm, undaunted, and impatient to be reveng'd on the Spaniards, he conferr'd with d' Almeida, Mendoza d' Almada, and Mello; who finding all things in ſuch a condition as they wiſh'd, agreed on Saturday the Firſt of December for the Execution.
author: Vertot, abbé de, 1655-1735.
title: The history of the revolution in Portugal in the year, 1640, or, An account of their revolt from Spain and setting the crown on the head of Don John of Braganza, father to Don Pedro, the present king

text: However, d'Almada did not dare to rely on his Oaths and Aſſurances, but was mightily diſturb'd at this Accident; And keeping a watchful Eye on this Man, he gave notice to the Conſpirators of this Adventure.
author: Vertot, abbé de, 1655-1735.
title: The history of the revolution in Portugal in the year, 1640, or, An account of their revolt from Spain and setting the crown on the head of Don John of Braganza, father to Don Pedro, the present king

text: I'm afraid, that inſtead of Reſtoring the Liberties of Portugal, your Attempt will only prove deſtructive to it, and furniſh the Spaniards with a Pretence, which they have long ſought for, to accompliſh the Ruin of this Kingdom.
author: Vertot, abbé de, 1655-1735.
title: The history of the revolution in Portugal in the year, 1640, or, An account of their revolt from Spain and setting the crown on the head of Don John of Braganza, father to Don Pedro, the present king

text: That it was not ſufficient for him to have the Nobility on his ſide, unleſs they were ſupported by the Great Men of the Kingdom, but very far from hoping they would come over to his Intereſt.
author: Vertot, abbé de, 1655-1735.
title: The history of the revolution in Portugal in the year, 1640, or, An account of their revolt from Spain and setting the crown on the head of Don John of Braganza, father to Don Pedro, the present king

text: Among theſe, none labour'd more effectually than Pinto Ribeuro, Comptroller of his Houſhold, to ſet all Machines on work, and form a Scheme for the Advancement of his Maſter.
author: Vertot, abbé de, 1655-1735.
title: The history of the revolution in Portugal in the year, 1640, or, An account of their revolt from Spain and setting the crown on the head of Don John of Braganza, father to Don Pedro, the present king

text: This was the Fate of Michael Vaſconcellos, a Portugueze by Birth, but an Enemy to his Country, and a Spaniard by his Inclination.
author: Vertot, abbé de, 1655-1735.
title: The history of the revolution in Portugal in the year, 1640, or, An account of their revolt from Spain and setting the crown on the head of Don John of Braganza, father to Don Pedro, the present king

text: He diſpatched able Embaſſadors to procure himſelf to be owned, to make Alliances, and raiſe new Enemies to the Houſe of Auſtria.
author: Vertot, abbé de, 1655-1735.
title: The history of the revolution in Portugal in the year, 1640, or, An account of their revolt from Spain and setting the crown on the head of Don John of Braganza, father to Don Pedro, the present king

text: The Conde Duke obſerv'd him with ſo ſtrict an Eye, that if his manner of Living had not been entirely the Effect of his Natural Inclination, that vigilant Miniſter would have ſoon deſcry'd it; and this muſt have been fatal to his Eaſe and Fortune.
author: Vertot, abbé de, 1655-1735.
title: The history of the revolution in Portugal in the year, 1640, or, An account of their revolt from Spain and setting the crown on the head of Don John of Braganza, father to Don Pedro, the present king

text: In vain, alas! had the wiſe men of this world, for about four thouſand years, exercis'd their wits, in ſearching out ſuch perfect Rules of living, as ſhine ſo illuſtriouſly in the lives of true Chriſtians.
author: Dawes, William, Sir, 1671-1724.
title: Christianity best propagated by the good lives of Christians a sermon preach'd before the gentlemen educated at Merchant Taylors School at St. Mary le Bow, Jan. 16, 1699 / by Sir William Dawes, Barone

text: To conclude all; If we really deſire to ſhow our love and reſpect for our School, as we pretend, and to give it a Character and Reputation in the world, let our good works become Advocates for it.
author: Dawes, William, Sir, 1671-1724.
title: Christianity best propagated by the good lives of Christians a sermon preach'd before the gentlemen educated at Merchant Taylors School at St. Mary le Bow, Jan. 16, 1699 / by Sir William Dawes, Barone

text: The Righteous, ſay the wicked, in the wiſdom of Solomon, c. 2. v. 12, &c. is not for our turn, and he is clean contrary to our doings, he upbraideth us with our offending the Law, and objecteth to our infamy the tranſgreſſing of our education.
author: Dawes, William, Sir, 1671-1724.
title: Christianity best propagated by the good lives of Christians a sermon preach'd before the gentlemen educated at Merchant Taylors School at St. Mary le Bow, Jan. 16, 1699 / by Sir William Dawes, Barone

text: In one word, we ſhould, as the Author of the Epiſtle to the Hebrews exhorts us, often conſider one another, to provoke unto love and to good works.
author: Dawes, William, Sir, 1671-1724.
title: Christianity best propagated by the good lives of Christians a sermon preach'd before the gentlemen educated at Merchant Taylors School at St. Mary le Bow, Jan. 16, 1699 / by Sir William Dawes, Barone

text: No certainly, the work was more than humane, and not to be accompliſh'd but by the infinite and multifarious wiſdom, which ſo richly dwelt in our Jeſus, who has been in theſe laſt days the Author of it.
author: Dawes, William, Sir, 1671-1724.
title: Christianity best propagated by the good lives of Christians a sermon preach'd before the gentlemen educated at Merchant Taylors School at St. Mary le Bow, Jan. 16, 1699 / by Sir William Dawes, Barone

text: That the unblameable, holy, and exemplary lives of Chriſtians are a very likely means, both of bringing over Ʋnbelievers, and converting wicked.
author: Dawes, William, Sir, 1671-1724.
title: Christianity best propagated by the good lives of Christians a sermon preach'd before the gentlemen educated at Merchant Taylors School at St. Mary le Bow, Jan. 16, 1699 / by Sir William Dawes, Barone

text: But ſince every line and feature of a true Chriſtian is exactly anſwerable and agreeable to all our pureſt and moſt refin'd notions of God, it ſeems highly unreaſonable, not to acknowledge him for his Father.
author: Dawes, William, Sir, 1671-1724.
title: Christianity best propagated by the good lives of Christians a sermon preach'd before the gentlemen educated at Merchant Taylors School at St. Mary le Bow, Jan. 16, 1699 / by Sir William Dawes, Barone

text: That this is true, as to Ʋnbelievers, might be ſufficiently prov'd from conſidering: That the holy Scriptures do recommend to Chriſtians this method of converting Ʋnbelievers, which, it is moſt certain, they would not do, were it not fit and proper for this end.
author: Dawes, William, Sir, 1671-1724.
title: Christianity best propagated by the good lives of Christians a sermon preach'd before the gentlemen educated at Merchant Taylors School at St. Mary le Bow, Jan. 16, 1699 / by Sir William Dawes, Barone

text: Secondly, The holy and exemplary lives of Chriſtians will be a ſure means of recommending them to the favour and eſteem, love and friendſhip of Ʋnbelievers: and conſequently a ſure means of gaining opportunities of converſing familiarly with them, inſinuating truth into them, and making them willing and eaſie to receive it.
author: Dawes, William, Sir, 1671-1724.
title: Christianity best propagated by the good lives of Christians a sermon preach'd before the gentlemen educated at Merchant Taylors School at St. Mary le Bow, Jan. 16, 1699 / by Sir William Dawes, Barone

text: Let us I ſay, having theſe opportunities, theſe encouragements, theſe obligations, be glad to diſtribute and willing to communicate.
author: Dawes, William, Sir, 1671-1724.
title: Christianity best propagated by the good lives of Christians a sermon preach'd before the gentlemen educated at Merchant Taylors School at St. Mary le Bow, Jan. 16, 1699 / by Sir William Dawes, Barone

text: Were there any thing in the lives of Chriſtians, led according to the Rules of their Religion, either unlike to, or unworthy of, God, this would be a ſufficient argument againſt the Divinity of it; for God certainly can do nothing, either unlike to, or unworthy of, himſelf.
author: Dawes, William, Sir, 1671-1724.
title: Christianity best propagated by the good lives of Christians a sermon preach'd before the gentlemen educated at Merchant Taylors School at St. Mary le Bow, Jan. 16, 1699 / by Sir William Dawes, Barone

text: And the reaſon of this is plain: becauſe the Arguments of ſuch men are always ſuſpected, and, they themſelves being manifeſt Hypocrites, their Arguments generally paſs for ſuch too.
author: Dawes, William, Sir, 1671-1724.
title: Christianity best propagated by the good lives of Christians a sermon preach'd before the gentlemen educated at Merchant Taylors School at St. Mary le Bow, Jan. 16, 1699 / by Sir William Dawes, Barone

text: And what can an erring Chriſtian poſſibly need or deſire more, in order to his amendment, than to be made ſenſible of his errours, and at once inſtructed and encourag'd to forſake them?
author: Dawes, William, Sir, 1671-1724.
title: Christianity best propagated by the good lives of Christians a sermon preach'd before the gentlemen educated at Merchant Taylors School at St. Mary le Bow, Jan. 16, 1699 / by Sir William Dawes, Barone

text: But had he given us Riches, Rank, and Name, And we'd attack'd his Life, and robb'd his Fame, You'd punish in one Culprit! with what Face?
author: Bentley, R. (Richard), 1708-1782.
title: A petition to the Right Hon. Mr. --, in favour of Mr. Maclean: By a lady.

text: Tho' Doctrine's fall before the Scythe of Time, Shall his believing what they taught, be Crime?
author: Bentley, R. (Richard), 1708-1782.
title: A petition to the Right Hon. Mr. --, in favour of Mr. Maclean: By a lady.

text: Too sure we beg, for Life we beg, 'tis true; If we had robb'd enough, we need not sue; We own our Guilt, with Tears Contrition-sent, Oh! let it hurt us not, that we repent!
author: Bentley, R. (Richard), 1708-1782.
title: A petition to the Right Hon. Mr. --, in favour of Mr. Maclean: By a lady.

text: Knowlege, Parts, and Sense; So, could thy Judgment in our Steerage err, Might E—t's Eagle-Eye wink o'er the Blur.
author: Bentley, R. (Richard), 1708-1782.
title: A petition to the Right Hon. Mr. --, in favour of Mr. Maclean: By a lady.

text: Would Tyrant Custom but so far recede, That for Maclean we might in Person plead, A hundred Hoops thy Levee-Room should crowd; Nay, shudder not, indeed we'd not be loud.
author: Bentley, R. (Richard), 1708-1782.
title: A petition to the Right Hon. Mr. --, in favour of Mr. Maclean: By a lady.

text: Un-plac'd, un-pension'd, as in Bribes unshar'd, What Gratitude to rob the Son debarr'd?
author: Bentley, R. (Richard), 1708-1782.
title: A petition to the Right Hon. Mr. --, in favour of Mr. Maclean: By a lady.

text: But English, Men of Business, know us ill, Think Pudding th' utmost Efforts of our Skill; Us, but Companions for the trifling Vein, And form'd to Satisfy, not Entertain.
author: Bentley, R. (Richard), 1708-1782.
title: A petition to the Right Hon. Mr. --, in favour of Mr. Maclean: By a lady.

text: Let selfish Man jostle for Power and Place, Barter his Vote, turn Patriot, lie, caress; Sincerer Woman has a nobler End, Unknown to Levees,—'tis to serve a Friend!
author: Bentley, R. (Richard), 1708-1782.
title: A petition to the Right Hon. Mr. --, in favour of Mr. Maclean: By a lady.

text: There Beauty often pacifies the Law, And tears a Fav'rite from its Iron Jaw; There the stern Judge remits the forfeit Life, T' a handsome Cousin, or a lovely Wife.
author: Bentley, R. (Richard), 1708-1782.
title: A petition to the Right Hon. Mr. --, in favour of Mr. Maclean: By a lady.

text: Yet, what we may — to Thee I write, And almost dry my Tears, and blame my Fright.
author: Bentley, R. (Richard), 1708-1782.
title: A petition to the Right Hon. Mr. --, in favour of Mr. Maclean: By a lady.

text: Reflecting, in Politeness you, as well As in your Politics, the French excell; And Heav'n-born Mercy can't from him be far, Who seal'd with Peace the Lyon-mouth of War.
author: Bentley, R. (Richard), 1708-1782.
title: A petition to the Right Hon. Mr. --, in favour of Mr. Maclean: By a lady.

text: Capricious Mistress! on the first she pours Her Vengeance, and Rewards on t'other show'rs; Brav'ry on Hounslow with a Gibbet pays, While look'd-on Sea-fights to new Honours raise.
author: Bentley, R. (Richard), 1708-1782.
title: A petition to the Right Hon. Mr. --, in favour of Mr. Maclean: By a lady.

text: IF ever Statesman melted at Distress, Nor chose to make it More instead of Less; If they retain a Sense of human Things, And deign to look on Mortals down from Kings, List! list! oh — whom Three Realms obey, To the sad Purport of my weeping Lay.
author: Bentley, R. (Richard), 1708-1782.
title: A petition to the Right Hon. Mr. --, in favour of Mr. Maclean: By a lady.

title: The lasses of Kinghorn. Tune of Clavers and his Highland men.

text: The Sailers they leugh heartily for to behold the ſport, To ſee the Captains run away for ſhelter to the Boat: But up ſpake General Paterſon. ſhe ſpake with Counſel good, And ſhe deſir'd to ſound retreat. for ſhe would have no Blood.
title: The lasses of Kinghorn. Tune of Clavers and his Highland men.

text: She took a Knock into her hand of Bleeching ſhe is good, She caus'd the Serjant ſtagger in the place where he ſtood.
title: The lasses of Kinghorn. Tune of Clavers and his Highland men.

text: And all the Battels we were at, we were never in ſuch Fears, O fy on you for Sogers that ever you took pay, The Laſſes of Kinghorn Town they made you run away.

text: How willingly driven, Impatient of ſtay, They take Wing and away, And crowd and preſs upward to Heaven!
title: The Consecration of Marcellus an ode in memory of the illustrious prince William, Duke of Gloucester.

text: Show her all the God: Let her look, and look again: This the reward of all her Pain, She once upon the Beauteous Work beſtow'd: Let her feed the Greedy Eye, Upon the lovely Effigie.
title: The Consecration of Marcellus an ode in memory of the illustrious prince William, Duke of Gloucester.

text: And fearful Clings about the Feather'd Neck: Stars, and Air, and Clouds, Float and Glide beneath him: Now he approaches the Empyreal Sphere; Now he's there, he's there: He comes, attend ye Deityes, All that Tread the Skyes.
title: The Consecration of Marcellus an ode in memory of the illustrious prince William, Duke of Gloucester.

text: Or when on Foot, how liftily he Treads, And with Commanding State the willing Squadrons leads: Know'ſt that Ruling, that Imperial Air?
title: The Consecration of Marcellus an ode in memory of the illustrious prince William, Duke of Gloucester.

text: Are we deceived? or was it Jove, Who in his Eagles form, Deſcended from above: And from the Burning Bed, Snatcht a better Ganymed?

text: Only for Caeſar's ſake the Capitol we ſpare, And give him Leave ſtill to Inhabit there: But let his other Statues fall.

text: Behind, another Proſpect fills the Eye: Advancing Youths in ſhining Armour dreſt, Move to the Great Solemnity, Their Sorrow in their Tears and Drooping Looks expreſt.
title: The Consecration of Marcellus an ode in memory of the illustrious prince William, Duke of Gloucester.

text: Laviſh in Reaching Rays Diſpence, A ſtrong Enliv'ning Influence, And to the Proſtrate Earth divide Impartial Light; Compar'd with This, how Fading and how Dim, Does Young Caeſareo's Glory ſeem!
title: The Consecration of Marcellus an ode in memory of the illustrious prince William, Duke of Gloucester.

text: Such was the Lovely Boy: So much their Pride, ſo much their Joy: To whom were due theſe Rites, and Univerſal Woe.

text: See from the Burning Pile aſcending Fire, And curling Flames aſpire: The frighted Eagle leaves the Top, And Gently ſtooping down, Takes the mighty Burden up, And pleas'd with the Prey, He Mounts the Bright way.
title: The Consecration of Marcellus an ode in memory of the illustrious prince William, Duke of Gloucester.

text: Fain would I with Ambitious Pace, A new extended Scheme of Future Glory Trace, But Oh! a warning Fear forbids my Haſt, And tells me, that thou ſhin'ſt too bright to laſt: I'ſt a Miſtake?
title: The Consecration of Marcellus an ode in memory of the illustrious prince William, Duke of Gloucester.

text: This was the Valiant Band, That once Enjoy'd the Princes firſt Command: How Beautifully ſad their Grief appears!
title: The Consecration of Marcellus an ode in memory of the illustrious prince William, Duke of Gloucester.

text: And by his Father Jove decreed a Deny: Learn from the Gods, ye Romans; learn to Give Thoſe Off'rings Virtues ſuch as His deſolve: Haſt, haſt, the Noble Pomp, and ſolemn Show, That gives him Altars, Vows, and Worſhip here below.
title: The Consecration of Marcellus an ode in memory of the illustrious prince William, Duke of Gloucester.
