text: No Officers or Servants are permitted upon Pain of Expulsion to take of any Tradesmen, Patients, or other Persons, any Fee, Reward, or Gratification of any kind, directly or indirectly, for any Service done, or to be done, on Account of this Infirmary.
author: London Hospital.
title: An account of the rise, progress, and state of the London Infirmary: supported by charitable and voluntary subscription, for the relief of sick and diseased manufacturers, seamen in merchant service,

text: The House is spacious and convenient, contains about forty Beds, properly and airily disposed, is furnished with Linnen, and all necessary Conveniencies.

title: An account of the rise, progress, and state of the London Infirmary: supported by charitable and voluntary subscription, for the relief of sick and diseased manufacturers, seamen in merchant service,

text: Under her, are Nurses, and Watchers, in proportion to the Number of Patients, of experienced Honesty and Tenderness, who are guided by written Orders to prevent Misconduct of any kind.

text: All poor, sick, and lame, who are recommended, or appear to the Committee to be truly necessitous, are received from the Hours of Eleven to One, who are supply'd with Advice, Medicine, Diet, Washing, Lodging, and every comfortable Assistance during their Cure.
author: London Hospital.
title: An account of the rise, progress, and state of the London Infirmary: supported by charitable and voluntary subscription, for the relief of sick and diseased manufacturers, seamen in merchant service,

text: No Persons with incurable or infectious Distempers, or of known Ability to pay for their Cures, are admitted to partake of this Charity; but all Accidents are received at any Hour of the Day or Night.

text: If such Provision is made for the diseased Inhabitants of Paris, those of London more immediately require our Regard; particularly, the British Manufacturers and Seamen, as they are the chief Support of both our foreign and domestick Trade.

text: But tho' we should escape the disasters which arise from the vicissitudes of war, are there not a thousand ways, in which God may blast in an instant all the mercies, which he has heaped upon us?
author: Gerard, Alexander, 1728-1795.

text: Who has raised up, in these degenerate days, a minister, actuated by the disinterested and incorruptible and steady principles of an old republican?
author: Gerard, Alexander, 1728-1795.
title: National blessings an argument for reformation: A sermon, preached at Aberdeen, November 29, 1759. ... By Alexander Gerard, ...

text: Every one shares in our publick blessings; to every one they should be arguments for repentance and obedience; and they will aggravate the future punishment of every particular person, by whom they are not thus improved.

title: National blessings an argument for reformation: A sermon, preached at Aberdeen, November 29, 1759. ... By Alexander Gerard, ...

text: WE deserve judgments; God showers down his richest blessings on us; they cannot be rewards of our righteousness; for what purpose then are they bestowed, but to be motives to repentance and obedience?

title: National blessings an argument for reformation: A sermon, preached at Aberdeen, November 29, 1759. ... By Alexander Gerard, ...

text: OUR successes in the present war are limited within the compass of a very few years; but they are so many and so great, that they would have rendered a whole long reign illustrious.

title: National blessings an argument for reformation: A sermon, preached at Aberdeen, November 29, 1759. ... By Alexander Gerard, ...

text: IT is now some years since this nation entered into war against a powerful neighbour, in defence of rights and possessions secured to us by sacred and recent treaties, but treacherously invaded and wrested from us.

title: National blessings an argument for reformation: A sermon, preached at Aberdeen, November 29, 1759. ... By Alexander Gerard, ...

text: I will not attempt to lessen your regard or your veneration for those, to whom we owe these illustrious transactions.

text: Were I to descend to a particular detail even of them, I should convert a sermon into an history of one of the most splendid periods of the British glory.

title: National blessings an argument for reformation: A sermon, preached at Aberdeen, November 29, 1759. ... By Alexander Gerard, ...

text: And let us not forget that, while our country has been carrying on war with success so unparalleled, we have never once felt the dangers or losses of war.

text: Who has given us commanders, who exert the valour and activity of health and youth, amidst the discouragements of excruciating pain, or the disheartening infirmities of old age?

text: I. First, I WILL turn your attention to those national successes, which God hath bestowed upon us, and which ought this day to fill our hearts with gratitude to him.

text: Soon, within my arms, Thy strange aversion shall be chang'd to love, And thou shalt wonder at thy own perverseness.
author: Dow, Alexander, d. 1779.
title: Sethona: A tragedy. As it is performed at the Theatre-Royal in Drury-Lane.

text: Let our guards Be chang'd; the traitors seiz'd; the gates secur'd; A chosen squadron of our bravest troops Reserv'd to guard us.
author: Dow, Alexander, d. 1779.
title: Sethona: A tragedy. As it is performed at the Theatre-Royal in Drury-Lane.

text: But if sincere Repentance—If the pangs of keen remorse Could e're attone for guilt, I stand absolv'd And hope for thy forgiveness.—Hope for more, Thy love—For which alone I risqu'd my life, And dar'd perdition!
author: Dow, Alexander, d. 1779.
title: Sethona: A tragedy. As it is performed at the Theatre-Royal in Drury-Lane.

text: I lov'd Sethona! she return'd my love; Now she is mine, by all the holiest vows, And would not violate, her plighted faith, To share thy throne!
author: Dow, Alexander, d. 1779.
title: Sethona: A tragedy. As it is performed at the Theatre-Royal in Drury-Lane.

text: What now remains Of all their glory, but these mould'ring piles, And these imperfect, mutilated forms Of what they were?
author: Dow, Alexander, d. 1779.
title: Sethona: A tragedy. As it is performed at the Theatre-Royal in Drury-Lane.

text: Tow'rd me he mov'd; then claspt me in his arms, And welcom'd me to liberty and life.— I knew him then for Orus.
author: Dow, Alexander, d. 1779.
title: Sethona: A tragedy. As it is performed at the Theatre-Royal in Drury-Lane.

text: He was a friend most worthy of thy tears: Humane, susceptible of the distress Of others, but unshaken by his own.
author: Dow, Alexander, d. 1779.
title: Sethona: A tragedy. As it is performed at the Theatre-Royal in Drury-Lane.

text: Stretch forth thy pale hand, from that airy shroud, And roll that cloud of sorrow from thy brow.
author: Dow, Alexander, d. 1779.
title: Sethona: A tragedy. As it is performed at the Theatre-Royal in Drury-Lane.

text: Thou shalt hear, But let not grief affect thy tender mind, Or throw a damp upon this hour of joy.
author: Dow, Alexander, d. 1779.
title: Sethona: A tragedy. As it is performed at the Theatre-Royal in Drury-Lane.

text: I had cause to fear Thy high displeasure, but thou giv'st me all, Without her there is nothing.— Ha! behold, The tyrant comes.
author: Dow, Alexander, d. 1779.
title: Sethona: A tragedy. As it is performed at the Theatre-Royal in Drury-Lane.

text: I'll join our friends, And lead the battle, 'till these lofty towers, These palaces, these temples of the gods, Shall mark the greatness of my rage with ruin.
author: Dow, Alexander, d. 1779.
title: Sethona: A tragedy. As it is performed at the Theatre-Royal in Drury-Lane.

text: Tho' dead, his image dwells within my soul, And leaves no room for others,—all my joys Were grafted on him.
author: Dow, Alexander, d. 1779.
title: Sethona: A tragedy. As it is performed at the Theatre-Royal in Drury-Lane.

text: When his bright eyes roll'd, I look'd not at the sun; and when he spoke My fingers dropt the lyre.
author: Dow, Alexander, d. 1779.

text: But 'tis objected, That if we do not uſe them here, the Dutch will get the Trade, who loſt it to us by the ſame Error.
author: Cary, John.
title: A reply to a paper delivered to the right honourable the lords spiritual and temporal, entituled, The linnen-drapers answer to that part of Mr. Cary's essay on trade that concerns the East-India trade

text: England is happy in a People who of their own Natures incline to Labour, and though ſome idle Vagrants herd among them, yet the Generality delight to be employed.
author: Cary, John.
title: A reply to a paper delivered to the right honourable the lords spiritual and temporal, entituled, The linnen-drapers answer to that part of Mr. Cary's essay on trade that concerns the East-India trade

text: THE Arguments therein uſed againſt prohibiting the wearing Eaſt-India wrought Silks and Calicoes in England, may be reduced to theſe Heads.
author: Cary, John.
title: A reply to a paper delivered to the right honourable the lords spiritual and temporal, entituled, The linnen-drapers answer to that part of Mr. Cary's essay on trade that concerns the East-India trade

text: That there will be a great abatement in the King's Cuſtoms if Indian Silks and Calicoes be prohibited to be worn in England.
author: Cary, John.
title: A reply to a paper delivered to the right honourable the lords spiritual and temporal, entituled, The linnen-drapers answer to that part of Mr. Cary's essay on trade that concerns the East-India trade

text: That the Dutch did once prohibit the uſe of Calicoes, which gave England advantage to beat them out of that Trade, but that they ſoon found their Errour, and therefore recalled their Placeat, but could never retrieve their Trade.
author: Cary, John.
title: A reply to a paper delivered to the right honourable the lords spiritual and temporal, entituled, The linnen-drapers answer to that part of Mr. Cary's essay on trade that concerns the East-India trade

text: That a Home-Conſumption is no advantage to a Nation, but that a Forreign Conſumption is clear profit; therefore we were better uſe Indian Silks and Calicoes at home, which are cheaper than our own Manufactures, and ſend them abroad to Forreign Markets.
author: Cary, John.
title: A reply to a paper delivered to the right honourable the lords spiritual and temporal, entituled, The linnen-drapers answer to that part of Mr. Cary's essay on trade that concerns the East-India trade

text: The Spaniards would wonder to ſee us come cloathed in Calicoes to ſell them our Woollen Manufactures; I am ſure they could not think we much encouraged their wearing them by our own Examples.
author: Cary, John.
title: A reply to a paper delivered to the right honourable the lords spiritual and temporal, entituled, The linnen-drapers answer to that part of Mr. Cary's essay on trade that concerns the East-India trade

text: That Trade or Commerce being the Riches of this Nation, ought to be free, ſheltered againſt all Prohibitions; That this hath been the Practice of Holland, whoſe Example we ſhould follow in taking off all Reſtraints from Commerce.
author: Cary, John.
title: A reply to a paper delivered to the right honourable the lords spiritual and temporal, entituled, The linnen-drapers answer to that part of Mr. Cary's essay on trade that concerns the East-India trade

text: That this will prejudice our Woollen Manufactures, inaſmuch as it will advance their Prices at home, and thereby leſſen their Sales aborad, becauſe Forreign Markets will be ſupplied cheaper elſewhere.
author: Cary, John.
title: A reply to a paper delivered to the right honourable the lords spiritual and temporal, entituled, The linnen-drapers answer to that part of Mr. Cary's essay on trade that concerns the East-India trade

text: The Force of theſe Arguments, I confeſs, I do not underſtand, or how they ſhould prevail on a Nation, whoſe Wealth ariſes from the Labour of its People, to encourage the Importation of Forreign Manufactures to be worn here, and thereby prevent the uſe of its own.
author: Cary, John.
title: A reply to a paper delivered to the right honourable the lords spiritual and temporal, entituled, The linnen-drapers answer to that part of Mr. Cary's essay on trade that concerns the East-India trade

text: The City of Briſtol hath within Seven years laſt paſt encreaſed their Stuff-making from Sixty pounds per Week to one Thouſand, by the help of the French Refugees ſetled there; which ſhews, that if we can find Sales for our Manufactures, we ſhall want neither Men nor Materials to make them.
author: Cary, John.
title: A reply to a paper delivered to the right honourable the lords spiritual and temporal, entituled, The linnen-drapers answer to that part of Mr. Cary's essay on trade that concerns the East-India trade

text: That the prohibiting theſe Commodities to be worn in England, will either ſettle that noble Trade (as they call it) on the Scotch, or divide it between them and the Dutch.
author: Cary, John.
title: A reply to a paper delivered to the right honourable the lords spiritual and temporal, entituled, The linnen-drapers answer to that part of Mr. Cary's essay on trade that concerns the East-India trade

text: Aye, you villain, you stepp'd aside, and let my dear wife tumble backwards, and knock her fine head against the brass fender—take a double hop out of your two boots, you jackdaw, how dare you stand before me with your horse-whip in your hand?
author: O'Keeffe, John, 1747-1833.

text: Can't find Nan, I would we were both safe again in the country —Well, I've saved this drop of cordial—who's you?

text: Uncle, you promis'd that when proved to be deceived in Antiquities, Belinda should be mine, Now zure besides the fifty pounds, give her to poor Taunton Dean.

text: I forgot to shew you my dress, had it made up for Cordelia, in our intended play at Mr Pathos's; as you were not there, I put it on to consult your taste.
author: O'Keeffe, John, 1747-1833.
title: The farce of the Modern antiques, or the merry mourners. In two acts. As performed at the Theatre-Royal, Smoke-Alley:

text: Sables! what, to celebrate my true-love's birth-day, no, now that my crusty uncle's out of town, and I have cash, I'll have such a roaring entertainment at home—Tol—derol lol.
author: O'Keeffe, John, 1747-1833.
title: The farce of the Modern antiques, or the merry mourners. In two acts. As performed at the Theatre-Royal, Smoke-Alley:

text: Thank you, Sir; though I do think you're an old fool, and that you're most confoundedly humm'd.

title: The farce of the Modern antiques, or the merry mourners. In two acts. As performed at the Theatre-Royal, Smoke-Alley:

text: I'm told you're so griev'd, you have sworn never to touch a drop of punch as long as you live.

text: Oh here's the parson striving to lay my mistress—but shell surely tear his head off—it's my poor dear master—help, murder!

title: The farce of the Modern antiques, or the merry mourners. In two acts. As performed at the Theatre-Royal, Smoke-Alley:

text: Ah, Belinda! confess the truth, wasn't it to see your uncle's nephew, Frank, that you've scamper'd up to town?

text: Thank'ee ma'am; but Miss Toepit's maid told me all of them, except your Ladyship, made a strange piece of bungling work of their play there last Wednesday.
author: O'Keeffe, John, 1747-1833.
title: The farce of the Modern antiques, or the merry mourners. In two acts. As performed at the Theatre-Royal, Smoke-Alley:

text: Old fool! get you out of my house you scoundrel, or I'll— blow you to Taunton Dean you dog, I will.
author: O'Keeffe, John, 1747-1833.
title: The farce of the Modern antiques, or the merry mourners. In two acts. As performed at the Theatre-Royal, Smoke-Alley:

text: Why then my dear Belinda, since your last letter, I've been planning schemes how to make you happy with the man you love.

text: I am heartily ſorry for the poor Quaker, I heard lately of, who hanged himſelf with G. K's Narrative in his Pocket; and the more for the exact parallel muſt make between him and Judas, both in his Life, and in his Death.
author: Bugg, Francis, 1640-1724?

text: No, here is no denial or Matter of Fact but of your Books, nor the natural Conſequences deduceable therefrom, or your practice agreeable to the ſame: And that it may appear ſo, take your Anſwer in your own words, viz. Thus Fran.
author: Bugg, Francis, 1640-1724?

author: Bugg, Francis, 1640-1724?

author: Bugg, Francis, 1640-1724?

author: Bugg, Francis, 1640-1724?

text: But your Temporizing is both ſeen, and diſcovered to be ſeen by others: And now for your Dedication to the Clergy.

text: Hitherto Men have not courted Adepts, nor been civil to them; far from that, they ſeem to have been under Perſecution every where, and in danger of every Body.
title: Annus Sophiæ jubilæus, The sophick constitution, or, The evil customs of the world reform'd a dialogue between a philadept and a citizen concerning the possibility of the sophick transmutation, the pr

text: What more common than to conſume at a Wedding what might ſufficiently maintain a Family moſt part of the Year; and, for ordinary People, to Spend at a Chriſtening more than they freely beſtow upon the Poor in all their Life?
title: Annus Sophiæ jubilæus, The sophick constitution, or, The evil customs of the world reform'd a dialogue between a philadept and a citizen concerning the possibility of the sophick transmutation, the pr

text: I believe ſomething may be done for Peace-ſake, the chief Eſſentials of Religion being retained in general, and the great Duties of Juſtice, Moderation and Charity, being witneſſed unto, and profeſſed.
title: Annus Sophiæ jubilæus, The sophick constitution, or, The evil customs of the world reform'd a dialogue between a philadept and a citizen concerning the possibility of the sophick transmutation, the pr

text: It is not impoſſible that there ſhould be ſuch Men as Adepts; and if there are any, it were extremely to be wiſhed that they might be perſuaded to communicate themſelves, which is here endeavoured, and the way made plain for it.
title: Annus Sophiæ jubilæus, The sophick constitution, or, The evil customs of the world reform'd a dialogue between a philadept and a citizen concerning the possibility of the sophick transmutation, the pr

text: All the Laws therefore that may be made by rich Chriſtians in favour of the poor, he will one day require from them.
title: Annus Sophiæ jubilæus, The sophick constitution, or, The evil customs of the world reform'd a dialogue between a philadept and a citizen concerning the possibility of the sophick transmutation, the pr

text: I thought an Adept would have had nothing to think of, but to make Endowments for Hoſpitals, Schools and Colledges, and the like.
title: Annus Sophiæ jubilæus, The sophick constitution, or, The evil customs of the world reform'd a dialogue between a philadept and a citizen concerning the possibility of the sophick transmutation, the pr

text: But true Men, who really think they have ſome Skill, and who ſincerely fear God, are moſt nice as to this point.
title: Annus Sophiæ jubilæus, The sophick constitution, or, The evil customs of the world reform'd a dialogue between a philadept and a citizen concerning the possibility of the sophick transmutation, the pr

text: All Playing for Mony, by which ſo much Time is loſt, and ſo many Families are ruined, ſhould be forbidden under ſevere Penalties, and the Mony, proved to have been played, ſhould be conſiſcated for the uſe of the Publick.
title: Annus Sophiæ jubilæus, The sophick constitution, or, The evil customs of the world reform'd a dialogue between a philadept and a citizen concerning the possibility of the sophick transmutation, the pr

text: The Prince that ſhould offer a ſhare of his Power to the Adepts, would never repent it, tho' it be probable they would not accept it, farther than to have and enjoy their Liberty without danger, as was ſaid under the firſt Head.
title: Annus Sophiæ jubilæus, The sophick constitution, or, The evil customs of the world reform'd a dialogue between a philadept and a citizen concerning the possibility of the sophick transmutation, the pr

text: Wherefore if Perſons that are able did join to that end ſome part of what they can well ſpare, it is probable that in time ſomething would be found that might be uſeful to the Society, if there be any thing in Chymiſtry.
title: Annus Sophiæ jubilæus, The sophick constitution, or, The evil customs of the world reform'd a dialogue between a philadept and a citizen concerning the possibility of the sophick transmutation, the pr

text: For it cannot but be the deſire of every well minded Man, to rectifie to the beſt of his power that which appears to him to be amiſs.

text: And I am happy to add, that, as well from the assurances I have received, as from the general appearances of affairs in Europe, I see no probability that the measures which you may adopt will be interrupted by disputes with any foreign power.

title: His Majesty's most gracious speech to both Houses of Parliament, on Thursday the 26th of October, 1775:

text: THE present situation of America, and my constant desire to have your advice, concurrence, and assistance on every important occasion, have determined me to call you thus early together.

text: On our part, though it was declared in your last session that the rebellion existed within the province of the Massachuset's Bay, yet even that province we wished rather to reclaim than to subdue.

title: His Majesty's most gracious speech to both Houses of Parliament, on Thursday the 26th of October, 1775:

text: I have also the satisfaction to inform you, that I have received the most friendly offers of foreign assistance; and if I shall make any treaties in consequence thereof, they shall be laid before you.

title: A poetical epistle from the late Lord Melcombe to the Earl of Bute: with corrections, by the author of the Night thoughts:

text: This Wisdom's laws, that first taught Virtue, teach, And place Esteem and Love in all Men's reach.

title: A poetical epistle from the late Lord Melcombe to the Earl of Bute: with corrections, by the author of the Night thoughts:

text: Whence then, and why, the Venal and the Vile, The Voice of Honour, and the Heart of Guile, Harden'd to crimes, and resolute to rise On Love and Friendship's violated ties?

title: A poetical epistle from the late Lord Melcombe to the Earl of Bute: with corrections, by the author of the Night thoughts:

text: Friendship well chose, of ev'ry blessing chief, Doubles our Pleasures, and divides our Grief: But view their Friendships, can we call them Choice?
author: Dodington, George Bubb, Baron of Melcombe Regis, 1691-1762.
title: A poetical epistle from the late Lord Melcombe to the Earl of Bute: with corrections, by the author of the Night thoughts:

text: CUNNING's the tim'rous Guide to sordid Ends: Compos'd of parts which Wisdom calls Defects, She apes her with the talents she rejects: Hence one proceeds with Firmness, one with Fear; There manly Caution, low Suspicion here.
author: Dodington, George Bubb, Baron of Melcombe Regis, 1691-1762.
title: A poetical epistle from the late Lord Melcombe to the Earl of Bute: with corrections, by the author of the Night thoughts:

text: Quick to discern, and wisely to pursue, And tread Life's labyrinth with Judgment's clue, Are parts that few, indulg'd by Heav'n, can fill; But all Men may be honest—if they will.
author: Dodington, George Bubb, Baron of Melcombe Regis, 1691-1762.
title: A poetical epistle from the late Lord Melcombe to the Earl of Bute: with corrections, by the author of the Night thoughts:

text: The crowds that Vice and Vanity pour forth, Whose claims are founded on their Wants, not Worth, Ill brook the manly manners of the Wise, Who scorn to flatter what they must despise.
author: Dodington, George Bubb, Baron of Melcombe Regis, 1691-1762.
title: A poetical epistle from the late Lord Melcombe to the Earl of Bute: with corrections, by the author of the Night thoughts:

text: Should Truth usurp suspicious Falshood's seat, And Honesty grow graceful in the Great; Should Wit presume to speak, and Learning write, And Pow'r and Lib'ral Arts at length unite; Pronounce that Land the fav'rite Land of Fate, Pronounce the Prince that rules it truly great.
author: Dodington, George Bubb, Baron of Melcombe Regis, 1691-1762.
title: A poetical epistle from the late Lord Melcombe to the Earl of Bute: with corrections, by the author of the Night thoughts:

text: POLLIO, to Thee, my Patron and my Friend, The secret counsels of my soul I send: Long since thy godlike Uncle held me dear (Fate gave me early to thy House's care); He dy'd, and left me unattach'd and free, Left me a legacy from Him to Thee.
author: Dodington, George Bubb, Baron of Melcombe Regis, 1691-1762.
title: A poetical epistle from the late Lord Melcombe to the Earl of Bute: with corrections, by the author of the Night thoughts:

text: And now let Envy all his actions scan, Then let her call me Flatt'rer, if she can: The vain reproach I shall with scorn receive; I wanted no distinction He could give, Save one, to all superior and supreme, His Friendship, his Affection, his Esteem.
author: Dodington, George Bubb, Baron of Melcombe Regis, 1691-1762.
title: A poetical epistle from the late Lord Melcombe to the Earl of Bute: with corrections, by the author of the Night thoughts:

text: Thus Prudence, Virtue, Parts, crowd Wisdom's train; Thus Cunning sweeps the Squand'rer, False, and Vain: Just to the Tiller's care, the crop succeeds, One binds the sheaf, and one collects the weeds.

title: A poetical epistle from the late Lord Melcombe to the Earl of Bute: with corrections, by the author of the Night thoughts:

text: And till they are proved beyond all Contradiction, the Doctrine built upon them, ought to be rejected with Detestation.

text: And, surely that Precept which enjoyns Obedience to Civil Laws, cannot it self with any Propriety be accounted a Civil Law; it must therefore either have no Obligation at all on the Conscience, or if it hath, it must be derived from the universal Voice of Nature and Reason.
author: Berkeley, George, 1685-1753.
title: Passive obedience: or, the Christian doctrine of not resisting the supreme power, proved and vindicated ... In a discourse deliver'd at the College-chapel. By George Berkeley, M.A. Fellow of Trinity-C

text: Secondly, This same Point may be collected from the Example set us by the Author of Nature, who, as we have above observed, acts according to certain fixed Laws, which he will not transgress upon the Account of Accidental Evils arising from them.
author: Berkeley, George, 1685-1753.
title: Passive obedience: or, the Christian doctrine of not resisting the supreme power, proved and vindicated ... In a discourse deliver'd at the College-chapel. By George Berkeley, M.A. Fellow of Trinity-C

text: Which must inevitably be granted, unless one of these three Things can be prov'd: Either, First, that Non-Resistance is no Moral Duty.

title: Passive obedience: or, the Christian doctrine of not resisting the supreme power, proved and vindicated ... In a discourse deliver'd at the College-chapel. By George Berkeley, M.A. Fellow of Trinity-C

text: Namely, That Loyalty is a Virtue or Moral Duty; and Disloyalty or Rebellion, in the most strict and proper Sense, a Vice or Crime against the Law of Nature.

text: And therefore, the least degree of Rebellion is with the utmost strictness and propriety, a Sin: Not only in Christians, but also in those who haxe the Light of Reason alone for their Guide.

title: The pleasures of melancholy. A poem:

text: And hark, methinks resounding from the gloom The voice of Melancholy strikes mine ear; "Come, leave the busy trifles of vain life, "And let these twilight mansions teach thy mind "The Joys of Musing, and of solemn Thought."
author: Warton, Thomas, 1728-1790.
title: The pleasures of melancholy. A poem:

text: Nor let me fail to cultivate my mind With the soft thrillings of the tragic Muse, Divine Melpomene, sweet Pity's nurse, Queen of the stately step, and flowing pall.
author: Warton, Thomas, 1728-1790.
title: The pleasures of melancholy. A poem:

text: But when the world Is clad in Midnight's raven-colour'd robe, In hollow charnel let me watch the flame Of taper dim, while airy voices talk Along the glimm'ring walls, or ghostly shape At distance seen, invites with beck'ning hand My lonesome steps, thro' the far-winding vaults.
author: Warton, Thomas, 1728-1790.
title: The pleasures of melancholy. A poem:

text: O tell how rapt'rous is the deep-felt bliss To melt to Melody's assuasive voice, Careless to stray the midnight mead along, And pour your sorrows to the pitying moon, Oft interrupted by the Bird of Woe!
author: Warton, Thomas, 1728-1790.
title: The pleasures of melancholy. A poem:

text: Or let me sit Far in some distant isle of the deep dome, There lonesome listen to the solemn sounds, Which, as they lengthen thro' the Gothic vaults, In hollow murmurs reach my ravish'd ear.
author: Warton, Thomas, 1728-1790.
title: The pleasures of melancholy. A poem:

text: But never let Euphrosyne beguile With toys of wanton mirth my fixed mind, Nor with her primrose garlands strew my paths.
author: Warton, Thomas, 1728-1790.
title: The pleasures of melancholy. A poem:

text: O wrap me then in shades of darksom pine, Bear me to caves by desolation brown, To dusky vales, and hermit-haunted rocks!
author: Warton, Thomas, 1728-1790.
title: The pleasures of melancholy. A poem:

text: O then how fearful is it to reflect, That thro' the solitude of the still globe No Being wakes but me! 'till stealing sleep My drooping temples baths in opiate dews.
author: Warton, Thomas, 1728-1790.
title: The pleasures of melancholy. A poem:

text: Ye youths of Albion's beauty-blooming isle, Whose brows have worn the wreath of luckless love, Is there a pleasure like the pensive mood, Whose magic wont to sooth your soften'd souls?
author: Warton, Thomas, 1728-1790.
title: The pleasures of melancholy. A poem:

text: The taper'd choir, at midnight hour of Pray'r, Oft let me tread, while to th' according voice The many-sounding organ peals on high, In full-voic'd chorus thro' th' embowed roof; 'Till all my soul is bath'd in ecstasies, And lap'd in Paradise.
author: Warton, Thomas, 1728-1790.
title: The pleasures of melancholy. A poem:

text: Illustrious objects strike the gazer's mind With feeble bliss, and but allure the sight, Nor rouze with impulse quick the feeling heart.

text: THus lurking as alone I lay, where there was no Repair, A Maid before me on the way, I heard a Greeting fair: Her Moan was loud, it mov'd the Air, to hear her ſtill I ſtood, She was lamenting evermair, for fault of Tocher good.
title: The sorrowful maiden for the want of Tocher-good. To an excellent old tune.

title: The sorrowful maiden for the want of Tocher-good. To an excellent old tune.

text: An old Maiden if that I be, no Man will of me make; Then great dolor will gar me die, fra time they me forſake; Alas! my Sorrow cannot ſlaik, which gars my Pleaſure fade, Alas! that I ſhould want my Maik, for want of Tocher-good.
title: The sorrowful maiden for the want of Tocher-good. To an excellent old tune.

text: Becauſe that I do ly alone, and Company's ſo good; I am in point, alas! to tine, for want of Tocher good.

text: This gars my Heart be like to burſt, and break in Pieces three, When Young men do their Cheeks oft clap, and will not look on me.
